News.title: 'I'm a doctor and 5 things you do every day could be increasing your blood pressure'
News.content:
'I'm a doctor and 5 things you do every day could be increasing your blood pressure'

According to the British Heart Foundation, high blood pressure can stretch your arteries, making them become stiff or narrow. This makes it easier for fatty material to build up

View Image Being aware of your blood pressure is key to keeping track of your health (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

A TV doctor has revealed how five things many people do every single day could be increasing their risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other serious health problems.

‌



Dr Amir Khan is a well-known face on ITV's Lorraine and Good Morning Britain, where he regularly dispenses invaluable health guidance. He has explained how five everyday habits could be sending your blood pressure soaring without you even realising it, reports the Express.

‌



In a TikTok video he said: "Your blood pressure is so important to your health, here are five surprising things that may raise it and why they matter for your heart."

‌



Stress

First on Dr Khan's list is hardly a shock. He said: "When you're stressed, your body releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol. They make your heart beat faster and your blood vessels narrow. That's your fight-or-flight mode. Fine for a few minutes, but if you're stressed all the time, your blood pressure stays high."

Too much caffeine

Dr Khan explained that, while a coffee or energy drink can give you a welcome pick-me-up, the caffeine will simultaneously cause your blood pressure to spike. "Caffeine blocks a chemical that helps your blood vessels relax, so they stay a bit tighter," he said. "If you're sensitive, even one strong cup can push your numbers up temporarily."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Not getting a good night's sleep

"Poor sleep means your body doesn't get its nightly reset," Dr Khan explained. "Your stress hormones stay higher during the day, and your blood pressure doesn't drop at night like it should. Over time, that can lead to chronic high blood pressure."

Over-the-counter medications

Dr Khan cautioned that certain over-the-counter medications, while potentially useful for tackling short-term health issues, can have damaging effects on blood pressure. He explained that decongestants available without prescription work by constricting blood vessels in the nose to relieve congestion — but also tighten blood vessels throughout the rest of the body. "Always check the label if you have high blood pressure, he said. " he advised. "And to be honest, there isn't much evidence they work."

Sitting down

"I go on about this all the time," he said. "When you sit for hours without moving, blood flow slows down and your blood vessels can stiffen. Even short breaks - a quick walk, stretching - help your vessels stay flexible and keep your blood pressure in check."

‌



Wrapping up, he said: "So if your blood pressure is creeping up, think about these five everyday habits too. A few small changes could make a big difference to your heart health."

What health problems can be caused by high blood pressure?

According to the British Heart Foundation (BHF), high blood pressure can stretch your arteries, making them become stiff or narrow. This makes it easier for fatty material to build up. It can lead to conditions such as

Heart attacks

Stroke

Kidney failure

Heart failure

Vascular dementia

‌



A number of factors can increase risk of high blood pressure, including:

Age

A family history of high blood pressure

Smoking

Drinking too much alcohol

Eating too much salt and not enough fruit and vegetables

Not getting enough exercise

Being overweight, especially around your mid-section

Ethnicity - people who are of Black African or Black Caribbean descent are at a higher risk of having high blood pressure

The following conditions can also directly cause high pressure, also called secondary hypertension. These can include:

‌



Kidney disease

Diabetes

Sleep apnoea

Some medicines such as oral contraceptives

Some over the counter and herbal medications

As many as five million adults in the UK have undiagnosed high blood pressure, according to the BHF. You can get your blood pressure checked at your GP or at some pharmacies. At-home blood pressure machines are also available to buy.

The BHF says: "If you’re a healthy adult aged 40 to 74, it’s a good idea to get your blood pressure checked every five years. You may be invited for an NHS Health Check in England once you turn 40. There may be other services available in Scotland and Wales. Ask your GP about how you can get your blood pressure checked.

Article continues below

"If you have been diagnosed with high blood pressure and it's under control, you’ll normally be monitored yearly, along with reviewing any medicines you take. When you start new medicines or have dose changes to existing ones, your blood pressure will need to be checked more than once a year.

"Check with your healthcare team how often to measure your blood pressure at home if you have your own monitor. Try keeping a diary of your readings. This will help your healthcare team spot patterns, and it might be motivating to see how your blood pressure improves over time."

News.title: 'UK missile vow risks being token gesture in face of Ukraine's bigger problems'
News.content:
'UK missile vow risks being token gesture in face of Ukraine's bigger problems'

Matthew Savill, RUSI's Director of Military Sciences, writes for The Mirror after Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed to share secret missile technology with Kyiv

View 2 Images 'Providing UK technology to allow the production of new cruise missiles inside Ukraine is giving a vote of confidence in Ukraine’s medium-term future' (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Providing UK technology to allow the production of new cruise missiles inside Ukraine is giving a vote of confidence in Ukraine’s medium-term future as well as probably supporting the development of their own missiles.

‌



But it is not a substitute for continuing ongoing support, as Ukraine faces another hard winter of heavy Russian aerial bombardment even as Ukrainian forces on the ground have blunted Russian advances, and begun to launch counter-attacks of their own.

‌



It will take time to construct and establish a new factory inside Ukraine – under wartime conditions – as well as to start producing new missiles. It is very unlikely any will be produced in the next year at the earliest.

Article continues below

Andy Burnham hits back after Russia accuses UK of 'participating' in war over missile blueprints READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as he visits Kyiv on his first foreign trip as PM (Image: SERGEY DOLZHENKO/EPA/Shutterstock)

More immediately helpful might be understanding some of the sophisticated features that make Storm Shadow so precise and adapting them for Ukraine’s own growing cruise missile production, used alongside their huge drone programme. International support is needed urgently to deal with Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s industry, infrastructure and civilian targets. The Russians use a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles and drones that are subject to ongoing upgrades: many are now jet-propelled and are better thought of as budget cruise missiles. There is still a need for air defences, especially interceptors from the US, which can defeat ballistic missiles – and France has promised to support production of missiles similar to those used by the Royal Navy for defence. But Ukraine will lose a game of industrial production that pits output of sophisticated interceptors against Russian missile production. So it needs to strike more Russian weapons before they are launched, and attack the military industrial facilities that produce them. That means more rapid production like the UK’s Project BRAKESTOP cruise missiles, intelligence support for Ukraine, and financial and technical support to its communications and weapons development so they can identify and attack these targets deep inside Russia. Without this additional support, the decision on SCALP licensing will remain a gesture that is appreciated, but one that is only a token gesture in the context of the much bigger problems that Ukraine faces.

News.title: First Brit 'dies' fighting for Russia in Ukraine after he's 'killed in drone strike'
News.content:
First Brit 'dies' fighting for Russia in Ukraine after he's 'killed in drone strike'

Bradley Townsend, 33, a fisherman from Barnsley in South Yorkshire left the UK in April to fight alongside Putin’s armed forces before being killed in a drone attack in the Donetsk region of Ukraine

View 2 Images Bradley Townsend featured in a video for the Russian International Volunteers Association saying he was a 'normal working-class lad from Yorkshire' (Image: Facebook)

The first Brit to die while fighting for Russia against Ukraine has been killed in a drone strike, according to reports.

‌



Bradley Townsend, 33, was killed by a drone near the city of Lyman in the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine.

‌



Mr Townsend, from Barnsley in South Yorkshire, had left the UK in April to fight alongside Putin’s armed forces - he was killed in the drone attack in June, the Telegraph has today reported.

‌



The Government has said it is “aware of reports” that a UK national had died in Ukraine and “in contact with his family”.

Bradley Townsend featured in a video on April 4, 2026, for the Russian International Volunteers Association, where he describes himself as a “normal working-class lad from Yorkshire” who chose to join Russia ’s fight against Ukraine.

However, reports have since suggested that Bradley died in June this year while fighting in the ongoing war. A fellow Briton fighting in Putin’s forces, Aiden Minnis, said he had “sacrificed his life for our cause”.

‌



View 2 Images Bradley Townsend, left (Image: YouTube/International Volunteers Association)

In a previous post on social media Mr Townsend said: “I came with the idea that I probably wouldn’t be able to go home. I’d definitely get persecuted if I went back. I’m not here for a suicide mission, but I understand that’s what can happen. This was my own decision, I wasn’t pushed into anything.”

The Yorkshire fisherman, who had no military training, said in another post that he was in the Donbas to “repay the favour” after miners from the region gave up a month’s wages to Yorkshire miners during the 1980s strikes.

‌



In a tribute posted on social media, Mr Minnis said: “Bradley Spencer Townsend, call sign ‘Badger’, our beloved comrade-in-arms went into the storm and fell on the battlefield near Liman [sic].

“He made the journey from Great Britain to Russia, he chose to walk in his grandfather’s footsteps and answered the call to fight fascism. I had the pleasure of spending some time with Bradley before he decided to sign his contract.

“We discussed the danger he would be facing, but he insisted that his mind was made up and he wanted to help the people of Russia defeat the Nazis. Ultimately, he sacrificed his life for our cause. His service was brief but he blazed the brightest star. Rest in Paradise brother. ‘To die a warrior in a Holy War is to live forever’.”

Article continues below

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office told the Mirror : “We are aware of reports that a British national has died in Ukraine and are in contact with his family.

“The FCDO advises against all travel to Russia, and our ability to provide consular support in these circumstances is severely limited.”

They asked that the privacy of Bradley Townsend’s family be respected at this time.

News.title: Calls for windfill tax grow as banks 'cash in on obscene profits while we face mortgage misery'
News.content:
Calls for windfill tax grow as banks 'cash in on obscene profits while we face mortgage misery'

EXCLUSIVE: A poll by trade union body the TUC has found overwhelming public support for Chancellor John Healey to tax banks more - including among Tory and Reform voters

View 3 Images Speculation is mounting that Chancellor John Healey could target banks in his October Budget (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The public back a windfall tax on banks’ "obscene" profits by a margin of more than three to one, exclusive polling has shown.

‌



The survey from the Trade Union Congress (TUC) found overwhelming support from across the political spectrum, including among Tory and Reform voters.

‌



The result was revealed on the eve of energy regular Ofgem announcing a price hike for tens of millions of households from October 1. Experts are forecasting that Ofgem will confirm on Wednesday that its price cap will rise another 4%, to £1,729 a year under its new measure of average household use, and £1,941 under its previous guide.

‌



The TUC wants the government to use the money raised from a bank windfall tax to pay for a social tariff that could bring down energy bills by up to £559 a year for those on low and middle incomes., it claims. The trade union body has called on PM Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey to act after Britain’s ‘big four’ banks - HSBC, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group, and NatWest - made more than £29billion profit in six months. Earnings have been partly fuelled by the Middle East war, which has driven up energy and other household bills and kept interest rates elevated for longer.

UK households threatened with more price hikes from looming 'Godzilla' El Niño READ MORE :

View 3 Images Profits at HSBC surged by almost a quarter to £14.5billion in the first half of 2026 (Image: Lucy North/PA)

TUC's proposals

The TUC argues upping the surcharge on banks’ profits to at least 8%, on top of the 25% corporation tax they pay, could raise £9billion over four years. Raising it even higher could bring in as much as £60billion over four years, it claims.

‌



It says the money raised could then be used to fund a permanent energy social tariff to cut energy bills for 18.7 million households. Under its proposals, the scheme would cost between £3.4billion and £5.9billion per year, depending on variations in the wholesale cost of energy and how long the current energy crisis lasts.

Setting out its idea, the TUC says there should be a standard social tariff used as a baseline for bill support which, as it stands, could slash bills by an average 25% - or £466 a year - for low income households, and up to £279 a year for those below average incomes. However, it has also suggests an "emergency ratchet" when - like now - energy bills are especially high.

View 3 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey are weighing up ways to boost the Treasury's coffers to fund Labour's spending plans

‌



Banks' profits described as 'obscene'

General Secretary Paul Nowak told the Mirror: “Big banks are cashing in on obscene profits while the rest of us have to put up with mortgage misery and bigger bills. It’s plain wrong – and the public knows it. It’s little wonder that voters from right across the political spectrum want banks to pay their fair share.

“Andy Burnham has been straight out of the blocks with action to ease the cost of living. But with no clear end in sight to Trump’s illegal war in Iran, energy prices are set to go up even further – and we’re going to have to see more from the government to protect living standards. That’s why the prime minister should do the common sense thing and tax bank profits to cut energy bills. This is the kind of decisive action which would show working people the prime minister is on their side.”

The TUC polling, conducted by Hold Sway, found 65% of those asked support a windfall tax on the profits of banks and other financial institutions that have made extra profits. That compared to just 18% who were opposed, with the remainder undecided.

‌



The move is backed by 73% of Labour voters, and 71% of Lib Dems, but also 69% of Tory and 64% of Reform voters. The level of support among Green Party voters was also 64% as the party formally proposed a 38% windfall tax on the domestic profits of the big banks.

According to the TUC, the ‘big four’ have been making profits of £6.7million an hour, or £1,850 a second.

There is speculation that Mr Healey will launch a tax raid on banks to fund Mr Burnham’s public spending plans.

‌



However, the financial sector has ramped-up warnings of the impact of any such move.

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of Wall Street giant JP Morgan, recently warned the Chancellor against taxing banks more, claiming it could push lenders overseas.

Lobby group UK Finance said the sector paid £43billion in taxes last year and warned hikes would “reduce UK competitiveness”.

Article continues below

How a windfall tax could work

Banks currently pay the standard 25% corporation tax on profits. But they also have a 3% surcharge levied on top.

The TUC is calling for this 3% to be upped to at least 8%, to the level it was before being cut by the Tories in April 2023, in a move the trade union body claims would collect £9billion over four years.

However, it also suggests going further. A 16% surcharge would raise £24billion over four years, it says, while a 35% surcharge, which would be the same level as the windfall tax the Conservatives imposed on energy companies, would bring in an estimated £60billion over four years.

News.title: 'Andy Slaughter helped free me when I was held hostage in Gaza - he deserves credit and not criticism'
News.content:
'Andy Slaughter helped free me when I was held hostage in Gaza - he deserves credit and not criticism'

Labour’s Andy Slaughter has faced Tory criticism over meetings with Hamas officials during visits to Gaza and the Palestinian territories - but former BBC journalist Paul Martin has defended the politician

View 4 Images

A top British documentary maker who was held hostage in Gaza for 26 days has defended the new Solicitor General after he was attacked for his links to Hamas.

‌



Labour’s Andy Slaughter has been criticised by the Tories for meeting Hamas officials in 2010. But former BBC journalist Paul Martin praised Mr Slaughter for his visit to Gaza in what Mr Martin called “very difficult circumstances”.

‌



Mr Martin had been held captive by Hamas and was threatened with mock executions. But three days after Mr Slaughter’s visit to Gaza City - against the advice of the Foreign Office - Mr Martin was dramatically freed. He was making a documentary.

‌



The Tories have attacked Mr Slaughter’s recent appointment, with Shadow Justice secretary Nick Timothy saying it was a disgrace.

Hamas hostage celebrates wedding as he finally marries his fiancee after spending 505 days in captivity READ MORE :

View 4 Images Documentary maker Paul Martin

But Mr Martin said: “When Andy Slaughter came to the Gaza Strip as part of a four-man delegation led by another MP David Steel, he was, in my opinion perfectly entitled to talk to senior figures from Hamas. “It is short-sighted to say that no British politician should in those days have met with people who were controlling that territory, even though in fact Hamas had violently taken over the territory from the security control of the Palestinian Authority.

‌



View 4 Images Mr Slaughter is our new Solicitor General (Image: Daily Mirror)

“Talking to those in control of a territory that has relevance to British foreign policy was, in my view, a legitimate thing to do, provided it did not provide any encouragement of further violence.

‌



“In any case, the presence of Andy Slaughter and David Steel was of direct benefit to me. I was being held captive by the Internal Security branch of Hamas, who locked me up because of a film I was making there.

“It was a pro-Palestinian film but one that showed the repression by Hamas of its own citizens, and was later shown eight times on BBC World News.”

‌



View 4 Images Palestinian students take part in a rally organised by the Between the Dream and the Crossing group (Image: Mohammed Salha/APAImages/Shutterstock)

Mr Martin, from north London is a freelance who has worked for the Mirror and the BBC added: “After 21 days in solitary confinement and after two mock executions, I was delighted when a top Hamas official came to see me and told me that Andy Slaughter and David Steel had met Hamas officials and in the course of their discussions had asked for my release.

‌



“Four days later I was set free - though I can only speculate whether Andy and David's intervention triggered my release. In any case, they deserve credit for their trip to Gaza in 2010, not condemnation."

Mr Slaughter was there with a delegation put together by the Council for Arab-British Understanding and by the All-Party Parliamentary Group for Palestine.

Article continues below

Mr Martin was 55 at the time of being held and is still working as a journalist, based in London.

News.title: Ex-snooker champion Graeme Dott found guilty of sexually abusing children
News.content:
Ex-snooker champion Graeme Dott found guilty of sexually abusing children

Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abuse, the High Court in Glasgow heard

View 3 Images Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott pictured outside the High Court in Glasgow (Image: Jane Barlow/PA Wire)

Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of sexually abusing two primary school age children.

‌



The 49-year-old subjected a girl and a boy to multiple incidents of abuse, with the girl targeted between 1993-1996 and the boy between 2006-2010.

‌



A five-day trial the High Court in Glasgow heard Dott exposed himself in front of both children, touched them inappropriately, and kissed them.

‌



On Monday, he was found guilty of two counts of lewd, indecent and libidinous behaviour towards them.

In both cases the abuse happened in the Glasgow area.

During the trial, jurors heard from one of Dott’s victims, a woman now in her 40s, who told the court Dott had sexually abused her on multiple separate occasions while she was a child.

‌



She said the abuse had started with Dott “caressing” her bottom over her clothing while giving her a piggy back.

View 3 Images Ronnie O'Sullivan and Graeme Dott pose with the trophy ahead of the Embassy World Snooker Final at The Crucible in 2004 (Image: Getty Images)

The woman also described an occasion when she said Dott suggested playing a “guessing game” where she had to guess what he was doing.

‌



She told the court she lay down and he exposed himself to her and then began touching her with different parts of his body, including his penis.

The woman told the court that Dott told her not to tell anyone he was sexually abusing her.

The second victim, a man who is now in his late 20s, said he was sexually abused by Dott on multiple occasions, with the snooker player touching him inappropriately, kissing him, and performing sexual acts.

‌



He told the court a lot of the abuse took place while he was in a shower, when Dott would come in either partly or completely undressed.

View 3 Images Graeme Dott was found guilty today (Image: Jane Barlow/PA Wire)

“He would… come into the shower and put soap on my body and wash me in the shower,” the man told the court.

‌



“While he was washing me he would touch me in inappropriate places.”

He said looking back at it now, Dott was “clearly getting sexual gratification from it”, and he was “pleasuring himself” while this was taking place.

The man said that because of his age at the time, he “did not know what was going on”, and it was only later he realised the interaction “wasn’t right”.

‌



The witness also described abuse which took place in a car, where he said Dott would kiss him on the face, head and lips, and “push himself up against me”.

Giving evidence last week, Dott had said there was “absolutely no way” he sexually abused two children.

Under cross-examination by prosecutor Lindsey Dalziel, Dott denied being attracted to the girl when she was young, calling the idea “disgusting”.

‌



When Ms Dalziel put it to Dott that he touched the first victim and told her what to do, he denied the allegation and called it “lies”.

Speaking about the second victim, Dott said he was “never in my company” and denied all allegations of abuse.

In her closing speech on Friday, Ms Dalziel called on the jury to find Dott guilty of both charges.

‌



She said: “The Crown’s case is that Graeme Dott subjected vulnerable children to the worst kind of abuse with a course of conduct which relied on opportunity, for his own gratification.”

Dott’s lawyer, Euan Dow, had invited jurors to clear his client of both charges.

But Dott was found guilty on Monday following the trial which began on Tuesday August 18.

News.title: Nigel Farage's Clacton by-election victory rally 'Farage Fest' investigated
News.content:
Nigel Farage's Clacton by-election victory rally 'Farage Fest' investigated

The organisers of Nigel Farage's Clacton by-election victory rally - dubbed "Farage Fest" - are being investigated for failing to get permission to hold it in time

View 2 Images Nigel Farage did not show up at the count of the Clacton by-election - and instead appeared at a 'Farage Fest' event (Image: AP Photo/Richard Pelham)

The organisers of Nigel Farage's Clacton by-election victory rally - dubbed "Farage Fest" - are being investigated for failing to get permission to hold it.

‌



The Reform UK leader faced criticism after he failed to show up for the result of the £250,000 contest he triggered earlier this month.

‌



Instead he appeared in the early hours of the morning in the Essex countryside several miles from the count at a "Farage fest", which boasted alcohol, ferris wheel, DJs and several fire pits. GB News was the only media outlet present.

‌



Mr Farage called the event "Clactonbury" when he spoke to cheering fans from the stage. Fans had to pay to enter the event, but could camp and park for free.

Tendring District Council confirmed it had refused to grant a Late Temporary Event Notice (LTEN) as the application had not been made within the legal timescale required.

View 2 Images Nigel Farage's main by-election rival was parody candidate Count Binface (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Mr Farage was re-elected as Clacton's MP - after resigning from the role at the start of July - during the by-election earlier this month. All the other major political parties boycotted the race, branding it a "gimmick" and a "stunt" to try to distract from questions about a £5million gift Mr Farage received shortly before the 2024 general election. Mr Farage's main rival was parody candidate Count Binface.

A Commons probe into the £5m gift Mr Farage received was suspended when he resigned as an MP. It was restarted when he was re-elected.

Lisa Hastings, Corporate Director for Law and Governance at Tendring District Council, said: "We can confirm that a Late Temporary Event Notice (Late TEN) was submitted in relation to an event on Thursday, 13 August, at Great Oakley Airfield.

‌



"This notice was refused, and a counter-notice served, as it was not submitted within the statutory timescales required under the Licensing Act 2003. No authorisation was therefore granted under a Late Temporary Event Notice for the event.

"As the matter may now involve potential enforcement considerations, Tendring District Council is unable to comment further on any ongoing or potential investigations by Licensing or other council departments; nor provide any further details about the Late TEN submission."

Reform UK spokesman: “Reform UK are confident that no rules were broken and the event was conducted in accordance with the law.”

‌



Earlier today, Richard Tice denied that Mr Farage is "hiding" despite him failing to make a public appearance since the Clacton by-election. Reform UK's deputy leader said his boss is on "good form" and will be "plenty" out at the party's annual conference in Birmingham next week.

Asked if he was in hiding, Mr Tice told a London press conference on social housing: "Nigel, I think, is 62. I'm not sure he's ever been in hiding. He's always on good form, and you'll see plenty of him if you come to party conference. But I do just repeat the point we are a broad team with a range of expertise, as you're hearing about today. And Nigel specifically gave us these tasks. Myself, spokesman for business, trade, energy, including housing, so that we get stuck into some detail."

Asked if Mr Farage had been interviewed by the Standards Commissioner, Mr Tice added: "With regard to timing on that, that's between Nigel and the Commissioners. There are, of course, quite strict rules around we can say what about when with the Commissioner."

Article continues below

A Labour source said: “Nigel Farage called a circus by-election to dodge questions on his secret £5million ‘gift’ from a crypto-billionaire. But the public is still waiting for answers. When Farage comes out of hiding, he should finally come clean. If he has nothing to hide, why has he gone to ground?”

News.title: Doxcycline 30-minute rule to follow if you're taking the antibiotic
News.content:
Doxcycline 30-minute rule to follow if you're taking the antibiotic

Doxycycline is a commonly-prescribed antibiotic

View Image Doxycycline is prescribed for a number of infections and conditions (Image: Peter Meade via Getty Images)

Doxycycline is a widely-prescribed antibiotic used to treat or prevent certain infections and is only available with a doctor's prescription.

‌



The medication is frequently given to those suffering from sexually transmitted infections (STIs), chest infections, gum infections, and urinary tract infections (UTIs). It can also be prescribed for acne or other skin conditions, or to prevent malaria when travelling to parts of the world where the disease is prevalent. The antibiotic typically comes in tablets or capsules to be swallowed, though there is also a dissolvable tablet that can be mixed with water to drink.

‌



The dosage and duration of treatment depends on the condition being treated. Most patients are required to take it once or twice daily for a period of days or weeks.

‌



Those taking doxycycline should be aware of an important 30-minute rule to avoid potential digestive discomfort or damage. NHS guidance states that doxycycline should be taken at the same time each day, swallowed with a full glass of water while sitting or standing upright, and that patients should not lie down for at least 30 minutes after taking it to prevent irritation.

It is crucial to complete the full course of medication, even if symptoms begin to improve beforehand. Should you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless your next scheduled dose is imminent.

Article continues below

If your next dose is nearly due, simply skip the missed one and resume your regular schedule. Never double up on doses to compensate for one you've missed.

Should you discover you've taken too much doxycycline, contact NHS 111 immediately. "If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance. Bring the doxycycline packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take."

Frequently reported side effects of doxycycline include headaches, nausea, vomiting, and a rash. These are not all of the possible side effects, however, and you should carefully read the leaflet supplied with your medication.

News.title: Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from Russia
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats", on his first official visit to Ukraine as UK prime minister.

Burnham met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

He said the coalition was "doing everything we can" while urging the US Congress to "ratchet up" economic pressure on Russia.

The government is set to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

During the meeting with France and Ukraine, Burnham said allies were doing "everything we can" to "dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks" of air defences to protect Ukraine.

"This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," Burnham said, praising the "strength" of the Ukrainian people.

"Ukraine has been Europe's protector, not a drain on our security but the front line in keeping Europe safe."

It comes after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.

He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them.

"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.

In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it."

He added the issue of missile interceptors would be the main topic at the coalition of the willing meeting.

News.title: UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most
News.content:
Instead, under Project Brakestop, it is developing its own long-range cruise missiles, free of foreign components, and less than half the price of a Storm Shadow.

Project Brakestop is also being done at break-neck speed. The UK hopes to have a new cruise missile ready by the end of the year. It is promising to supply the new weapon to Ukraine.

It is Ukraine which has shown the world how to produce relatively cheap, mass produced weapons, necessary for a long, protracted conflict.

Douglas Barrie, Senior Fellow for Military Aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) told the BBC: "The decision to share UK classified information on the MBDA SCALP missiles with Ukraine, as France and Ukraine work toward local assembly lines in Ukraine, is notable. Any impact, however, will in part depend on how quickly Ukrainian assembled SCALP cruise missiles can be introduced into service.

"Given that Ukraine has already operated both Storm Shadow and SCALP, familiarity with the missile may help speed the overall process, but this will also be dependent on the extent and pace at which local assembly can be established."

At the start of the war its armed forces relied on old Cold War-era Soviet weaponry.

A slow supply of Western weapons helped it adapt. But now Ukraine produces 70% of its own weapons.

Key has been its rapid development of drone technology â from small First Person View (FPV) one-way attack drones for the front line, to larger long-range drones capable of striking deep into Russian territory, further than Storm Shadows can strike.

Kyiv is on track to build 10 million drones by the end of this year. And they can do it cheaper than the West, by using mass-produced Chinese parts.

Nato allies' equivalent drones can be twice as expensive as they try to shun Chinese components.

However, there are still weapons that Ukraine needs and struggles to produce on its own. From fast fighter jets to the most urgent example, interceptors to take down Russian ballistic missiles

The most effective weapon to do that, by far, is the US-made Patriot interceptor. Ukraine has all but run out of them and Russian ballistic missiles now make it through Ukrainian air defences with ease.

America's war in Iran has meant they're in even shorter supply.

They're also expensive â at around Â£3m a missile â and production rates have been slow. The US is planning to double production rates from around 600 Patriot missiles per annum to 2,000, but that will take several years.

President Donald Trump signalled last month that he would be willing to share Patriot technology with Ukraine, but has since rowed back.

Even if he had given approval, it would have taken a while for Ukraine to make Patriots themselves - some estimate at least a year. Ukraine would also be relying on the same sophisticated components that are in high demand across the globe.

Ukraine has embarked on a programme to develop its own interceptor missiles with European support â known as Project Freya.

But there are huge technological challenges in building a high-speed missile to take down another missile travelling at thousands of miles per hour. It is expensive and often time consuming.

Ukraine's military and its weapons manufacturers have shown themselves to be fast learners.

One of its own companies, Fire Point, is developing its own ballistic missiles which it hopes will be ready to fire in anger next year.

But Russia has already ramped up its own ballistic missile production, to around 100 a month.

Developing sophisticated weapons is expensive and cannot be done quickly. Ukraine is short of both time and money.

So, the move to hand missile blueprints to Ukraine will be welcome, but it is not an immediate fix for Ukraine's most pressing problems, and it wwill not dramatically alter Kyiv's ability to strike Russia in new ways.

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.

The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.

During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.

Dott covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.

He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

News.title: Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies aged 61 one year after son's death
News.content:
A former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.

Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.

Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.

Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".

News.title: Prince Harry steps down from African wildlife charity board
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts attempt to move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after their announcement last week they were returning to the UK imminently their children enrolled in school to start at the beginning of September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

News.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
News.content:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon.

The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.

That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.

Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.

"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.

"El NiÃ±o is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.

News.title: Victims describe 'house of terror' abuse by mother, grandmother and stepfather
News.content:
A mother, grandmother and stepfather who subjected three children to years of abuse in a "house of terror" have avoided jail.

Shirley Freeman, Julia Stephen and David McColl's victims were beaten, starved and psychologically tormented between 2003 and 2012.

Freeman, 51, and Stephen, 69, were earlier found guilty of cruel and unnatural treatment. McColl, 50, admitted the crimes.

At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Sheriff Craig Findlater said no sentence could "repair the awful childhoods" of the trio's victims.

Freeman was sentenced to 18 months probation, 240 hours of unpaid work, and a 12-month restriction of liberty order, as a direct alternative to custody.

Stephen was ordered to carry out 150 hours of unpaid work and given 18 months probation.

And McColl was sentenced to 220 hours of unpaid work, 18 months probation, and an 11-month restriction of liberty order.

Warning: This article contains descriptions of child abuse

Victims William and Meaghann Murphy, who are now 25 and 28, told BBC Scotland News the violence and cruelty they experienced as children became normal.

William said he was "utterly disappointed" at what he described as the "leniency" of the sentence.

"Violence and psychological terror resulted in nothing more than unpaid work and a curfew," he said.

"This system has failed my sisters and me, but we refuse to let it silence us. We must do better. We must stop child abusers from walking away with a slap on the wrist."

News.title: 'It's not Alton Towers' - rows break out over queuing at Wales' highest mountain
News.content:
Visitors to Wales' highest mountain are being urged to respect others by not skipping queues to reach the top following rows among climbers.

Recent hot weather means there have been bumper summer crowds at Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, where people have reportedly waited more than one hour to reach the 1,085m (3,560ft)-high summit.

Social media videos have shown arguments among queue-jumpers and those patiently waiting their turn to touch the metal plate that marks the top.

A recent video showed Marc Screeton, from Manchester, being heckled as he bypassed the line, saying: "Imagine queuing on a mountain? No chance."

But others have said queuing is necessary for safety reasons.

Eryri National Park Authority said its policy remained one of "self-policing" at the summit.

News.title: Teen pleads guilty over Channel boat with 165 migrants
News.content:
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has pleaded guilty to endangering others during a sea crossing.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, originally from South Sudan, admitted the offence at Canterbury Crown Court in relation to a crossing on 23 July.

Rescuers said they were astonished and alarmed to see the number of people packed onto the dinghy.

It was said to have been about the same length as a bus before it began deflating in the world's busiest shipping lane.

Prosecutors said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat.

Endangerment at sea is a new offence created to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the Channel.

At the time of the crossing, the dinghy set a record for the largest number of people brought over in a single boat since dinghy arrivals began on the south coast in recent years.

The figure has since been surpassed, and earlier this month, a record 230 people reached the UK in a so-called "mega dinghy".

Atak is due to be sentenced on 11 September.

News.title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
News.content:
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.

Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.

Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.

Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.

The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.

Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.

Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.

Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.

They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.

Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.

The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.

But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.

A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall.

"We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our Â£2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."

News.title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
News.content:
The government has urged social media companies to remove posts celebrating dangerous driving, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham branded sharing them "truly reprehensible".

Earlier Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that "social media companies could take the content down easily and adjust their algorithms to stop it being distributed".

Two police officers died when a car going the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Five passengers in the other car were also killed.

A TikTok account believed to belong to one of the five passengers, 18-year-old Makai Saddington, previously shared videos appearing to show dangerous driving, which have since been removed.

But Cleveland Police said "there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok".

News.title: Woman pleads guilty to breaching anonymity order in Jeffrey Donaldson case
News.content:
A 55-year-old Ballynahinch woman has pleaded guilty to breaching a lifetime anonymity order by posting information likely to reveal the alleged identity of a victim in the Jeffrey Donaldson sex abuse case.

Donna Toman of Lord Moira Park appeared at Downpatrick Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A defence lawyer said she was entering a guilty plea to a charge relating to a social media post earlier this year.

The charge states the post "was likely to lead members of the public to identify a person as the person against whom a qualifying offence is alleged to have been committed".

On 29 July police stated that the woman's arrest related to the Jeffrey Donaldson trial.

District Judge Magill said he wanted a pre-sentence report by 12 October adding that it was a "serious offence".

The court heard the offence can bring a six-month sentence.

Donaldson, who was an MP from 1997 until 2024, was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

He was told by the judge that the sentence would be a lengthy one.

It has since been confirmed he is to appeal his convictions.

News.title: Pubs and hotels could see business rates reformed after review
News.content:
A review is being launched into the way business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, and could lead to a reform of the system.

The Treasury says business rates expert Jerry Schurder will lead the review into rate valuations and report back in March 2027, with the government calling for the views of landlords, hoteliers and business owners to feed in to the process.

Last month, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, to come into effect in April.

Pub groups have argued they face disproportionately higher rates bills, but other businesses have called for a wider reform of the rates system.

According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), 161 pubs closed in the first three months of this year across England, Scotland and Wales, equating to the loss of around 2,400 jobs.

Rising business rates are cited as one issue facing the sector, although there have also been complaints that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made staff costs more expensive.

James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the new review would look at "a rethink of valuations - so that we can build a fairer system for the future".

Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: "For years pubs have paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open, so this review is sorely needed and hugely welcome."

The BBPA says pubs are valued differently for rates than retail venues. Instead of being based just on floor area, they are judged by a measure called Fair Maintainable Trade (FMT) - which means when a pub's turnover increases, so does its rates bill.

Jonathan Lawson, the chief executive of Butcombe Group, which has 120 pubs across the south and south west of England, told the BBC's Today programme that the use of FMT meant pubs were effectively being "punished for success", while large online retailers that operate out of warehouses were not subject to revenue-based rates calculations.

Their rates, he said, "are calculated based on what is deemed to be the market rent for that area, and takes very little on board in terms of revenue driven through that site".

"You can have a very large site paying a relatively low level of business rates versus a relatively small pub... paying a very high level of business rates."

Schurder is a former business rates policy lead at advisory firm Newmark UK, and his review will feed into the next rates revaluation in 2029.

Northern Ireland and Scotland set their own valuations, while Wales presently chooses to align its methodology with England. As the same approach is used across England and Wales, the review will be looking for responses from both nations.

Schurder's appointment was welcomed by Craig Beaumont of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) who said he would bring "crucial heavyweight business rates expertise into the Treasury".

However, Beaumont said the government needed to address the wider business rates system and exempt more smaller firms by increasing the rates relief threshold for small businesses.

Jonny Haseldine from the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) also said the review of valuations should be wider.

"The full reform of business rates, promised by the government at the last election, is urgently needed. This continued piecemeal approach to reform is the wrong approach," he said.

While the BCC said hospitality was the sector most worried about rates, Haseldine warned firms in every sector were struggling with the "complex and outdated" system.

Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the review was "far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off".

"Tax hikes on business premises and jobs, alongside job-destroying regulation in the Employment Rights Act, have left many hospitality businesses on the brink," he said.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said reform of business rates was "long overdue", but also called for an emergency VAT cut and a reverse to jobs tax changes "which have hammered hospitality in particular".

News.title: Girl gets tumour diagnosis 12 hours after eye test
News.content:
A mum said she "fell apart" after finding out her four-year-old daughter had a brain tumour, just 12 hours after an eye test.

Katie, 41, said her daughter Phoebe, now five, started to be sick and was getting severe headaches in February, but was told "it was just migraines" by a GP.

Following an eye test in May, Katie was called by the optician who told her to take her daughter straight to A&E at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. Just hours later, she was diagnosed with a brain tumour.

"I fell apart and just sobbed and sobbed," said the mum from St Neots, Cambridgeshire. Thankfully, Phoebe's tumour was not cancerous and she is now under the care of specialists.

Katie said: "I felt like we were probably wasting the hospital's time because Phoebe was running around playing like normal but, looking back, she was probably the sickest kid there.

"I kept thinking, how am I going to tell her dad and the other children?

"I kept asking if Phoebe would survive but the doctors said they were unable to answer that at that time, which is the worst thing in the world as a parent."

News.title: Reform says it will prioritise British-born workers for social housing
News.content:
Tice said he wanted the rules on who was allocated a home to be changed away from need to suitability, putting British families, workers and veterans at the front of the queue, saying: "This comes down to fairness."

"We're saying that the first people we should be looking after are young, British workers - under 35, young British married couples, young British veterans - who have done the right thing," he said.

"They've got a job, they're doing their best, working in their community, setting a fine example, because the role of the British government is actually to look after British citizens first."

Rules would be changed to reserve at least half of all social homes in England for British-born workers aged under 35, with prioritisation also given to married couples, veterans, victims of domestic violence and care leavers.

Tice claimed there were currently 540,000 existing affordable social homes occupied by overseas nationals and he wanted that to change.

"It's not fair that young British working families can't get on the housing ladder when overseas nationals have come to the UK and, because of the current rules based on need rather than suitability, they have jumped ahead in the queue," he said.

"We just don't think that's right: I can't think of another country where you rock up with a family and you expect the local taxpayer in that country to pay for your housing needs."

UK or Irish nationals made up 88.5% of main social home householders in 2024/25, according to the English Housing Survey.

That means around 11.5% of main householders, the perÂ­son in whose name the social home is renÂ­ted, were non-UK or Irish nationÂ­als.

For its part, Reform estimates 540,000 social homes are currently occupied by foreign nationals.

Reform has previously announced it would evict foreign nationals from social housing - a plan criticised by housing charity Shelter which said building more homes is the solution, rather than "changing the order of the queue" and "stoking division".

Tice also said Reform would raise Â£10bn a year to build new homes, in part by reintroducing the Right to Buy scheme of the 1980s, allowing people to buy council homes at a discount.

"The failure then was they didn't reinvest the proceeds into building more affordable homes," he said, adding he believed reinvestment would raise a third of the investment needed to build 50,000 homes a year over a decade.

Tice said another third would be raised via housing authorities, and the final third would be money from local government pension schemes.

A Labour Party spokesperson said the plan was "unworkable and unserious", adding: "It would blow a Â£10bn blackhole in the public finances, would create years of wrangling with the EU, and could leave British citizens without a place to call home.

"This Labour government is investing billions to deliver the biggest boost to social and affordable housing in a generation, to fix the housing crisis we inherited from the Tories."

The Conservative Party, which also said it would revoke the right of foreign nationals to social housing, accused Reform of "trying to catch up" with its policies.

The Tories have said their plan, which would allow Irish citizens and some EU nationals to remain in social housing, would free up around 230,000 homes.

Sir James Cleverly, shadow housing secretary, added: "The Conservatives have already set out comprehensive plans to ensure British nationals are at the front of the queue for social housing. Now Reform are trying to catch up.

"We also believe in a home owning society and that those who work hard should be able to buy their own home, without unnecessary barriers standing in their way."

Liberal Democrat spokesperson Gideon Amos said that Reform's plan was a "cruel gimmick".

Green MP SiÃ¢n Berry said her party would tackle housing issues by ending Right to Buy, building and buying hundreds of thousands of new council homes, and introducing rent controls.

She added: "Another blatantly racist and cruel policy from Reform, adding to a host of plans to create a two-tier Britain â one for those born in the UK and one for everyone else."

News.title: Rain to return this week with chance of thunderstorms and flooding
News.content:
The weather is set to turn more unsettled this week as rain returns with a chance of thunderstorms and localised flooding.

Some places could see a return to showery conditions by Tuesday, but it is from Wednesday onwards that more widespread and persistent rain will arrive from the south.

The wet weather will be welcome for parched regions of the UK, but a lot more will be needed before drought conditions start to ease.

As well as the rain, temperatures will also be on the rise once more, as warmer air moving in could push midweek highs close to 27C (81F) in places.

News.title: ‘Reagan would be throwing up:’ Ontario premier unloads on Trump and threatens to cut electricity to US as trade dispute escalates
News.content:

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said that Ronald Reagan would be "throwing up" over President Donald Trump’s trade policy as the expanding Canada-U.S. trade confrontation deepens.

Ford said Monday that Trump has miscalculated the determination of the Canadian public to sustain financial hardship rather than submit to American pressure.

"He underestimates Canada. We’re all in," Ford said. "Up here, we’re at a fever pitch, everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice."

Ford said that Trump had "declared war, economic war against his closest friend and ally" before turning his attention to Reagan, whose classic opposition to tariffs Ford previously highlighted in an American television ad campaign.

open image in gallery Ontario Premier Doug Ford (left) has threatened to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the United States ( AFP/Getty )

Ford highlighted that Trump keeps a portrait of Reagan near his desk. Reagan consistently advocated for open trade and repeatedly cautioned that protective duties could provoke counter-measures and harm American consumers and workers.

"He’d be throwing up on him from the picture if he knew what was going on, spinning around in his grave right now," Ford said. "He should maybe take that picture off the wall and move it somewhere else. Because right now, Ronald Reagan would be disgusted with President Trump."

The Premier’s remarks followed Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to exit trade talks with the Trump administration late Friday, citing excessive demands from Washington in exchange for duty relief. The United States enacted 50% tariffs Saturday on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, prompting Carney to announce matching dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs starting Sept. 8.

Trump intensified the conflict further on Monday, threatening a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts, and steel starting next year.

"Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years," Trump wrote on social media Monday morning. Criticizing what he called Canada’s "ridiculously high tariffs" on American farmers, Trump added: "Not sustainable, and NOT ANYMORE!"

Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity

Ford warned that "everything is on the table" should the dispute deteriorate, including shutting off electricity exports and critical mineral shipments from Ontario. He also urged Canada to consider using oil and potash as leverage.

open image in gallery With Prime Minister Mark Carney walking away from discussions late Friday, Ford stated that "everything is on the table” ( Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press v )

"I’ll cut them off," Ford said of critical minerals. "You won’t get a grain of sand out of Ontario."

Critical minerals carry increasing weight for U.S. national defense and industrial manufacturing. The Pentagon has worked to secure reliable supplies of raw materials utilized in military aircraft, missiles, munitions, and advanced electronics as Washington aims to diminish its reliance on China, which controls the mining and refining of several key strategic minerals.

Ford explicitly highlighted high-grade nickel exported to the United States and uranium processed in Ontario.

"What would they do without the high-grade nickel that we ship down to the U.S.?" Ford said.

Ford argued that Canada should weigh increasingly harsh retaliatory measures if Trump continues targeting Canadian industrial sectors, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise power rates or cease sending electricity across the border.

"We power 1.5 million homes and businesses," Ford said. "Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes."

If Trump persists in trying to dismantle Canadian industry, Ford added, "he better have a pack of batteries."

Ford has leveraged electricity in past disputes. During an earlier stage of the trade row, Ontario levied a 25% surcharge on power sent to Michigan, Minnesota, and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum before both sides stepped back.

Auto industry becomes a central battleground

Ford accused Trump of pursuing more than just an improved trade agreement, arguing he intends to dismantle Canadian industrial capacity and transfer manufacturing south.

Ford said Trump wants to turn Canada into a vassal state.

"He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.," Ford said.

The automotive industry plays a crucial role in Ontario, serving as the core of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing base. Plants and supply lines across Ontario are deeply integrated with facilities in Michigan and other U.S. states, with components routinely crossing the border multiple times during assembly.

Major automakers including Ford, General Motors, and Stellantis maintain major assembly operations in Ontario, supporting tens of thousands of jobs across the broader supply network. Trump’s warning of a 50% tariff on Canadian-built vehicles and components places the sector directly at the heart of the growing conflict.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer stated on Monday that "the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place" was the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada leveraged access to its domestic market to foster northern vehicle assembly.

"If he thinks the Canadian people are going to roll over and just continue buying American-made vehicles, it’s not going to happen," Ford said.

Ford says he opposed preliminary deal

Ford also revealed that he had resisted the tentative draft agreement Carney was reviewing prior to Canada walking away from negotiations.

"I wasn’t supporting the deal," Ford said.

Ford stated he was unwilling to allow American liquor back onto Ontario store shelves as part of a settlement and was prepared to break publicly with the proposed agreement.

"I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves," Ford said. "I was ready to go out there and call a press conference ... and say I’m not buckling over."

Ford noted his understanding that Washington sought provisions late in the talks that would have restricted Canada’s freedom to conclude trade pacts with other nations without U.S. consent. Carney has called that requirement unacceptable and an infringement on Canadian sovereignty.

"Who does he think he is?" Ford said of Trump. "You gotta be kidding."

Reagan fight returns

Ford’s comments regarding Reagan reignited a previous confrontation with Trump. Last year, Ontario funded U.S. television s featuring clips from a 1987 Reagan address cautioning that import tariffs trigger retaliation and trade conflicts.

Trump accused Ontario of misrepresenting Reagan and abruptly halted trade discussions with Canada. Ford subsequently agreed to pause the ad campaign so talks could resume.

"He doesn’t respect anyone," Ford sad.

Despite the sharp rhetoric, Ford maintained that Canada should remain open to dialogue.

"I never believe in walking away from the table," Ford said. "Continue negotiating and see where we go."

“Ffs RKID announce the tour we’re all losing our minds.” So said the latest tantalising post from the world’s biggest wind-up merchant Liam Gallagher. Fans might stay sceptical... but could this in fact be the clearest indicator yet that another Oasis reunion is on the cards?

By now, a new tour might seem less of a surprise than those long-awaited 2025 shows. The rock band made history when brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher put an end to their years-long feud and reunited onstage for the first time in almost 16 years to play a record-breaking world tour, including a series of homecoming shows in Manchester.

Even before the 2025 tour concluded, fans predicted that Oasis would be keen to get back out on the road again, given the run of shows were a defining cultural event – as well as a very lucrative one. Oasis Live ‘25 was estimated by Forbes to have generated over $400m (£293m) in revenue, with Noel and Liam each pocketing between $50m-$100m. As a result, the pair cracked the Sunday Times Rich List this year with a combined net worth of $375m.

The Independent’s sources have said they understand that a Knebworth residency is on the cards but have yet to confirm any specific dates. This year marked the 30th anniversary of the band’s legendary Knebworth shows in 1996, where they played to a combined audience of 250,000 (more than four per cent of the population applied for tickets), including the rumoured 7,000-strong guestlist.

open image in gallery Oasis at Knebworth, August 1996 ( PA )

Sources have also said that Noel has been writing new music – it remains to be seen if this will emerge in the shape of the first Oasis album since 2008’s Dig Out Your Soul, with Liam on vocal duties.

Earlier this month, it was announced that SJM Concerts, the promoter behind the Oasis reunion tour, had secured a licence to host events at Knebworth indefinitely.

The promoter has also worked on shows with Take That and The Prodigy, as well as comedian Peter Kay.

The licence allows events for up to 125,000 people, with live music and dance performances permitted until 3am.

In July, The Sun claimed that Oasis would play six nights at Knebworth over a three-week period in September 2027. Meanwhile, the Manchester Evening News reported that same month that the rock’n’roll stars would headline 12 nights at the Etihad stadium, with an insider telling the paper: “It will be 12 nights at the Etihad Stadium across May and June. They could even add more dates to that as well, there’s talk of up to 20. The wider tour is also going to include a return to Knebworth.”

Before that, there was speculation in 2024 – after the band announced their comeback tour – that they would return to the site. Oasis denied this on X in a statement: “Contrary to reports in some UK tabloid media today, Oasis will not be playing Knebworth Park in the future.”

The Independent has contacted Oasis’s representatives for comment.

open image in gallery Brothers Liam and Noel Gallagher during their 2025 reunion tour ( AFP/Getty )

Contrary to tabloid media reports, sources told The Independent that the mood backstage during Oasis’s 2025 reunion was jubilant, with both Noel and Liam in great spirits as their famous friends – from football stars to pop singers, including Manchester City star Jack Grealish and the Happy Mondays’ Shaun Ryder – rubbed elbows.

“It’s been a proper love-in backstage,” one source said. “There’s a friends and family bar which is basically free booze – Guinness on draft (of course) (sic), beer, wine and champagne. It’s like going to a wedding every night.”

They continued: “Cast and Richard Ashcroft [Oasis’s support acts] are having the time of their lives – it’s been so nice to see Noel and Liam’s guests vibing off each other. Everyone’s been making new friends.”

And while it was true that Liam had left early each night – this was nothing to do with animosity towards his older brother and everything to do with him ensuring he was in peak condition for each concert.

“Liam has been completely zen, focusing on his voice and arriving shortly before each show, then getting straight off to avoid temptation,” a source told The Independent.

The 2025 reunion tour is the subject of a forthcoming documentary directed by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, due for release in IMAX cinemas on 9 September and on Disney+. Titled Don’t Look Back In Anger, the film follows Noel and Liam as they undertake the Live ‘25 tour, which kicked off just over a year ago in Cardiff.

A 46-second teaser trailer, released last month, showed cheering fans before cutting to footage of the Gallagher siblings backstage getting ready for their first shows together since their split in 2009.

“Oasis Live ‘25, one of the most anticipated rock ‘n’ roll comebacks of our time,” Disney+ said in a statement. “The film is an unapologetically uplifting account of the biggest musical event of 2025, capturing the experience and emotions of the band and their fans across the world.

“The unique perspective includes rehearsal, backstage, and onstage access as well as the first joint interviews with Noel and Liam in over 20 years.”

When it comes to Glastonbury, Liam insisted over the weekend that an Oasis headline performance is “not happening” next year. Organiser Emily Eavis recently confirmed that all headliners have been booked.

As for a 2027 tour, for now, Oasis fans will just have to roll with it... the band are taking their time.

A Dutch broadcaster announced on Monday that it is boycotting the Eurovision Song Contest for a second consecutive year, calling the event a "platform for division" because of tensions over Israel’s involvement.

The decision by AVROTROS comes after television organisations in the Netherlands, Iceland, Ireland, Slovenia and Spain refused to take part in this year's contest because of Israel's participation.

It stated: "AVROTROS will not participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027 because the event can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict."

The Dutch broadcaster, which has a long history of involvement with the competition, said it was leaving it to the public network NPO to decide on any Dutch involvement.

AVROTROS director-general Taco Zimmerman said in a statement: "The Eurovision Song Contest was originally created to bring people and countries together. It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character," adding: "The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division."

Next year's contest will take place in the Bulgarian port of Burgas, but AVROTROS will not be there ( AP )

NPO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

AVROTROS said it has called on the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) to establish transparent rules for countries involved in military conflicts. "However, the recently announced changes by the EBU do not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored," it said.

The Geneva-based EBU — a group of public broadcasters from 56 countries that runs Eurovision — did not immediately comment.

While AVROTROS did not mention Israel by name, it confirmed it will boycott Eurovision in 2027 "because the event can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict."

It added: "The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years."

The contest was founded in 1956, in part to help unite a shattered continent after World War II, pitting acts from dozens of countries against one another for the musical crown. Bulgarian singer Dara won this year with her infectious party anthem "Bangaranga."

A number of performers and countries have called for the exclusion of Israel, which has participated in Eurovision since 1973 as one of a few non-European competing nations.
