World.title: Algeria’s schools put Shakespeare before Molière in break from France
World.content:
Algerian primary schools will begin teaching English before French for the first time, signalling the country’s break from France.

Share Algeria’s schools put Shakespeare before Molière in break from France on social media

Ahmed Krim spent 30 years teaching English in Algeria’s middle schools. Now retired, the 60-year-old watched the language he loved remain firmly behind French as the country’s second language.

English was less valued than French, which might have been the language of Algeria’s coloniser, but continues to be present in every dialogue, six decades after independence.

On July 25 , Algeria’s Education Minister, Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui, announced that English will become the sole foreign language taught in the third year of primary school in the new academic year for 2026-2027.

French would be pushed back to the fourth year, ending its domination of foreign language classes in Algerian schools.

From next month, eight-year-olds across Algeria will become the first to learn English before French.

“It is a very good decision. But it requires thinking, planning and resources,” Krim told Al Jazeera.

It is among the first steps in President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s linguistic overhaul for Algeria, which he first outlined in 2022 with English being introduced to primary schools.

Since then, medicine and science faculties have begun switching from French to English.

The French language has been erased from some utility bills and Air Algerie tickets. Road signs are beginning to feature English alongside Arabic, while government ministers’ websites will also have English as an option.

The shift from French to English as Algeria’s secondary language is both sweeping and structural.

It comes amid the most serious diplomatic crisis between the two countries since Algeria’s independence from France in 1962.



In July 2024, French President Emmanuel Macron publicly backed Morocco’s sovereignty claim over Western Sahara.

Algeria, which supports the Sahrawi Polisario Front and hosts over 170,000 Sahrawi refugees, viewed that as highly provocative.

That, and other issues, saw Algeria expel French diplomats, and vice versa.

Algeria’s replacement of French as the country’s second language accelerated after the diplomatic crisis grew.

A classroom without enough teachers

A rethink of the whole education system in Algeria may be needed.

“First and foremost, specialised training centres must be restored and candidates must not be forced into the teaching profession without wanting it – we need people who genuinely want to do this work,” Krim said.

He refers to dedicated institutes established after independence, where primary and middle school teachers, like himself, trained via a model that combined classroom instruction with direct school placements to meet the gap in Arabic instructors.

The centres operated until the late 1990s, when an economic crunch replaced them with the fewer and more selective Ecoles Normales Superieures.

Most teachers today are university graduates, but lack the practical, classroom-first grounding that the older model provided.

Krim said that school curricula must be designed and entrusted to “a qualified body that includes both linguistic and pedagogical expertise, free from all ideology”.

But journalist and analyst Noureddine Bessadi said the ideological dimension matters in Algeria, which overthrew colonialism following a bloody and bitter struggle against the French.

“Since independence in 1962, every shift in language policy has been fought as much on political as pedagogical grounds,” Bessadi told Al Jazeera.

After independence, Algeria’s Arabisation drive, when French was displaced from government and education, was “part of state building and enforcing Algeria’s identity, centring Arabic and Islam”, Bessadi added.

Tamazight, a non-Semitic language spoken by around a quarter of Algeria’s population, was marginalised until 1995, Bessadi said, shaped by an “ideological perception of unity that prioritised linguistic and cultural harmony”.

Critics argue that the transition from French to English is happening faster than the system can keep up with. For one, it is believed that there are not enough qualified English teachers to make the language reforms work.

But one source familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that there are enough teachers to roll out this programme in primary schools and that any shortage could be filled through contractors.



In February, Algeria’s education ministry reportedly recruited about 15,000 English language teachers for primary schools.

Rafik Laceb, a lecturer in English at Mouloud Mammeri University in Tizi Ouzou, is cautiously optimistic about the primary school reform. But he considers the parallel push to teach university subjects in English to be rushed and poorly executed.

“Frankly, and beyond any chauvinism, I believe this decision is positive… I believe there is, today, sufficient supervision and evaluation work from the first experience,” Laceb said, in reference to the previous introduction of English in later primary school years.

The university experiment that began in 2023-2024 produced insufficient contact hours, a lack of genuine assessment of students’ English levels and no tracking of their progress.

Around 50 percent of teaching at Tizi Ouzou University’s English department is by younger contract staff, which brings other challenges.

“A young contract teacher must first master the basic principles of medicine before attempting to teach medical terminology in English,” he said.

Levelling the playing field

Currently, children only begin learning a foreign language in the third year of state primary schools, whereas multiple languages are taught at private schools from kindergarten.

Djamel Merah, whose daughter attended private schools before transferring to public secondary school, studied Arabic, French and English simultaneously from kindergarten level.

Merah welcomes the government’s language reforms at state primary schools, which will provide more children with the opportunity to learn English.

“It addresses a question about the gap in opportunities between children who get multilingual education from the start and those in public schools who don’t get the same chance,” he said.

Shakespeare’s rising shelf space

There also appears to be a more organic response among the public that precedes the government’s promotion of the English language.

Krimo Taleb, a bookseller at the Libre Pensee bookshop in Tizi Ouzou, has seen a growth in English-language book sales, particularly among female readers.

“In my opinion, it has nothing to do with government decisions. The majority of young readers today speak three languages fluently,” he said.

His own daughter, a middle school student, reads fluently in Arabic, English and French.

Colleen Hoover, Ana Huang and J. K. Rowling are some of the best-selling authors at his shop.

“Previously, our bookshops provided for English literature students the works of Shakespeare,” Taleb says. “Today, there is a diverse range of English-language titles aimed at the general public.”



However, French remains Algeria’s most influential foreign language. According to the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), Algeria has approximately 15 million French speakers, nearly a third of its population.

There is not a single newspaper published in English and written English by Algerians remains in its infancy.

But there are signs that former colonies are turning their backs on France’s linguistic legacy, particularly in Africa, where Paris’s military and political presence made a resurgence in recent decades.

In March 2025, Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso withdrew from the OIF, accusing it of being a political instrument of Paris.

“Mali made its national languages official in 2023, demoting French to a working language. Burkina Faso followed the same year and Niger in 2025,” Bessadi added. “Even Senegal, which has not removed French as an official language, has begun encouraging local languages at its expense.”

For Krim, Algeria’s linguistic ambitions are not far-fetched, but for it to work, the country needs the “necessary resources… and transparency”.

World.title: Saudi Arabia’s MBS visits Macron in France: What to expect
World.content:
Saudi crown prince and French president are set to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy.

Share Saudi Arabia’s MBS visits Macron in France: What to expect on social media

Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, (MBS), is on the second day of his two-day state visit to France, where he’s meeting President Emmanuel Macron.

In this explainer, we outline what they are expected to discuss and examine how their latest meetings build on an already evolving relationship.

What is on the agenda?

MBS’s visit to Paris began on Sunday evening alongside President Macron at the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup. It was the first time the Esports tournament, which includes competitions ranging from video games to chess, had been held outside Saudi Arabia.

On Monday, Macron and Bin Salman are expected to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy.

French media reported that a deal to build a Dragon Ball-themed amusement park, backed by a Saudi investment fund and inspired by the iconic Japanese manga series, could be signed.

Valerie Pecresse, President of the Regional Council of Île-de-France in Greater Paris, told French broadcaster TF1 that the regional government had been working on the project for 18 months.

“There is a very important meeting at the Elysee today that may result in the signing of this agreement. We are waiting for the signature,” she said, describing the project as “on the scale of Disneyland”.

Bin Salman and Macron are also holding bilateral discussions on regional security and their economic ties.

That is expected to include discussions about energy routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, such as new pipelines, capacity upgrades and alternative port networks.



France is a major buyer of Saudi oil and mineral products.

Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on February 28, shipping has been severely disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz – the vital waterway on which oil exporters in the Gulf are heavily reliant and where 20 percent of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies are shipped from during peacetime. The disruption sent oil prices soaring.

Before the war, a barrel of Brent crude – the global benchmark – cost about $66. Over the course of the conflict, prices have climbed above $100 – hitting a high of $119 early on in the war.

On Monday, Brent was trading around $93 a barrel.

Bin Salman and Macron are also expected to discuss the war in Iran, the bloodshed in Palestine, as well as developments in Syria and Lebanon, where Israel occupies around one-fifth of its territory.

Other expected topics on Monday’s agenda include global events that Saudi Arabia is set to host in the coming years, including Expo 2030, focusing on sustainability and urban innovation, and the 2034 football World Cup.

How much trade does Saudi Arabia do with France?

The two countries have a fairly equal trading balance.

In 2024, France exported $4.5bn worth of goods to Saudi Arabia and imported $4.6bn worth, according to data from the Observatory of Economic Complexity (OEC), an online platform that compiles and visualises international trade statistics.

Refined petroleum accounted for 72 percent of Saudi Arabia’s exports to France in 2024. Besides refined petroleum, Saudi Arabia exported crude petroleum and other mineral products to France. It also exported small amounts of machinery, chemicals and cars.

France’s exports to Saudi Arabia in 2024 were more diverse, including airliners, helicopters, gas turbines, pharmaceutical products and perfume, among other products.

What have relations between Saudi Arabia and France been like?

Sunday’s visit marked the third time MBS has visited France after trips in 2022 and 2023.

In December 2024, Macron visited Riyadh, where the two countries founded the Saudi-French Strategic Partnership Council, which formalised and upgraded political and economic ties between Saudi Arabia and France.

The current visit is also MBS’s first international trip since the August 7 signing of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, known as the Mecca pact – the mutual defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan.

Signed by the prince, Turkiye’s President, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistan’s Prime Minister, Shehbaz Sharif, the agreement commits all three states to treat an armed attack on any one of them as an attack on all three.



Analysts say the pact shows that Saudi Arabia is taking steps to diversify its security partnerships beyond Washington.

World.title: Four arrested over fatal shooting of South African boxer Zolani Tete
World.content:
Tete, who won world WBF flyweight and WBO bantamweight titles, was killed outside his home in Eastern Cape last week.

Share Four arrested over fatal shooting of South African boxer Zolani Tete on social media

South African police say they have arrested four people in connection with the murder of two-time boxing world champion Zolani Tete, who was shot last week.

The four suspects arrested over the weekend are aged between 22 and 28, police said in a statement on Monday. One has been formally charged with murder.

Tete, 38, was attacked on Friday evening as he returned to his home in Mdantsane in the Eastern Cape province.

A 27-year-old woman who was with him in the car survived but is in hospital, police said.

Tete won the IBF junior bantamweight world title in 2014 and the WBO bantamweight world title in 2017.

In 2017, he entered boxing history when he took just 11 seconds to flatten his opponent with his first punch to retain his WBO bantamweight crown.

It was the fastest knockout victory in a world championship bout.

In 2023, the United Kingdom Anti-Doping agency hit Tete with a four-year ban that ended on July 29, and he was preparing to return to professional boxing.

“South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced,” Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said in a statement following the murder.

“He was training for a return to the ring. He believed he still had something to give this country. He was right, but he will not get the chance now. He, and all of us, have been robbed.”

World.title: South Korea says US cancelled upcoming joint marine exercises over Iran war
World.content:
Share South Korea says US cancelled upcoming joint marine exercises over Iran war on social media

South Korea says the United States has cancelled a large joint amphibious landing exercise scheduled for next month due to constraints on force availability caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.

“The US Marine Corps formally notified our forces in June that its ability to deploy forces during this year’s Ssangyong exercise would be constrained due to the situation in the Middle East,” Han Seung-jeon, a spokesman for the South Korean Marine Corps, told reporters at a news briefing on Monday.

The biennial Ssangyong drills involve marine forces from South Korea and the US and are designed to strengthen combined operations, typically involving warships, aircraft and ground forces rehearsing amphibious landings.

Seoul and Washington were continuing consultations on resuming the amphibious exercise, the spokesman said, without giving details.

There was no immediate comment from the Pentagon.

The announcement follows US President Donald Trump’s surprise order last week to scale back a separate annual joint military exercise that ended last Friday, citing the cost and Seoul’s refusal to take part in the war on Iran.

The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were cut from 11 days to five.

Trump has also sought to revive the relationship he developed with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un during his first term.

He wrote on his Truth Social platform last week that the Ulchi Freedom Shield drills sent “a signal that was totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful”.



Despite the reduction of the exercises, North Korea fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles last week and issued a statement denouncing the drills.

North Korea has long condemned such joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion.

The US president also said last week that it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons. Seoul estimates that North Korea has 80 to 120 such weapons.

Trump met Kim three times during his first term, but Pyongyang accelerated its nuclear programmes after their second summit in Hanoi in 2019 collapsed without an agreement on North Korea’s denuclearisation.

World.title: Activists occupy UK aircraft parts factory over Israel links
World.content:
NewsFeed Activists occupy UK aircraft parts factory over Israel links

Pro-Palestine activists from the ‘People Against Genocide’ group occupied a Martin-Baker factory in the UK, accusing the company of supplying ejection-seat components for aircraft used by Israel’s military. The group says the action aims to disrupt Britain’s military support for Israel.

World.title: Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US treasury secretary
World.content:
The US treasury secretary has threated Iran with "the single greatest financial offensive ever", claiming the US-Israel war with Iran was "entering its endgame".

Scott Bessent said the US would sever all economic ties with the country in "an economic D-Day" and that any nation partnering with Iran financially would also be isolated.

Bessent's threat to the Iranian regime follows several U-turns and extended deadlines from US President Donald Trump's administration on previous threats.

Iran dismissed Bessent's comments and said it would shut down all oil exports from the region "if the war continues", according to news agency Reuters.

The Iranian regime has also issued a new warning to shipping not to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, the agency reported.

One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through strait, a waterway south of Iran, but the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February.

Bessent made the comments in an opinion piece for the Financial Times, external. He did not detail what the economic pressure on Iran would involve, but he is expected to do so in a press conference in the US at 13:00 local time (18:00 BST) on Monday.

"The world should understand that our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," he wrote in the piece.

The US has made several threats to Iran over the course of its war with the country, including Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz.

The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy.

The economic impact of the Iran war is being felt in the US and across the world. Higher oil prices have fuelled concerns over the cost of living, with petrol and diesel prices much higher than they were a year ago.

In the US, gasoline prices have surpassed $4 a gallon and affordability is among the top concerns of American voters ahead of the mid-term elections in November.

On Monday, a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, was $93.

Last week, Bessent announced the US government would intervene in the bond markets and buy back more government debt in a bid to boost demand for bonds and lower borrowing rates.

But the impact of the annoucenment was short-lived, with long-term borrowing costs bouncing back up a day later.

World.title: Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes
World.content:
Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated.

Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan.

Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%.

When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was "working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation".

The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon's site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured.

Following that strike, Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday: "Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy's logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole.

"After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon's turn."

Meanwhile, in Ukraine's Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region's head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram.

Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia's first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country.

Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points.

The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians.

Both companies have been described as "Russia's Amazon" and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population.

In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances.

But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments.

This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses.

The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies.

World.title: Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza
World.content:
Four kites were found in Kibbutz Nahal Oz, which is about 800m (2,620ft) from the Gaza border, on Friday and Saturday. Several more were found elsewhere in southern Israel last week, according to local media.

The Israeli reports cited military sources as saying they believed Hamas was behind the kites and that they might have been intended to test Israel's response.

No suspicious materials were attached to the kites and they did not pose a threat, the military said.

But Katz warned there would be "zero tolerance" and said: "A balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone, with or without explosives."

Residents of Nahal Oz said in a statement that they feared the return of incendiary kites and balloons, adding: "We will not accept a policy of containment when it comes to our security."

Hamas warned of "the danger of the allegations and threats" from Israel and said the kites were "basically children's toys from displacement camps".

"These threats are based on fabricated pretexts and are an attempt to justify the continuation of the aggression and violations against our people," a spokesman for the group added.

On Sunday, Palestinian health officials said two people were killed and seven others injured in two Israeli strikes in Nuseirat refugee camp and the town of al-Zawayda, both in central Gaza.

A four-year-old boy called Mohammed Taha was killed when a building in al-Zawayda, just north of Maghazi refugee camp, was bombed, according to local media.

The Israeli military said it killed the commander of a Hamas weapons manufacturing site in the Maghazi area, whom it identified as Ismail Abu Ful, and that it had warned the residents to evacuate beforehand.

"There is no ceasefire, there is nothing," Abu Ahmed, a displaced man who had been sheltering nearby, told Reuters news agency. "We want solutions, we want to live in peace."

On Monday, Palestinian media reported that a man called Mohammed Abu Asad was killed in an overnight Israeli strike on a tent in the central town of Deir al-Balah.

The Israeli military said Abu Asad was a member of the elite Nukhba forces of Hamas's military wing who had taken part in the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the cross-border assault, during which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

More than 74,420 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including 1,288 since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

World.title: King of Norway's health has worsened, palace says
World.content:
King Harald V of Norway's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream.

The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice.

The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago.

His son, Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave.

King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.

In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia.

The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026.

Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018.

The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg HÃ¸iby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence.

HÃ¸iby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure.

Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

World.title: Nearly three million Teslas recalled in China over hidden door handles
World.content:
Minimalistic door handles became a signature feature of electric vehicles (EVs), but the controversial designs are now at the centre of China's biggest car recall, affecting more than 4 million vehicles.

The recall, which includes 2.98 million Chinese-made Teslas, follows safety concerns that the hidden door handles are difficult to locate and open in emergency situations.

Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely.

The recalled vehicles will have a warning label stuck on the interior door and receive a software update to automatically lower the windows in a crash.

The designs have come under scrutiny after two fatal crashes in China involving Xiaomi EVs, in which power failures were suspected to have prevented doors from being opened.

Tesla said in a statement on Friday that it was recalling some of its Model 3, Y, S and X vehicles due to door handles that are "difficult to identify and operate because their colour is similar to the interior trim".

"In extreme situations such as a severe collision causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail, this could hinder occupants from quickly opening the doors to escape and impede rescue efforts by those outside the vehicle, posing a safety hazard," it said.

Tesla said it would place warning labels on the recalled vehicles and issue a software update to automatically lower a vehicle's windows after a collision.

It is not clear if the affected firms plan to make a similar recall for the rest of the world.

The BBC has contacted Tesla, XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely for comment.

The use of hidden handle designs has "snowballed" after Chinese brands were quick to copy the "sleek" look of Tesla's Model S sedan since 2014, said Tu Le, the founder of consultancy Sino Auto Insights.

The use of warning labels and a software update is more of a "band-aid" than a lasting solution for the issue, he added.

In February, Chinese authorities announced a ban on hidden door handles.

Under new rules due to take effect on 1 January 2027, cars will only be allowed to be sold in China if they have a mechanical release on both the inside and outside of their doors.

Tesla's door handles were also involved in a probe by US safety regulators after reports that they suddenly stopped working, leaving children trapped in the cars.

In July, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggested creating a new formal safety standard for all carmakers.

The BBC has contacted the agency for comment.

World.title: Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison
World.content:
Sean Grayson, the white US police officer convicted of murdering a black woman, Sonya Massey, during an incident at her home in 2024, has died in prison at age 32.

Grayson shot dead Massey, 36, during an exchange that took place after she reported a suspected intruder at her residence in Illinois. The killing reignited the debate about police brutality in the US.

Grayson said he fired because he thought Massey was about to throw a pot of boiling water on him. He was last year found guilty of second-degree murder.

The former police officer was undergoing treatment for colon cancer. His lawyer Daniel Fultz confirmed to the BBC that Grayson had died on Sunday, but did not disclose the cause.

The BBC has asked the Illinois Department of Corrections for comment.

Lawyers for Massey's family said: "Grayson's death in custody from cancer does not bring Sonya back."

"We wish his family prayers of peace, as we do for all who grieve a loved one. Sonya's family knows that pain all too well and will grieve her loss the rest of their days," the lawyers said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

Protests took place across the US in the aftermath of Massey's death, and then-President Joe Biden declared that the late woman "should be alive today".

World.title: Access to Zambian courts prevented as election petition deadline looms
World.content:
Court premises in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, and elsewhere have been shut as the deadline for filing a petition against the outcome of the recent presidential election approaches.

An unusual police presence has been reported at some courts, which have been taped off to prevent access.

Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile said he would challenge the election result, citing irregularities, after coming second with a 38% share of the vote. Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema won a second term with 60%.

Mundubile is in hiding over alleged threats made against him, amid a post-election period marked by controversy, including the shooting dead of an opposition figure and the arrest of others.

Monday is the last day on which petition against the presidential election result can be filed. Such a petition could potentially affect the inauguration of Hichilema, which is scheduled for 1 September.

On Monday, lawyers who arrived at the courts were being asked to depart.

One lawyer told the BBC that three armed men approached his vehicle, identified themselves, and instructed him to leave the area.

The courts that have been sealed off include the High Court in Lusaka, the Supreme Court, which also houses the Constitutional Court, and several local courts.

It is unclear when the premises will reopen. The BBC has contacted the Zambian police and the judiciary for comment.

Local media cite a directive by a judiciary administrative official telling all staff not to report to work following the closure of courts for "security reasons".

The memo, which has also been shared online by some opposition figures, does not give details of the security situation.

Some commentators have raised concerns over the closure while questioning the independence of the judiciary.

A prominent voice for the opposition, Emmanuel Mwamba, alleged the action was aimed at preventing Mundubile from filing his presidential election petition.

The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) said it was concerned by the closure of the courts and the presence of heavily armed military personnel around court premises in Lusaka.

It said there was no formal public explanation for the closure nor its expected duration.

Referring to the "unsigned memorandum" from the judiciary addressing staff, it said no further official information had been provided to lawyers and the public.

"The closure of the courts has immediate implications for access to justice, particularly for persons requiring urgent judicial intervention," it said in a statement

It said the timing was "particularly significant in the present electoral context", citing a "seven-day period" in which a person may "petition the Constitutional Court to nullify the election of a President-elect".

World.title: Four arrested over suspected poisoning of elephants in Kenya
World.content:
Four people have been arrested in Kenya as part of an investigation into a spate of mysterious elephant deaths over the past two months, officials have said.

Three Kenyans and one Tanzanian have been detained on suspicion of poisoning at least 18 elephants in the Amboseli National Park, the Kenya Wildlife Service told the BBC.

The investigation is looking into whether the elephants died from cyanide poisoning after eating large quantities of tomatoes sprayed with illegal pesticides.

Preliminary laboratory tests have found traces of cyanide in samples of the crops taken from the elephants' stomachs.

All of the affected elephants - mainly female adults and their calves - had also shown signs of paralysis, which authorities believe also points to cyanide poisoning.

Tomato farms are found in the Kimana area, which is part of a corridor between Amboseli National Park and the Tsavo National Park in southern Kenya.

It is a vast area known as the Amboseli ecosystem, which straddles the border near Tanzania where more than 2,000 elephants move along in search of food and water.

Pesticides prohibited in Kenya are sometimes smuggled across this porous border with Tanzania and used in farms within the Amboseli area, where elephants live near human settlements and are known to raid farms for food.

While regulations against illegal agrochemicals exist, there is weak enforcement and little attention paid to how they can affect animals.

The suspects have been released on bail and the investigation continues.

World.title: ‘We did everything possible to save him’ — Yayi mourns Ogogo
World.content:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate in Ogun State, Solomon “Yayi” Adeola, has mourned veteran Nollywood actor Taiwo “Ogogo” Hassan, recalling the efforts made to save him during his battle with stage-four cancer.

Yayi, the senator representing Ogun West Senatorial District, was one of the major financiers of the actor’s treatment during his illness. Ogogo’s daughter, Kira, had publicly acknowledged the senator’s support days before the actor’s death, saying he had been footing the medical bills while the family searched for further treatment options.

In a tribute issued after Ogogo’s death, the politician said he and those around the actor had done everything humanly possible to secure the medical care he needed.

The 57-year-old said: “During those difficult moments, we stood closely with him and his family, supporting his treatment and doing everything humanly possible to ensure that he received the necessary medical care.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We remained hopeful and prayerful that he would overcome the illness and return to the family, friends and countless admirers who cherished him. Sadly, despite all efforts, it has pleased Almighty God to call him home. Indeed, God knows best.”

Painful

Furthermore, Yayi described Ogogo’s death as painful, especially after the veteran actor’s courageous battle with illness and the collective hope and prayers for his recovery throughout his treatment.

He said Ogogo was not only an accomplished veteran of the entertainment industry but also a dear brother and a proud son of Ilaro, Ogun State.

Yayi added that the 66-year-old actor’s remarkable career brought joy to generations of Nigerians and contributed significantly to the growth and development of the Nigerian film industry.

“His talent, humility and enduring body of work will ensure that his memory lives on. At this extremely difficult time, we extend our heartfelt condolences to his wife, children and entire family, the good people of Yewaland and Ogun State, his colleagues and associates in the entertainment industry, and everyone whose life he touched.

“We share in their grief over this sad and irreplaceable loss. We pray that Almighty Allah forgives his shortcomings, accepts his good deeds, grants him Al-Jannah Firdaus, and gives his family and all of us who mourn him the strength and fortitude to bear this painful loss.”

Backstory

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that Ogogo died on Sunday after battling stage-four cancer. His family subsequently buried him at his residence in Ilaro, Ogun State.

Since his death was announced and his burial held, Ogogo’s colleagues, friends, associates and fans have continued to mourn him, remembering his kindness and describing him as a man who brought joy to those around him and touched many lives.

Ogogo began his acting career in 1981 while working as a mechanic. He later left his job with the water corporation in 1994 to pursue acting as a full-time career.

Before his death, Ogogo appeared in numerous films, including “Atitebi”, “Agbelebu”, “Agbo-Odaju”, “Danfo Driver”, “Owo Blow”, “Amerah”, “Aníkúlápó”, “Bank Alert”, “IGE” and “Aníkúlápó: Rise of the Spectre”, among others.

World.title: Transfers: Super Eagles’ Terem Moffi joins German club Hamburger SV
World.content:
Super Eagles striker Terem Moffi has completed his move to German Bundesliga side Hamburger SV, with the club confirming the signing of the 27-year-old Nigerian on Monday.

Moffi joins HSV from French Ligue 1 outfit OGC Nice after completing his mandatory medical examinations at the Athleticum at Volkspark last weekend, before putting pen to paper on his contract.

The Nigerian striker will wear the No. 9 shirt at his new club as he begins another chapter in a career that has already taken him across several European leagues.

HSV sporting director Kathleen Krüger believes Moffi’s experience and versatility will add another dimension to the club’s attack.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Terem fits perfectly with our orientation. With his commitment, we are setting ourselves even wider and more variable in the Sturmzentrum and thus increasing our quality,” Krüger said.

“Through his career path so far, he brings extensive experience at a high international level and can also pass this on to our talents. We are pleased that Terem is at the HSV, and welcome him warmly.”

Sports director Claus Costa also highlighted the physical qualities and attacking versatility Moffi will bring to the squad.

“We are very pleased that we have succeeded in signing Terem. Terem is a striker who is difficult to control due to his physique, determination and style of play,” Costa said.

“He can attack the depth, has an enormous presence in the penalty area and brings the necessary quality with his back to the goal.

“We are convinced that Terem will give our game additional punch and our squad additional variability. Now it is important to integrate him quickly so that we can start the new Bundesliga season as a team with a lot of energy and conviction.”

Moffi begins seventh-country adventure

At 27, Moffi has already built an impressive European football journey, with Germany becoming the seventh country in which he has played professionally.

Born in Calabar, Nigeria, in May 1999, Moffi moved to England at 17, where he attended the Buckswood Football Academy before beginning his professional career in Lithuania.

He first played for FK Kauno Zalgiris before moving to FK Riteriai. In January 2020, he moved to Belgium to join KV Kortrijk before later that year moving to France with FC Lorient.

His performances at Lorient earned him a move to OGC Nice in early 2023, while he spent the second half of last season on loan at Portuguese giants FC Porto.

Across those clubs, Moffi recorded 88 goals and 13 assists in 228 competitive appearances. The striker has also been a Nigerian international since 2021, making 23 appearances for the Super Eagles, with six goals and two assists to his name.

Moffi made his international debut alongside his new HSV teammate Jordan Torunarigha for Nigeria in October 2023.

Moffi excited by HSV challenge

The Nigerian revealed that conversations with the coach played an important role in convincing him to make the move, while Hamburger SV’s stature and history also appealed to him.

“The coach was really very convincing in the talks. The location with its great fans and the entire orientation of the club also played a role in my decision,” Moffi said.

“Even if the HSV spent a few years in the 2. League, the club is still a big name, all over the world.

“When I told my father about the interest, he immediately knew which club it was and was full of anticipation. For me, that was crazy in a positive way. I’m all the happier to be a part of history and the club myself.”

Moffi also outlined what HSV supporters can expect from him, insisting that while scoring goals remains his primary responsibility, he is equally committed to contributing to the collective effort.

“As a striker, I love to score goals, but I also love working for the team and keeping the whole group together,” he said.

“I’m now the new guy in the team, which is always a bit strange for yourself at first, but I’m very happy to get to know everyone now and get started together soon.”

With HSV now preparing for the new Bundesliga campaign, Moffi will hope his goals, physical presence and experience can help the club make a strong return to the German top flight.

World.title: Cross River gov’t seeks $25m international support for landslide, flood recovery at COP17
World.content:
The Cross River State Government has taken its July–August 2026 landslide and flood disasters to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) COP17 in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, seeking $25 million in international support for emergency response, ecological restoration and long-term resilience.

The state government made the call in its proposed Cross River Restore Hope Initiative report currently being pitched to potential investors and partners at the COP17 in Mongolia by two members of the Cross River State House of Assembly, Martins Achadu, Chairman House Committee on Education and Vice Chairman Committee on Environmental Matters and Catherine Ubi, Clerk of the Cross River State House of Assembly.

In the document reviewed by PREMIUM TIMES, the government said its proposal would address the immediate humanitarian needs arising from the disasters while tackling underlying environmental and infrastructure vulnerabilities that have worsened flooding, erosion and landslide risks.

The appeal was presented as the Cross River delegation joins governments, development partners, financial institutions and environmental organisations at COP17 to discuss land restoration, climate resilience and financing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the state’s evidence note prepared for the conference, prolonged heavy rainfall triggered a series of landslides and floods across Calabar and surrounding communities between July and August.

At Ikot Anwatim in Calabar Municipality, the government said a landslide reportedly killed five people, including four children from the same family, while destroying two houses and injuring other residents.

Days later, it said another landslide at Boro Pit/Satellite Town killed a child and destroyed residential property.

According to the report, flooding also affected several communities, including Ekorinim 2 , where an assessment by the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) and the Cross River State Emergency Management Agency (CR-SEMA) found more than five residential buildings affected and over 15 households displaced.

The state also reported that a one-month-old baby was swept away by floodwaters at Elijah Henshaw Street.

By late July, a major mudslide at Diamond Hill near the Calabar Jetty prompted state authorities to warn that the scale of the ecological threat was beyond the capacity of a single institution.

$25m recovery plan

Under the proposed initiative, Cross River is seeking a catalytic $25 million over 36 months.

The state proposed allocating $3 million to humanitarian protection, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and household recovery.

Another $6 million would go to emergency slope stabilisation, critical drainage and erosion-control works, while $4 million would support risk mapping, geotechnical and hydrological studies and early-warning systems.

The plan also proposes $6 million for watershed, forest, riparian, wetland and urban nature-based restoration, $4 million for resilient community infrastructure and livelihood recovery, and $2 million for programme management, safeguards, monitoring and contingency.

The state stressed that the $25 million figure was an advocacy and planning target rather than a final engineering cost, saying it would need to be validated through detailed damage-and-needs assessments and technical investigations.

‘From emergency response to resilience’

Cross River said its proposal was designed to move beyond repeated emergency relief to a broader programme of prevention and restoration.

The initiative has five pillars: protecting vulnerable people, stabilising critical sites, making Calabar and other priority towns flood-resilient, restoring forests and wetlands, and building a risk-informed state.

The state is seeking support for geotechnical investigations of high-risk locations, hydrological and drainage modelling, multi-hazard mapping, satellite and drone-based monitoring, early-warning systems and risk-informed land-use planning.

It also wants restoration of degraded watersheds, riparian buffers, mangroves, wetlands and unstable slopes to be integrated with engineering interventions.

“Cross River is not asking partners to fund repeated emergency clean-up,” the state said in its COP17 appeal. “It is asking for a transition from response to resilience: protect people, repair systems, restore land, reduce exposure and create the institutions that keep risk from rebuilding.”

Why Cross River says the crisis matters

The state argued that its ecological importance makes the crisis relevant not only to Nigeria but also to global restoration efforts.

Cross River is home to more than half of Nigeria’s remaining tropical high forest, according to UN-REDD, and contains lowland rainforest, freshwater swamp forest, mangroves, wetlands and montane ecosystems.

But the state said its ecological assets are under growing pressure, citing a recent sustainable development report which estimated that Cross River lost about 134,000 hectares of tree cover between 2001 and 2023.

It said forest loss and land degradation could reduce watershed and slope resilience, while unplanned development, excavation, blocked drainage and poor waste disposal could intensify local runoff and flooding.

However, the state cautioned against attributing the 2026 disasters solely to climate change.

“Heavy rainfall is an immediate trigger in several reported incidents, but the precise contribution of climate change, soil conditions, slope geometry, land-use change, drainage obstruction and other human pressures cannot be assigned without event-specific hydrometeorological and geotechnical analysis,” the report said.

It added that the documented exposure and vulnerability were sufficient to justify urgent intervention.

Six demands at COP17

The Cross River delegation is asking COP17 partners to recognise the state’s landslide and flood emergency as an urgent land-restoration and human-resilience issue.

It is also seeking a multidisciplinary technical mission involving geotechnical, hydrological, ecological, urban-planning and humanitarian experts to validate priority sites and develop an investable recovery plan.

Other demands include immediate humanitarian and anticipatory-action financing for vulnerable communities, funding for stabilising critical slopes and drainage corridors, establishment of a geospatial risk and early-warning platform, and a multi-year landscape restoration programme.

The state said such investments would help protect its forests, watersheds, wetlands and livelihoods while reducing future flood and erosion risks.

Cross River also proposed a governance structure involving state and federal agencies, local governments, communities, technical experts, humanitarian organisations, women and youth groups and civil society.

It called for public disclosure of project sites, procurement milestones, contractors, disbursements and outputs, alongside independent technical and financial audits.

The state’s appeal comes as COP17 focuses on financing, water, land, people and food systems, under the conference theme “Restoring Land. Restoring Hope.”

For Cross River, officials said, the message is particularly urgent as communities continue to face the consequences of landslides, flooding, erosion and displacement.

“Restore the land. Restore hope. Restore lives,” the state said in its appeal to COP17 delegates.

In an interview with PREMIUM TIMES on the sidelines of COP17 in Mongolia, Mr Achadu said Cross River State is not in COP17 to merely report the problems confronting her people.

“We are here with evidence, experience, ecological assets and a sub-national commitment to develop practical solutions. From London Climate Action Week to Ulaanbaatar, our objective is to transform international climate engagement into restoration, resilience, investment and measurable outcomes for our communities,” he told PREMIUM TIMES.

On her part, Mrs Ubi, said the state government is at COP17 to call for direct investment for proper utilisation of the state’s huge and untapped potentials from amongst the Overseas Private Sector Investment Corporations (OPIC)

World.title: Osun police confirm shooting amid alleged killing of five over garage takeover in Ikire
World.content:
The Osun State Police Command has confirmed that there were shootings around the Naira and Kobo Garage in Ikire, Irewole Local Government Area, amid reports that five people were allegedly killed during a dispute over control of the motorpark.

According to the Facebook posts by Osogbo Updates and Adeleke Youth Development Initiative, the reported victims were said to include three commercial bus drivers and two passersby. However, the police said they were still gathering information before confirming whether there were casualties.

The state police spokesperson, Abiodun Ojelabi, confirmed the shooting to PREMIUM TIMES via a phone call on Tuesday.

“We are still gathering the information as to what is happening there. I can only confirm there were shootings around that area,” Mr Ojelabi said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The reported incident has heightened concerns over the growing political tension in Osun following Governor Ademola Adeleke’s victory in the 15 August governorship election and attempts by his supporters to assert control over APC-led garages and local government secretariats across the state.

What happened in Ikire

The reports about the Ikire incident began circulating on social media, with claims that a confrontation broke out at the Naira and Kobo Garage after some individuals allegedly attempted to take control of the facility.

A report posted by Oshogbo Update claimed that three commercial bus drivers and two passersby were killed during the incident.

The report also alleged that the Divisional Police Officer in Ikire, Olatona Bamidele, went to the garage to clear the road and facilitate access for people described as thugs to take over the garage.

READ ALSO: Police arrest two over death of former world boxing champion Zolani Tete

Although the claims could not be independently verified by PREMIUM TIMES, as Mr Ojelabi said the Command is still investigating the incident and had not established the reported death toll.

The development comes against the backdrop of heightened political competition in Osun, where disputes over control of transport unions and grassroots political structures have continued even after the governorship election.

Disputes are rooted in the prolonged contest over who should control Osun’s transport garages, with major rival political parties, Accord and the All Progressives Congress, laying competing claims to the union leadership.

The post-election developments have therefore raised concerns that the political transition following Mr Adeleke’s re-election could trigger fresh confrontations at the grassroots level.

Mr Adeleke won the governorship election on the Accord Party platform, securing 511,067 votes to defeat his closest challenger, Bola Oyebamiji of the APC, who polled 444,815 votes.

World.title: Lagos Housing Crisis: AAC candidate rejects Hamzat’s advice to young workers
World.content:
The African Action Congress (AAC) governorship candidate in Lagos State, Oluwadamola Sol-Nuyi, has rejected Deputy Governor Obafemi Hamzat’s advice to young workers struggling with high rents to consider living with their parents, relatives or sharing accommodation.

In a statement shared with PREMIUM TIMES on Monday, Mr Sol-Nuyi stated that the advice amounted to an acknowledgement of Lagos’ housing crisis rather than a solution to it.

Mr Hamzat, who is also the governorship candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC), gave the advice during a question-and-answer session on Nigeria Info FM recently.

He was responding to a question about how a 22-year-old earning N100,000 monthly could afford a self-contained apartment or mini-flat reportedly costing about N1 million a year.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Hamzat noted that young workers should choose accommodation they could afford rather than feel pressured to rent apartments beyond their means.

“If I start work as a young person and I’m not married, a lot of us live with our parents. A lot of us live with our cousins,” he said.

He also advised residents not to spend more than 40 per cent of their income on rent, saying they had other expenses such as food, clothing and transportation.

“In fact, if you spend more than 40 per cent of your income on rent, it is too high because you must eat, you must buy clothes, you must do transportation,” Mr Hamzat stated.

The deputy governor also advocated mortgage financing as a way of making home ownership more accessible to residents.

He stressed that Lagos could no longer rely on a system where people were expected to pay the full cost of a house at once.

Mr Hamzat cited a N7 million property as an example, saying a buyer could pay a 10 per cent deposit and spread the balance over 10 years, with the monthly repayment determined by the buyer’s income.

He said the Lagos State Residents Registration Agency (LASRRA) system would also help the government establish residents’ identity, address and place of work when assessing their ability to access housing finance.

But Mr Sol-Nuyi stated that the government should do more than advise residents on how to cope with high rents.

“While responsible personal financial management is important, telling hardworking Lagosians who cannot afford housing to simply move back to their parents or share accommodation is not a housing policy,” he said.

AAC calls for more affordable housing

Mr Sol-Nuyi explained that successive administrations had failed to adequately address the housing needs created by Lagos’ growing population and rapid urban expansion.

He questioned why workers earning legitimate incomes still struggle to find decent accommodation in the city where they work.

“Lagos is an economic powerhouse. It should also be a place where teachers, nurses, engineers, artisans, civil servants, entrepreneurs, security personnel, transport workers and other ordinary residents can afford to live with dignity,” he said.

The AAC candidate noted that housing should be treated as an essential part of economic planning because of its effect on family stability, public health and workers’ productivity.

He promised that his proposed administration would expand affordable and social housing for low- and middle-income households and essential workers.

He also proposed community-based housing schemes involving cooperatives and private developers, improved access to housing finance and investment in infrastructure in underserved communities.

Mr Sol-Nuyi said urban renewal should not result in the destruction of communities without adequate resettlement and compensation.

He also called for greater transparency in land allocation and housing programmes.

Mortgage financing

Lagos State has previously promoted mortgage-based housing schemes, including the Lagos State Home Ownership Mortgage Scheme (LagosHOMS), which allows subscribers to pay for homes over several years.

READ ALSO: Court orders final forfeiture of 52 Lagos housing units adjudged proceeds of crime to FG

Mr Hamzat stated that such arrangements were necessary because many residents could not afford to pay for houses outright.

He also acknowledged that housing affordability was linked to the wider economy, saying residents needed better incomes to cope with the cost of living.

“What is important is we must also build our economy in such a way that people earn better,” he said.

Mr Sol-Nuyi, however, explained that the housing crisis required more direct government intervention, including increased housing supply, infrastructure investment, affordable financing and better urban planning.

He urged Lagos residents to demand clear commitments from political candidates on housing, including specific targets, budgets, locations and delivery timelines.

“Lagos must not merely be a city where people come to work. Lagos must be a city where the people who build, serve and sustain it can afford to live,” he said.

World.title: Lagos govt mourns veteran actor Ogogo
World.content:
The Lagos State Government has mourned the death of veteran actor and cultural icon, Taiwo Hassan, also known as Ogogo.

The state Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture, in a statement issued on Sunday, and posted on the X page of the Lagos State Government described Mr Hassan as a distinguished ambassador of Yoruba heritage whose career contributed significantly to Nigeria’s creative and cultural industry.

The statement signed by the Commissioner for Tourism, Arts and Culture, Toke Benson-Awoyinka, said the actor was not only an entertainer but also a custodian of Yoruba culture and a gifted storyteller who used his career to promote the heritage.

“Taiwo Hassan was more than an actor. He was a custodian of culture, a gifted storyteller, and a proud ambassador of Yoruba heritage,” the commissioner said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to her, Mr Hassan’s work on stage and screen helped preserve Yoruba cultural values while entertaining generations of Nigerians.

Mrs Benson-Awoyinka said the actor’s contributions helped shape the cultural landscape of Lagos State and Nigeria, adding that his legacy would continue to inspire future generations.

The ministry extended its condolences to Mr Hassan’s family, friends, colleagues and members of the Nollywood and wider creative arts community.

She prayed for the repose of the actor’s soul and for strength for his family, friends, colleagues and other loved ones to cope with the loss.

“His departure is a great loss to the creative and cultural community.

“We pray that Almighty God grants his soul eternal rest and gives his family, friends, colleagues, and loved ones the strength and fortitude to bear this irreplaceable loss,” Mrs Benson-Awoyinka said.

Ogogo

Ogogo died on Sunday, 23 August, at the age of 66 after battling stage-four cancer. His daughter, Kira Taiwo, confirmed his death during an emotional social media broadcast, while veteran actor Jide Kosoko also confirmed the development and announced arrangements for his burial in Ilaro, Ogun State.

The actor’s death came days after his family disclosed his cancer diagnosis and sought assistance for his treatment. His remains were subsequently taken to Ilaro, where burial rites were scheduled for Monday, 24 August.

Born on 31 October, 1959 in Ilaro, Mr Hassan trained as an automobile mechanic before venturing into acting. He began acting in 1981 while working at the Lagos State Water Corporation and eventually left government employment in 1994 to pursue acting full-time.

His transition from mechanic to actor marked the beginning of a career that lasted more than four decades. He became a prominent figure in Yoruba-language cinema, working not only as an actor but also as a producer, director and screenwriter.

Mr Hassan featured in several Yoruba and English-language productions, including Owo Blow, Omo Ghetto, Aníkúlápó, Aníkúlápó: Rise of the Spectre and Tenant of the House. His long career and distinctive presence made him one of the recognisable figures in Nigeria’s Yoruba film industry.

His death has since drawn tributes from colleagues and others in the entertainment industry, with burial activities taking place in his hometown of Ilaro.

World.title: INTERVIEW: How my role on UN panel on nuclear war effects can benefit Nigeria – Prof Rabia Sa’id
World.content:
Rabia Sa’id, a professor of physics at Bayero University, Kano (BUK), was appointed last year by the United Nations Secretary-General to a 21-member scientific panel studying the physical effects and societal impacts of nuclear war.

Established under UN General Assembly Resolution 79/238, the panel of some of the world’s premier scientists is evaluating existential global nuclear threats. It is scheduled to present its findings later this year. The findings are expected to inform international policy on nuclear risk reduction, global security, and humanitarian protection.

Professor Sa’id, from Kano State, is one of the first two female lecturers in BUK’s Department of Physics. Her strides have inspired young women across Nigeria to pursue careers in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM).

Beyond her foundational contributions to atmospheric, space weather, electronics, and particle physics, Mrs Sa’id is widely recognised for applying scientific solutions to real-world environmental challenges. Her notable achievements include developing eco-friendly fuel briquettes, reducing rural reliance on firewood, and combating regional deforestation, and leading pioneering, low-cost air quality monitoring initiatives that combine ground sensor data with satellite observations to enhance local climate tracking.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In this exclusive interview with PREMIUM TIMES’ Ahmadu Maishanu in Kano, Sa’id speaks on her appointment, how Nigeria can leverage the opportunity it presents, and what the country stands to gain from the panel’s work.

Excerpts:

PREMIUM TIMES: What does your presence on this global panel signify for Nigeria’s standing in international science and global diplomacy?

Professor Rabia: Nigeria plays a key role as a voice within the United Nations. Also, Nigeria routinely pushes for UN Security Council reforms to secure permanent representation for African nations and to contribute to policies that ensure world peace; it is a signatory to the Agreement on the Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy and to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. I believe that even though I am on the panel in my individual capacity, it should still be positive for Nigeria’s standing in international science and global diplomacy

PREMIUM TIMES: How can your role on this panel benefit local scientific research, climate action, and policy development back home in Nigeria?

Professor Rabia: There is so much that I have learnt since the start of the panel work. I am an atmospheric physicist and climate action advocate, with expertise in nuclear nonproliferation. Being in the circle of eminent scientists across various fields related to nuclear impacts on climate, food sources, human health, agriculture, etc., provides valuable insights we can use to mitigate environmental impacts locally.

PREMIUM TIMES: Through your appointment as one of the pioneer female academics at BUK’s Department of Physics, you broke institutional gender barriers. What message does this UN appointment send to young women across Northern Nigeria and the rest of the nation?

I have always been a strong advocate for women’s participation in science careers, and I have demonstrated this through career talks in secondary schools across Kano and extended to other states in Nigeria. The message that this UN appointment sends to young women is that if they work hard and become visible, their work and expertise will speak for them, and they will not need to lobby.

PREMIUM TIMES: Women remain underrepresented in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics disciplines across Africa. How can this global platform bolster women’s inclusion in science?

Professor Rabia: The UN panel provides a platform for experts to meet across various scientific fields. One can interact, exchange contact information, and share ideas. It becomes a networking platform that one can leverage to connect with other women working in the same field in Nigeria. For example, my contact with the panel’s experts provides a platform to leverage for my students’ benefit. Reaching out to these experts is much easier now because we met in person, and they saw my capabilities firsthand. It serves as an excellent platform for collaboration, bolstering women’s empowerment, and driving other key benefits.

PREMIUM TIMES: How can Nigeria benefit from this global platform?

Professor Rabia: The primary work of this panel is anticipatory. While the UN always strives for peace, we must acknowledge that the threat of conflict remains real. In the event of a war, the panel’s main duty is to evaluate the potential consequences of a nuclear exchange. When Hiroshima and Nagasaki occurred during World War II, the world was caught unprepared. Today, given rising global geopolitical tensions, we must ask: if a nuclear conflict were to happen, what specific impacts should we expect? Unless we accurately predict these outcomes, we cannot properly prepare for them. This necessity prompted New Zealand to advance the initiative, resulting in the adoption of UN Resolution 79/238 to investigate these scientific impacts.

Although Nigeria does not possess nuclear weapons, it is a key signatory to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), and the findings of this investigation will benefit our nation. Nigeria can pursue nuclear energy to secure a stable electricity supply. Nuclear power provides a reliable, clean energy solution that aligns with global environmental protection goals, which is why many nations rely on it today. Critics in Nigeria often argue that a weak safety culture could lead to disaster. However, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) enforces rigorous global safeguards designed specifically to prevent operational failures. The scientific research from this UN panel will directly inform and strengthen Nigeria’s own safety protocols for future nuclear infrastructure.

We already have a track record of safe operation. The Centre for Energy Research and Training at Ahmadu Bello University (ABU) in Zaria has safely operated a miniature neutron-source research reactor for years without incident. This proves that Nigeria possesses the capability to manage nuclear technology responsibly. Public anxiety surrounding nuclear power is understandable and surmountable; the fear stems largely from a lack of awareness. Nothing in life is to be feared; it is only to be understood. The technical safeguards available today ensure that nuclear power can be operated even more safely than our current energy infrastructure.

PREMIUM TIMES: Could you please share your experience so far and how you were nominated for the appointment?

Professor Rabia: Because of the network of scientists I have on different platforms and the visibility I have already built, I happened to be on the mailing list of some of these organisations. I received a notification for a call for nominations. Usually, such an opportunity comes with the requirement that you are nominated either by your institution or by the government of your home country. Most of the times, I shy away a little because I have tried on several occasions and found that the government or the institution already has its own candidate to nominate, making it very difficult.

However, in the case of this nomination for the UN Panel, your government can nominate you, your institution can nominate you, an expert can nominate you, or you can self-nominate. Knowing all the difficulties one can face when seeking a government or institutional nomination, I decided to self-nominate. I submitted the self-nomination form with all the required information. I was not very confident because I thought many institutions within Nigeria might have nominated other people, given that it is a high-level expert panel. I didn’t think I was going to make it, but I told myself that everything is worth trying.

Sincerely, I almost even forgot I had sent the nomination form, though I knew I beat the deadline, which was November 2024.

I didn’t hear anything until July 1, 2025. In fact, it was someone else who saw the UN press release and noticed my name among the 21-member panel selected for appointment by the United Nations Secretary-General, António Guterres, to study the effects of nuclear wars. That person sent it to me on WhatsApp. I opened it and thanked God Almighty for the opportunity.

After that, I looked at the names of the other experts on the panel, and it was unbelievable. There was the Deputy Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency, directors who have been with the World Health Organisation, agricultural scientists, and many other prominent scientists whose papers I had read but never expected to meet. I was really excited; at one point, I kept looking at the list to make sure it was actually my name (laughter). Finally, I realised that it was indeed me, and I had truly been selected. I then contacted the UN Nigeria House Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Nigeria, Mohamed Malik Fall, who responded to my message informing him of my appointment and hosted me at UN Nigeria House.

Panel activities began last December following its inauguration at UN Headquarters in New York. Since then, the panel has convened virtually on several occasions and held an in-person meeting in Vienna, Austria, in March. The next meeting is scheduled for Geneva, Switzerland, in September, alongside several consultations with regional stakeholders, ahead of the final report’s submission to the UN General Assembly in 2027.

World.title: Fidelity Bank gets extension to publish H1 2026 audited results
World.content:
Fidelity Bank Plc has announced a potential delay in the publication of its audited financial statements for the half-year ended 30 June, after securing an extension from the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX).

The lender said it secured an extension from NGX Group to 30 September to publish its half-year financial statements, according to a regulatory filing by its Company Secretary, Ezinwa Unuigboje, on Monday.

Fidelity Bank said the extension became necessary because the audit of its H1 2026 financial statements is still being finalised.

According to the bank, upon completion of the audit, the financial statements will be presented to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) for approval before publication in line with the NGX Rulebook and other applicable regulations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The financial institution said it obtained the NGX’s approval for the extension, subject to receiving regulatory approval from the CBN for the H1 2026 audited accounts.

“Premised on the foregoing, the approval of the NGX was obtained for an extension of time to September 30, 2026, subject to receipt of regulatory approval from the CBN for the H1 2026 audited accounts,” the lender said.

Meanwhile, Fidelity Bank said the trading window for its insiders and connected persons remains closed.

The bank said the trading restriction will remain in place until 24 hours after the publication of its half-year audited financial statements.

For Nigerian listed companies whose financial year ends on 31 December, H1 results covering January to June must be filed with NGX by the applicable half-year reporting deadline, subject to regulatory requirements for banks.

Fidelity Bank, one of the leading Nigerian financial institutions, reported gross earnings growth of 45.6 per cent from N1.04 trillion in 2024 to N1.52 trillion in audited financial results for the year ended 31 December 2025.

The growth reflected stronger topline momentum across core business segments of the financial institution.

It also recorded a profit after tax (PAT) of N242.4 billion, which was underpinned by a 38.7 per cent year-on-year increase in interest income of the lender.
