A 23-year-old pilot’s courage in safely ditching her twin-engine Piper in the Atlantic Ocean off Boca Raton, Fla., this weekend was matched by her calm humility in a statement thanking others rather than her own heroism.

"During the descent, my primary focus was ensuring the safety of everyone around me," Faith Tenkley, 23, said in a statement to Fox News. "I was able to navigate toward open water, successfully avoiding all nearby buildings, paddleboarders and swimmers (as well as individuals using metal detectors)."

Viral video shared on social media showed the unusual and markedly smooth water landing Saturday morning as onlookers gasped; yet, video showed a man with a metal detector keenly focused on his beach treasure hunt as the stunning events unfolded around him.

FDNY DEPLOYS 140+ PERSONNEL TO JFK AFTER DELTA FLIGHT REPORTED WITH FLAT TIRES ON APPROACH TO LANDING

Tenkley, meanwhile, was dodging buildings and a busy beach while trying to find a safe way to land a crippled aircraft.

"I want to express my deepest gratitude for the concern and support following my unexpected water landing yesterday," her Sunday statement began. "I am incredibly fortunate and relieved to share that I was able to swim away from this incident.

"After deciding a landing at Boca Raton Airport was not the safest option I continued to the coast."

Cleared by air traffic control (ATC) to land on a runway, her landing gear was malfunctioning, leaving her concerned about a hard landing with a plane still full of fuel.

FAA UNVEILS NEW AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLER HIRING PLAN AFTER CHIEF WARNED SYSTEM WAS ‘CHRONICALLY UNDERSTAFFED’

"I want to extend my thanks to ATC for being prepared, as well as the lifeguards, firefighters and the police officers whose rapid response and professionalism ensured everyone's safety – as well as any witnesses who called for help," her statement concluded. "Thank you all for your kind messages."

Tenkley, who has been flying for four years, was the only person aboard her family’s twin-engine Piper PA-30 when it developed mechanical trouble Saturday on a flight from Page Field in Fort Myers, Florida, to Bimini in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

She was flying to the Bahamas to pick up her parents when the trouble began about 15 miles west of Boca Raton. She initially planned to divert to Boca Raton Airport before the plane’s landing gear malfunctioned and its right engine failed.

ARGENTINIAN FLIGHT INSTRUCTOR JUMPS TO DEATH FROM PLANE, 22-YEAR-OLD STUDENT FORCED TO LAND ALONE

As she approached the coast, Tenkley guided the disabled plane to the open stretch of water just offshore.

Video captured by a beachgoer shows the aircraft descending low over the busy Boca Raton beach before gently landing on the ocean’s surface. The Piper remained largely intact as Tenkley, wearing a bikini, swam away from the aircraft with the help of a lifeguard who arrived in moments to assist.

PILOT DECLARES MAYDAY BEFORE SEAPLANE COMES DOWN IN NEW YORK CITY’S EAST RIVER

A Boca Raton Ocean Rescue fire boat arrived shortly afterward. She was taken to a hospital as a precaution and was not reported injured.

World.title: Browns pick Deshaun Watson as their starting QB despite home crowd booing and his '17 away games' comments
World.content:
It's going to be Deshaun Watson as the starting quarterback for the Cleveland Browns to open the NFL regular season, which means one thing: Get your popcorn ready because this should be entertaining.

No, not entertaining in the typical star-player-doing-amazing-things kind of way.

Entertaining in the cinema drama kind of way because what we have here is the NFL equivalent of a villain being given the opportunity to redeem himself and then deciding – by his actions – if he continues to be reviled based on what happens next.

DESHAUN WATSON BOOED BY BROWNS FANS, FIRES BACK AFTER POOR OUTING OPENS DOOR FOR SHEDEUR SANDERS

What happened Sunday evening is Browns coach Todd Monken and general manager Andrew Berry picked Watson to be their starter over Shedeur Sanders, to culminate a competition that spanned the entire offseason and into the first two preseason games.

That decision was announced to the players on Monday morning.

And now we see the next chapter of what has been the tremendously disappointing story of Watson in Cleveland. It's a story that has compounded on-field failure, Personal Conduct Policy suspension, and one injury after another the last three years.

It's a story that seemed to have a climax on Saturday when Watson was booed lustily by Browns fans – at home at Huntington Bank Field – from the moment he entered the game in the second half pretty much until the game was over.

DESHAUN WATSON'S FIRST GAME SINCE 2024 A SUCCESS BECAUSE HE WASN'T AS BAD AS SHEDEUR SANDERS OR DILLON GABRIEL

And then Watson conducted a viral press conference in which he called what Browns fans did "personal," and "disrespectful," making it seem possible that his time with the team was about to end because how does an NFL team keep a QB that gets booed at home?

Watson, indeed said, he would be playing "17 away games" if he won the starting job.

But these are the Browns, folks.

They do Browns things.

A source confirmed to OutKick the Browns did not take Watson's words into account when deciding on him as the starter.

They obviously also didn't take the booing into account.

They picked Watson over Sanders because, well, Watson is more experienced. He's more ready to face what NFL defenses will show the Browns once the season begins. A source said he was also slightly better than Sanders throughout the competition, the Saturday preseason meltdown notwithstanding.

Sanders, who had a higher completion percentage than Watson but threw one more interception, had better stay ready.

That was the coaching staff's message to the son of Pro Football Hall of Famer Deion Sanders.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Watson, you see, has been named the starter for the regular-season opener. But not for the season.

The Browns have made no guarantees to him if he plays poorly. If that happens, the team reserves the right to pivot to Sanders.

Watson has thrown 19 TD passes in his 19 games with the team, which is nowhere near what the Browns expected when they traded away six draft picks, including three first-rounders, to the Houston Texans, then signed him to a $230 million contract.

Watson has a chance to finally reward that investment to start the 2026 season. It's a small window of opportunity, but it beats the alternative for him, which was getting cut outright.

So we shall see what happens next starting with the Browns' regular-season opener, a road game at the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sept. 13.

Get your popcorn.

World.title: Alaska Senate race’s absurd name problem gets even harder to untangle
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former Anchorage Mayor Dan Sullivan is taking sides in Alaska’s unusual same-name Senate fight, endorsing incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan over a third Dan Sullivan, whose candidacy has already triggered legal challenges and allegations of an effort to confuse voters.

The intervention from Dan A. Sullivan adds another twist to a potentially competitive race in which Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and his Republican allies have accused teacher Dan J. Sullivan of running as a GOP candidate to siphon votes from the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has denied those accusations and says he is a legitimate moderate Republican challenger.

"As the OG Dan Sullivan, I urge Alaskans to vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. He’s been great for Alaska," the former mayor wrote on social media.

DAN SULLIVAN ACCUSES SAME-NAME CHALLENGER OF TRYING TO 'RIG' ALASKA SENATE RACE

Republicans have attempted to use legal mechanisms to remove Dan J. Sullivan, who is himself running as a Republican, from the ballot. They point to the fact that he has worked with a Democratic-aligned consultant as evidence that he is part of a liberal plot to mislead voters.

Dan J. Sullivan has defended himself from the accusations by arguing that he is genuinely a moderate Republican that has real dissatisfactions with Dan S. Sullivan’s representation of the state.

It is unclear how many Dan Sullivans live in Alaska.

Alaska has a unique electoral system, something Republicans have argued could further contribute to confusion when voters head to the polls in November.

GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING

The state holds a nonpartisan primary where the top four vote-getters advance to the general election regardless of their party affiliation. Once the four candidates are chosen and Election Day arrives, Alaskans use ranked-choice voting.

Under the system, voters rank candidates in order of preference. When their first choice is eliminated, their support passes to their next choice and so on until one candidate is victorious.

Advocates of the system argue that it gives voters greater control over who ultimately wins office as well as more options to choose from. Critics, meanwhile, argue the system could cause confusion in November.

Dan S. Sullivan and Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola have advanced to the general election, though it is unclear whether Dan J. Sullivan will join them as votes are still being counted, according to the Associated Press.

JUDGE RULES REPUBLICAN WITH SAME NAME AS SEN DAN SULLIVAN CAN STAY ON ALASKA PRIMARY BALLOT

Following a Republican legal challenge, the Alaska Supreme Court held last month that Dan J. Sullivan could remain on the ballot after he was initially removed by the state’s Division of Elections. Now, federal and state prosecutors are reportedly investigating whether he is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters.

The Sullivan campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

World.title: Why Wyndham Clark deserves PGA Tour Player of the Year, LIV Golf's final hoorah, and Scottie Scheffler's money
World.content:
Wyndham Clark picked up his third win of 2026 on Sunday after flipping a switch down the stretch at the BMW Championship and fending off Rory McIlroy. With the victory, the PGA Tour Player of the Year debate has become a legitimate one for the first time in four years.

With the POY chatter at full volume, it's worth mentioning that two things can be true at once: being the best player on the planet doesn't make you the player of the year, and being the player of the year doesn't mean you're the best player on the planet. We'll get more in-depth on that down below, but spoiler: I think Clark has done plenty to end Scottie Scheffler's four-year streak of taking home POY honors.

While Clark was out playing McIlroy at Bellerive Country Club - a major championship venue - Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau, and Michael La Sasso were battling at LIV Golf Indianapolis at The Club at Chatham Hills, a non-major championship venue. The potentially final chapter of LIV's story being closed out with La Sasso besting the two biggest LIV stars was certainly a scene.

Welcome to Par Talk, a weekly read to get you caught up on all the happenings that took place in professional golf that you need to know. You can follow Mark on X @itismarkharris and email him at mark.harris@outkick.com .

Wyndham Clark is the PGA Tour Player of the Year, for now

The PGA Tour Player of the Year award isn't all that significant in the grand scheme of things. Approximately 99.9% of the golf world won't look back in five years and be able to name the player who took home the honors in 2026, yet that same crowd would be able to tell you who won the Masters 30 years ago.

The POY award does, however, create debate and discussion, two things we humans in sports love more than anything; therefore, we have to get into it.

Scottie Scheffler is the best golfer in the world. Nobody in their right mind would debate that statement, but that doesn't mean that he's put together the best year, and after his win at the BMW on Sunday, Clark is the one who (currently) owns that title.

Scottie Scheffler's 2026 highlights: Two wins, The American Express and the FedEx St. Jude Championship (by eight strokes), five second-place finishes, 12 total top-five finishes, lowest scoring average on the PGA Tour, zero major championship victories.

Wyndham Clark's 2026 highlights: Three wins, the CJ Cup, the U.S. Open, and the BMW Championship, six top-five finishes, one major championship victory.

Scheffler has had an incredibly strong and lucrative campaign, but Clark has him beat in the two categories we care about the most: total wins and major championships. While we can acknowledge that Scheffler's five runner-up finishes bolster his season resume, we can also admit that, even as a collective, they don't carry enough weight to trump Clark's extra victory.

If you want to play the game that Clark and Scheffler are neck-and-neck in the Player of the Year race ahead of the Tour Championship, that's perfectly fine, but only one player can win the award, and the one who hoisted a trophy at a major championship should win the theoretical tiebreaker.

LIV GOLF CEO SAYS LEAGUE IS HOPEFUL IT CAN 'DO RIGHT BY' VENDORS SUING THEM OVER ALLEGED MISSED PAYMENTS

Speaking of the Tour Championship, if Clark gets the job done in Atlanta to win back-to-back Playoff events, he would slam the door shut on the POY debate. If Scheffler, the odds-on favorite, finds the winner's circle, then we get to go through this exercise this same time next week. I'll be here.

As for Sunday's final round at the BMW Championship, it was a pillow fight between Clark and McIlroy, with Wyndham giving his five-shot lead away and looking completely out of sorts on the opening nine holes. McIlroy didn't earn any momentum really; he was more so handed it, but never grabbed hold of it.

Clark carded three consecutive birdies to close out Sunday's round to earn a three-shot victory. We'd be lying if we said it was overly exciting, but a three-shot win in a FedEx Cup Playoff event playing alongside career Grand Slam winner and fan favorite in McIlroy will always fall into the noteworthy category.

After securing his victory at Bellerive, Clark spoke about how he's one of the best players in the world. That confidence is understandably back, and he's absolutely correct in his assessment of being one of the best in the game today.

Scottie Scheffler is mega rich

While Scheffler finished T-12 and 10 shots back of Clark at the BMW, that's not to say he didn't have a uniquely impressive week.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Following Sunday's action, he revealed he had been dealing with hand, foot, and mouth disease. Any parent to young children can attest that HFM is nasty, incredibly contagious stuff, especially if adults contract it, as it causes blisters in all three areas. Having blister-covered hands and feet while trying to play golf at the highest level seems both miserable and impossible, yet Scheffler shot four-under over the weekend to climb up the leaderboard.

With his T-12 finish at the BMW, Scheffler has earned just under $21 million this season, which is a crazy number given he's 'only' won twice. What's even more eye-opening is that the No. 2 player on this year's money list, Cameron Young, has earned $6.5 million less than Scheffler.

LIV Golf doesn't get its ideal ending

LIV Golf apparently has an investor in place to push the league into 2027. The emphasis on the word 'apparently' seems to be growing by the day, as only time will tell whether LIV Golf '2.0' will become a reality.

Speaking of reality, there is one where LIV Golf Indianapolis was the last LIV event the golf world ever saw. It will almost certainly be the last LIV event we see in its current form, with ginormous purses and a leaderboard with some of the game's biggest names involved.

Sunday's finish in Indianapolis was unique, with Michael La Sasso besting Jon Rahm by one shot and Bryson DeChambeau by two, but it also serves as a perfect microcosm of LIV's non-existent luster.

FRUSTRATED BUBBA WATSON CONFRONTS UNRULY FAN AT LIV GOLF INDIANAPOLIS IN INTENSE SCENE

A 22-year-old former NCAA champion from Ole Miss beating two of the best players in the world should create some sort of buzz, yet given the circumstances of the complete unknown and the fact that LIV has been on its final leg for months now, it's done virtually nothing.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The fact of the matter that will rile up the LIV Golf truthers is that if the same scenario unfolded on the PGA Tour, on a golf course people have at least heard of before, it would have been headline-worthy, at the very least.

Maybe it's oversaturation, maybe it's the fact that sports fans can only pay attention to so much. Perhaps it's the players involved or the Saudi's past-funding of the league that remains to be the biggest hold-up of interest.

I think it's more than fair to say it's a combo of all of the above, but it will be fascinating to see what unfolds with the league, and more so its players, in the coming months.

World.title: Washington Post ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after being terminated over Charlie Kirk posts
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Washington Post was ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after she was fired last year for social media posts she made after Charlie Kirk's assassination.

Sarah Miller Espinosa, the arbitrator overseeing Attiah's legal challenge against The Post, said the paper "did not have good and sufficient cause" and that it "violated" her labor agreement, according to The New York Times, which first reported on Espinosa's ruling last Thursday.

"The Washington Post failed to establish the grievant engaged in gross misconduct," Espinosa concluded.

TEACHERS WHO CELEBRATED CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION NOW CASH IN WITH TAXPAYER-FUNDED SETTLEMENTS

Attiah told The Times she is "relieved to finally have that record set straight," adding, "This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion writer, and this was wrongful termination."

The columnist announced her legal victory, saying on X, "The Washington Post fired me last year for speaking the truth after Charlie Kirk's killing. I fought back. I'm happy to announce: I won my case against the Washington Post. They have been ordered to reinstate me immediately."

A spokesperson for The Washington Post said the paper respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further. Attiah didn't immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Fox News Digital reached out to Talking Points USA for comment.

Attiah sparked outrage for her posts about the slain conservative icon on the liberal social media platform Bluesky.

TENNESSEE UNIVERSITY TO PAY PROFESSOR $1.9M AFTER CALLING CHARLIE KIRK A 'DISGUSTING PSYCHOPATH'

GEORGIA TEACHER RECEIVES ALMOST $300K SETTLEMENT OVER CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION POST

"Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a White man that espoused violence is… not the same as violence," Attiah wrote at the time. In a separate post, she wrote, "Part of what keeps America so violent is the insistence that people perform care, empty goodness and absolution for White men who espouse hatred and violence.’"

Critics also slammed Attiah for misquoting Kirk in another post, attributing to him saying, "Black women do not have the brain processing power to be taken seriously. You have to go steal a White person's slot."

On a July 2023 episode of "The Charlie Kirk Show," Kirk actually said, "If we would have said three weeks ago [...] that Joy Reid and Michelle Obama, and Sheila Jackson Lee, and Ketanji Brown Jackson were affirmative-action picks, we would have been called racist. But now they're comin' out and they're saying it for us! They're comin' out, and they're saying, 'I'm only here because of affirmative action.' Yeah, we know. You do not have the brain processing power to otherwise be taken really seriously. You had to go steal a White person's slot to go be taken somewhat seriously."

Following the backlash, Attiah revealed she had been fired by The Post, saying in a termination letter her posts were "unacceptable" and "gross misconduct."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Attiah filed a legal challenge against The Post over her termination last fall, and previously announced in June that she and the paper would enter arbitration.

Arizona authorities have arrested a man in connection with a home invasion shooting that killed a Tucson police recruit and left his fiancée hospitalized.

Carlos Ramirez, 23, was shot dead at his home in southwestern Tucson early Wednesday morning, according to the Pima County Sheriff's Department (PCSD). He was expected to graduate from the police academy on Aug. 27 and had previously worked for PCSD as a corrections officer. His 23-year-old fiancée, whose name has not been released, also works as a corrections officer in the department.

Deputies arrested Santiago Jorge Rogers, 39, at a hotel on South Palo Verde Road in Tucson on Saturday morning, the sheriff said in a statement. He is being held without bond at the county jail.

SUSPECTS AT LARGE AFTER TUCSON POLICE RECRUIT KILLED, PIMA COUNTY CORRECTIONS OFFICER WOUNDED IN SHOOTING

Hours later, surveillance video taken from a parking lot shows a third man parking the suspect vehicle, a gray Acura MDX SUV, and walking away.

World.title: John Candy's family calls out Hollywood for weight criticism the actor endured throughout his career
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

John Candy's family is calling out Hollywood for how their father was treated.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital at Televerse 26, the late actor's daughter, Jennifer Candy-Sullivan, and her mother, Rosemary Candy, slammed Hollywood for the way their father's weight was discussed during his fame.

"I think everyone who had some sort of difference was kind of put under a magnifying glass. So for him, it was his weight. And he kind of... he took it like a gentleman," Jennifer said. "And I think as his career went on, he was able to be more comfortable with himself and kind of vocalize and speak up for himself."

She went on to say that because of his career, people "thought he was the everyday guy and everyone loved him" so it would be okay to "pal around" and "joke around him," but that "in reality, it wasn't that okay. It's not cool."

JACK OSBOURNE FIRES BACK AT BODY SHAMERS CALLING HIM 'GROSSLY UNDERWEIGHT'

Rosemary noted that "he was able to handle it really well," but that it was still "upsetting" and "a challenge" he was dealing with early in his career, "from the beginning when I met him."

WATCH: John Candy’s daughter says actor ‘took it like a gentleman’ when Hollywood focused on his weight

Jennifer doesn't think the public or the media would be any less harsh on her father if his rise to fame occurred today, saying, "I think there would be a different type of kind of critique to him."

"I think if he tried losing weight, then it would be like, 'You're too skinny, you're no longer funny.' So I think Hollywood would find something," she said. "It would be... he doesn't... he would do something wrong. Ultimately, I think anyone in Hollywood does something wrong."

The two attended a special FYC presentation of the documentary about the comedian, "John Candy: I Like Me," as part of Televerse 26, the Television Academy festival.

The film, which originally premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in September 2025, was directed by Colin Hanks, and features interviews from many of his former co-stars, including Steve Martin, Macaulay Culkin, Bill Murray, Catherine O'Hara, Martin Short and others.

WATCH: John Candy’s daughter says Hollywood would have criticized him even if he lost weight: ‘You’re too skinny’

"When we would see John on the screen, we felt like he was one of the most relatable people," Hanks said. "And I think in working on the film and talking with people and learning more about John's past, I just felt like we didn't even understand just how relatable he was."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

He explained that talking "about things like mental health and therapy" has only become popular in recent years and "wasn't something that was discussed back then." With today's lenses on, "John was even more like one of us than we even realize."

WATCH: John Candy's daughter got to see a vulnerable side of her father in the documentary 'John Candy: I Like Me'

Hanks wasn't the only one who learned something new about the "Planes, Trains and Automobiles" actor.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I think for us, it was to see his vulnerability with those interviews. He was really good about keeping his business at work, and then family life was family life. So he tried not to bring it into the house," Jennifer said. "My mom probably understood it more because they would have conversations about it, obviously. But for us, we didn't really see it. So I think to see that on camera on the big screen was challenging."

John rose to fame as a member of the sketch comedy show, "Second City Television," on which he also worked as a writer. His writing on the show earned him two Emmy Awards.

World.title: Father of sailor aboard USS Lincoln detained by immigration authorities, family says
World.content:
The immigrant father of a sailor on board the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln was detained Saturday by immigration officials, family members said.

Luis Manuel Aviles, originally from Nicaragua, was detained shortly after 11 a.m. ET in Key West, Florida, where he lives, stepdaughter Katty Delgado told NBC News on Saturday evening.

She said that Aviles has been in the U.S. for roughly 20 years and that she has no knowledge of an arrest history or criminal allegations against him.

“He’s doing everything the right way,” she said.

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Sunday that the Border Patrol arrested Aviles during a traffic stop in Key West. The agency said Aviles entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location and would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

“We are simply enforcing the laws passed by Congress. This Administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce,” a DHS spokesperson said.

Delgado said she learned the news from family members, including Aviles’ wife and his son Joshua Aviles, who posted a note about the detention on Facebook. Her stepfather, Delgado said, was arrested near a Publix supermarket as he was headed to a mechanic.

Luis Manuel Aviles and his son Joshua Aviles. Katty Delgado

Joshua Aviles said on Facebook that he’s on board the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which is on its way back to the U.S. after its prolonged stretch at sea, including its deployment to the Middle East to engage in the war with Iran.

“I’ve been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything,” he wrote Saturday.

He said that his father is hard-working, giving and humble and that he has a work permit, a Social Security card and a driver’s license.

“This is heartbreaking for me,” Joshua Aviles said. “I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal.”

Asked to confirm whether Luis Manuel Aviles had a Social Security number, a work permit or pending immigration cases, as his family indicated, DHS told Telemundo, NBCUniversal’s Spanish-language network, that “work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States.”

The Lincoln left its home port of San Diego on Nov. 25, and, with more than eight months since it visited a port in December, it broke the Navy record for time without a port call. Relatives of sailors on board the carrier have described reports of deteriorating conditions and morale. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said claims about the situation on board have been “completely misrepresented.”

The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln has officially left the Middle East en route to the West Coast, a journey that could take a month or more.

Joshua Aviles, who told NBC News he has limited internet access, wrote on Facebook that he’s doing everything he can to get his father released from detention.

“I love you with all my heart. Please stay strong. I’m coming home, Dad,” he wrote.

President Donald Trump has stood by his administration’s immigration crackdown, including ICE’s expanded enforcement and arrests, which in recent months have included the arrests of children and spouses of service members, a San Diego Padres minor-league catching coordinator and a grandmother from India who’s a schoolteacher with a green card.

Immigration authorities have detained more than 50 parents and spouses of service members during Trump’s second term, according to a recent Associated Press investigation. There has been backlash to the detentions, which come despite programs for military members that can sometimes offer immediate family protection from deportation.

The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services website says those “discretionary options” are offered on a “case-by-case basis.”

It was not immediately clear whether Luis Manuel Aviles was in the program.

The DHS spokesperson said in a statement Sunday that “having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws.”

“Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” the spokesperson said.

Delgado lamented that her stepbrother has spent nine months out at sea, without seeing his family, “and this is what his father gets.”

World.title: Trump hits back at Carney, threatens to hike auto, truck, metals tariffs to 50%
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Monday hit back at Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who on Friday had announced he would retaliate against any new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods.

Writing on Truth Social, Trump threatened to hit imported cars, trucks, automobile parts and steel with 50% tariffs starting Jan. 1, 2027.

“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote. “On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with.”

Canada ranks as the third-highest source of U.S. imports. In 2025, more than $380 billion worth of goods were brought over the border, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.

Monday’s escalation follows a wave of new tariffs that hit Canada early Saturday after weekslong negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down.

Carney pulled Canadian negotiators out of those talks late Friday after he said the U.S. “proposed new terms that were uneconomic” and “unfair.”

Those 50% duties, which came into effect at 12:01 a.m. ET Saturday, ensnared a wide swath of Canadian goods, from hockey sticks to building materials.

“We cannot control the storm blowing in from Washington,” Carney said Saturday. “Canada will match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Moments before Trump’s social media post, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer tried to publicly downplay the impact of the tariffs that hit Saturday morning.

“I think the markets understand that this affects a very small amount of trade,” Greer told CNBC. He added that he would not use the term “trade war” to define Saturday’s tariffs.

In Carney’s view, however, Canada has been attacked by the United States, which for decades has been one of its closest partners and allies.

“You’re at war when you get attacked,” Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Saturday. “We got attacked.”

Carney noted that Canada had waited to retaliate “until the United States decided to actually implement these so-called [Section] 338 tariffs.”

On Sunday, Bloomberg News reported that Carney was designing Canada’s retaliation measures to remain in place for the duration of Trump’s term as president, if necessary.

In his Monday post, Trump did not specify whether automobiles and parts that are compliant with the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade pact would continue to be exempt from additional tariffs. Canadian-made vehicles that do not meet USMCA requirements currently face a 25% U.S. tariff.

Steel imported from Canada currently faces a U.S. tariff of 50%. It was not clear Monday whether Trump’s announcement meant that the tariff would rise to 100%.

If fully implemented, the increased tariffs on autos and parts could be the most disruptive for consumers and automakers.

The U.S., Canada and Mexico have a deeply integrated auto supply chain and manufacturing process. Vehicles often cross borders multiple times before they are fully assembled and sent to dealerships.

Trump’s latest waves of tariffs could also spell further doom for the USMCA trade deal, which Trump negotiated and signed during his first term after ripping up the 1992 North American Free Trade Agreement, or NAFTA.

On July 1, the Trump administration announced that it was not going to renew the USMCA in its current form, plunging it into uncertainty with a series of rolling annual reviews and negotiations.

World.title: Dan Sullivan endorses Dan Sullivan to beat Dan Sullivan in perplexing Alaska Senate race
World.content:
A new Dan Sullivan has entered the conversation surrounding the Alaska Senate race, in which incumbent Dan S. Sullivan faces a candidate with the same name.

The Republican former mayor of Anchorage, Dan A. Sullivan, endorsed GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan for re-election over retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola on Tuesday.

“As the OG Dan Sullivan, I urge Alaskans to vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. He’s been great for Alaska,” the former mayor wrote on Facebook.

Both Dan S. Sullivan and Peltola advanced to the general election in November after the all-party primary last week. The primary is decided by ranked-choice voting, and the top four finishers advance, regardless of political affiliation. NBC News has not yet made a call regarding who the other two candidates will be, but Dan J. Sullivan could be among them.

Alaska’s Senate race is considered one of the most competitive this cycle, when control of the upper chamber hangs in the balance. With primary votes left to count, Peltola so far has 48% of the vote, with Sen. Dan S. Sullivan taking 43%. Dan J. Sullivan — who is running as a Republican — has 2.4%, with other candidates getting considerably fewer votes.

Democrats view the election as a seat they could flip in November. The Cook Political Report rates the race a tossup.

The Sullivan saga has drawn attention as former teacher Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy has faced legal challenges. Dan S. Sullivan and Republicans have alleged that the teacher was placed on the ballot to confuse voters and detract from the senator’s share of the vote, claiming he’s working with Peltola.

Dan J. Sullivan has denied coordinating with the Peltola campaign. Peltola has also denied any involvement with the second Sullivan campaign.

Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, R-Alaska, placed second in the primary last week. Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images file

The Alaska Supreme Court ruled last month that Dan J. Sullivan can stay on the ballot after the state Division of Elections originally disqualified him. NBC News has reported that state and federal prosecutors in Alaska were investigating whether the race could be part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. A grand jury issued subpoenas this month to compel information from witnesses linked to Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign.

World.title: Navy sailor on USS Lincoln says dad was arrested by immigration officials
World.content:
U.S. Navy sailor Joshua Aviles said he learned his father was arrested by federal immigration officials while on his ninth month aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier that has been at the center of reports of mental health challenges and subpar conditions faced by service members.

"I just got a call that my dad was taken by ICE. If you know my dad, you know he is a hardworking, humble man who is always willing to help anyone if he can," Aviles wrote in a Facebook post this weekend.

"This is heartbreaking for me. I don't know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal," he added.

Asked by CBS News about the arrest, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed Luis Manuel Aviles Roa, a native of Nicaragua, was arrested by Border Patrol during a traffic stop in Key West, Florida, on Saturday, saying he entered the U.S. illegally. The department said Aviles remained in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, facing deportation proceedings.

DHS did not dispute the family's statements that Aviles lacks a criminal record, but said that "(h)aving a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation's laws."

"We are simply enforcing the laws passed by Congress," the department said in a statement Sunday. "This Administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce."

Katty Delgado, Joshua Aviles' half-sister, told CBS News that her stepfather was on his way to the mechanic when he was arrested by Border Patrol. She said he's been living in the U.S. for roughly 20 years and that he has a pending immigration application to obtain legal status.

She said communication with her half-brother has been "on and off" since he's still deployed overseas, but she said he's told her he's having trouble sleeping and eating.

"His mind is focused now on 'Where is my dad? And how is he doing?'" she said.

Aviles' arrest is the latest immigration enforcement operation to affect a U.S. military family over the past year and a half.

Historically rare, immigration arrests of military spouses and parents have become more common under the second Trump administration, which rescinded prior limits on arrests by ICE and Border Patrol as part of its mass deportation campaign.

DHS officials have consistently said anyone in the country illegally is vulnerable to being arrested and processed for deportation, even in cases involving military families.

In his Facebook post, Aviles noted the USS Lincoln's extended deployment in the Middle East.

"I've been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything," he wrote.

The aircraft carrier and its roughly 5,000 crew members left the Middle East last week to head back to the U.S., a journey that could take several weeks.

World.title: Jared Kushner and Hakeem Jeffries met as midterm elections loom
World.content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and President Trump's adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner met recently, a source familiar with the details confirmed to CBS News.

The private discussion comes less than three months before the midterms. Democrats are aiming to take control of the House in the November elections, with Jeffries in line to possibly become the next House Speaker if they win the majority. It also comes as Republicans — led by Mr. Trump — have cast Democrats as the party of dangerous extremes.

The New York Times first reported the meeting, which took place in New York City and covered a broad range of topics and potential areas of common ground such as housing, immigration and cost of living. The White House and a Kushner spokesperson did not immediately respond to CBS News' requests for comment.

In a statement, Jeffries did not confirm the meeting but said Democrats will not tolerate Republicans' "my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people."

"To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition," Jeffries said.

Kushner has no formal role in the White House, but he serves as a key adviser to Mr. Trump in overseas diplomatic negotiations. He and Jeffries worked together on criminal justice reform legislation during Mr. Trump's first term.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday that he first learned of this meeting from news reports.

"I don't know what that's about," Johnson said to Fox News' Peter Doocy. "I know Jared has interests and lots of other things going on. He's not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House."

While Mr. Trump met frequently with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and the former House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi in his first term, he has only met with Schumer and Jeffries once so far this term.

Mr. Trump has instead used his social media to insult both of them, including referring to Jeffries as "low IQ" and a "thug." Earlier this year, Jeffries called Mr. Trump "the dumbest president ever."

However, in an interview this month with Punchbowl News, Mr. Trump said he could work with the Democratic leader and described him as a "nice guy."

"People are harsh on me. I'm harsh on them. It's part of the world," Mr. Trump said. "I'd probably get along with him very well."

"Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

World.title: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to unveil new economic sanctions on Iran
World.content:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to unveil new economic sanctions on Iran

toggle caption Jacquelyn Martin/AP

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to unveil a new round of economic sanctions on Iran on Monday, in what he has described as the "single greatest financial offensive ever."

President Trump has called it an "economic D-Day" and pledged to go after other countries who extend an economic lifeline to Tehran.

In anticipation, the Iranian currency, the Rial, has plunged to a record low.

What are these new sanctions and how much more pressure can they pile on?

The U.S. already has extensive sanctions on Iran, some stretching back almost 50 years, and as recently as June had imposed further penalties for entities that helped Iran evade existing financial restrictions. There has also been a months-long U.S. naval blockade of Iran, which has cut off most goods to Iran from the outside world.

Sponsor Message

This latest suggestion from President Trump and Secretary Bessent appears to be focused on putting more pressure on the countries and governments — not just the businesses — that host the entities providing cashflow for Iran.

In an editorial for the Financial Times published overnight, Bessent wrote, "our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." He appeared to reference countries that still trade with Iran, saying they should "consider the consequences of doing so."

That includes China, Iran's biggest oil customer, which Bessent criticized last week for historically buying about 90 percent of Iran's oil.

But some analysts question the actual utility of fresh economic sanctions.

Alan Eyre, a former American diplomat who was part of the U.S. negotiating team over Iran's nuclear program until 2015, told NPR's Emily Feng that the U.S. has already targeted "the low-hanging fruit, the mid-hanging fruit, the high-hanging fruit, the tree," and that "there are no new sanctions that are effective."

Iran vows a "seismic" retaliation to any sanctions

Iran's new security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said in an interview on state TV over the weekend that Iran would retaliate in a "seismic manner" to Trump's latest attempt at economic warfare. Rezaei, a hardliner who used to lead Iran's Revolutionary Guards, is now a military adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.

Sponsor Message

Rezaei warned Gulf states that any countries partnering in these new economic restrictions would be considered an enemy of — and a target for — Iran.

Since the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran nearly six months ago, Iran has attacked U.S. bases in Jordan and Gulf countries including the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Several have led to serious injuries and fatalities.

Rezaei said Iran would retaliate by further targeting oil tankers that are transiting the Persian Gulf on the Omani side of the Strait of Hormuz, warning that "not even a single drop of oil will leave the region."

Iran is not currently interfering in these routes, so such actions could further hamper oil supplies. Energy exports from the Gulf region have already suffered the biggest disruption in their history because of the war and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Gulf countries that invested billions on pipelines that can help avoid the Strait of Hormuz, have not yet commented on the U.S. plans for fresh sanctions.

New sanctions will make a dire economic situation worse for ordinary Iranians

Iran has weathered some U.S. sanctions for almost half a century, since the Islamic Revolution of 1979, with ordinary Iranians bearing the brunt of the subsequent economic pain.

The Iranian economy was already struggling when the U.S. and Israel launched this war against Iran in February, with double-digit inflation and currency devaluation. According to the Iranian government agency, the Statistical Centre of Iran, inflation is now at almost 90 percent.

NPR spoke to one 30-year-old Iranian woman, who said most ordinary Iranians are now buying food using a credit system because they do not have enough cash.

"Since I am in debt to the grocery store, I couldn't even buy tomato paste to cook pasta," she told NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi. She did not want to be named for fear of retaliation from the Iranian government.

Sponsor Message

She said lifesaving medicines like insulin have become too expensive for many, and that daily life is becoming increasingly difficult, with frequent power cuts and unemployment rising.

Economic pain and the high cost of living were among the factors driving Iranians to protest on the streets earlier this year, in demonstrations that were met with a deadly government crackdown.

A fast-growing wildfire in Reno, Nev., has forced around 42,000 people to evacuate, with thousands more told to prepare to leave. Dozens of American cities have canceled their contracts with Flock Safety over privacy concerns about its automated license plate readers. More than 20,000 people in northwest Indiana are still without power, nearly two weeks after severe storms.

This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

World.title: Washington, D.C.'s first IndyCar race packed the National Mall
World.content:
Washington, D.C.'s first IndyCar race packed the National Mall

toggle caption Nathan Howard/Reuters

In the end, it was an American who took the crown.

The first-ever street race in the nation's capital ended with Florida native Kyle Kirkwood on the podium. He led 128 of the 147 laps, finishing with a commanding win.

toggle caption Chris Graythen/Getty Images

toggle caption Finn Gomez/Getty Images/Getty Images

toggle caption Aaron Schwartz/Reuters

Over the weekend, the Freedom 250 Grand Prix transformed some of the nation's most famous streets – Pennsylvania, Constitution, and Independence avenues – into a race track.

Tens of thousands of people packed into the National Mall to attend each day of the two-day event. There was no shortage of American flag paraphernalia: red, white and blue hats, shirts, earrings and dresses. Many in the crowds sported bald eagles splashed on bright shirts as well as "Freedom 250" merch. (And a real bald eagle flew over the racetrack during the singing of "God Bless America" before returning to its handler.)

toggle caption Tierney L. Cross/Reuters

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Allison Robbert/AP Photo/Allison Robbert/AP

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

"Oh man — patriotic and electric," Cameron Graves said, describing the energy at the event. Graves wore American flag pants and a Freedom 250 shirt and hat. He already had a front row seat by 8:15am on Sunday.

Sponsor Message

Pre-race celebrations were filled with pomp and circumstance. There were multiple flyovers and military bands flooded the racetrack. Before waving the green start flag, President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump took a ceremonious lap in Trump's armored car, nicknamed "The Beast." Crowds cheered and chanted "U.S.A."

toggle caption Tierney L. Cross/Reuters

toggle caption Doug Mills/Pool/The New York Times/AP

toggle caption Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

toggle caption Jacquelyn Martin/AP

toggle caption Mike Kropf/Getty Images

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix was pulled together in just seven months – a relatively short period of time to overcome security issues, satisfy permit requirements and address safety issues. Over 200 manhole covers had to be welded down because otherwise they could be road hazards.

The race brought people together from across the country. Devoted IndyCar fan Mick Bryant, a dealer of collectibles, including IndyCar cards, came from Greenfield, Ind. He was decked out in a full black-and-white checkered outfit down to his socks.

"I'll tell you what, I've been going to the [Indianapolis] 500 for decades... and I still get goosebumps," Bryant said. "There's nothing like it. I just love the sound. Love the smell."

Kathleen Lazorchack and her husband travelled from West Virginia for the race. Lazorchack is a director at Summit Point Motorsports Park. She said the best part about motorsports is the people.

"If you ever have an opportunity to walk through the paddock and talk to people, it'll make your hair stand up on your arms," Lazorchack said.

Sponsor Message

Along with the longtimers, there were also brand new fans.

toggle caption Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Allison Robbert/AP

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

toggle caption Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

In the front row of the stands, Omar Saenz and his 14-year-old step-son Damien Macwithey were carrying racing helmets signed by drivers. They had traveled from Dallas, Texas for their first IndyCar race.

"It's like a bum rush of people," Damien said, holding his helmet tight in his lap with the protective wrapping still on it. "It's going to be very loud."

And it definitely was.

Michael Milton, a D.C. resident wearing a bald eagle hat, was struck by the thundering sounds at his first IndyCar race.

"It does something to you, right? It gets inside of you," Milton said as the cars shot by. "It's almost a visceral feeling."

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk for NPR

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk for NPR

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk for NPR

The Grand Prix also received plenty of pushback. Some D.C residents were wary of one more stamp President Trump was putting on their city. Others complained about the traffic jams and parking restrictions in the runup to the event.

Johnny Ring, who lives in D.C. and was there with his husband, said he had mixed feelings. (He might have been the only person reading a book at the track before the race began.)

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk

toggle caption Gabriella Demczuk for NPR

He was excited to view a once in a lifetime event, but said he also does not support the Trump administration.

"It feels like it's kind of shoved down our throats," said Ring. "But, you know, I want to be able to be kind of a little bit a part of history."

World.title: In candid interviews, National Guard members speak out about D.C. deployment
World.content:
In candid interviews, National Guard members speak out about D.C. deployment

toggle caption Illustration by Mari Fouz​ for NPR

As the sight of armed, uniformed National Guard troops became ubiquitous in Washington, D.C., over the past year, one voice has been notably absent from the public discourse around the deployment: the guard members themselves.

"I will say very frankly that the bad taste that this mission left in my mouth, it actually embarrasses me to be involved in any way," one guard member who was part of the deployment for several months recently told NPR.

Thousands of National Guard members have been patrolling the streets of Washington, D.C., for more than a year now, in what has become President Trump's largest and longest domestic military deployment. Their presence has become a common, and controversial, topic of conversation among D.C. residents and constitutional experts alike, raising concerns about the normalization of armed troops in a city for an extended period of time.

Sponsor Message

Members of the military are not allowed to speak to the press without authorization. Under this administration, those rules and the ramifications for breaking them have gotten even stricter.

But some members who are no longer a part of the mission have become more open to sharing their thoughts as the deployment enters its second year — and has been extended to the end of President Trump's term.

"I don't want to think about the National Guard. I don't want to necessarily discuss my affiliation with the National Guard. I don't want to fulfill my normal National Guard duties just because of the abuses of the National Guard in this D.C. mission," the guard member said, noting that isn't how he's felt after previous domestic deployments.

That guard member was one of three who spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity because they are still serving and are barred from speaking publicly. All of them were deployed as part of the D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission for many months, and each has more than a decade of service.

In candid interviews, the guard members described their feelings throughout their time on the deployment, and their worries about the new norms it's establishing. They discussed the cost, which is expected to run into the billions. And they say they worry that Trump's unprecedented use of the troops is damaging the National Guard's reputation with the American public.

Sponsor Message

All were skeptical about the administration's original reason for the deployment — to help with law enforcement after declaring a "crime emergency", despite a 30-year low in violent crime in the city.

"Now, with it being a year, it's hard to feel like that justification holds any water," said one guard member. "It feels like the guard is being exploited in a sense."

Another said it feels more like a political stunt, pointing out the way the guard has been inserted into certain narratives by the administration, like being ordered to patrol the perimeter of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool following its faulty renovation.

toggle caption Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

"I hope that there will be some accounting someday — probably after President Trump is gone — about why we were there, and was it worth it? But none of that is gonna happen right now," that member said.

NPR reached out to both the White House and the D.C. Joint Task Force regarding the concerns raised by the guard members.

The White House responded by reiterating how safe D.C. is now, without providing evidence that the guard is responsible for decreasing crime.

In a statement, Brig. Gen. Leland Blanchard II, the interim commanding general of the D.C. National Guard, called the deployment "unique" and pointed to "significant accomplishments" that guard members contributed in the past year, including assisting law enforcement with apprehensions, rendering medical aid and reuniting lost children with their families.

"Whatever individual perspectives they carry away from their experience, their service and sacrifice deserve our respect," Blanchard wrote.

"My initial reaction was just shock"

Trump first deployed the D.C. National Guard in August of 2025 — something he can do since the president controls the district's guard. Hundreds of guard members in the district were pulled from their civilian jobs and immediately called up.

"My very initial reaction was just, I guess, shock and feeling like this context and this situation just felt like a very authoritarian move that kind of felt uncharacteristic of something you would see in our country," said one member of the D.C. guard, adding that the reasoning behind the deployment contributed to the confusion.

Sponsor Message

In the days and weeks that followed, Republican governors began sending members of their guard to help with the mission.

"Walking into it, we had no real specifics," one guard member who was deployed from West Virginia remembered thinking. "The president is calling out the guard to make D.C. safe. Well, what the what the f*** does that mean?"

All remembered a scramble in the early days to figure out what everyone should be doing, as more and more troops — who were all deputized as special law enforcement and armed with a handgun — arrived. They said that despite the confusion, there was a collective effort to figure out how to be useful and effective. Military members are trained to be apolitical and follow orders.

"All of these people showed up, and then it was more of an after-the-fact figure out what we're going to do," one said, saying everyone was really trying to be as helpful as possible to the community with whatever resources they were given, like providing Naloxone to counter the effects of an opioid overdose or helping a bicyclist who had been hit by a car. "We can argue about why they were there and whether they should be there, but soldiers and airmen were trying to do the best with what they had."

In the early days, troops were largely assigned to help with beautification projects around the city: clearing trash along the road, bagging leaves in public parks or trimming trees at the National Mall. The guard member from West Virginia said that many of the members he had arrived with — most of whom had raised their hand for the deployment — became quickly disillusioned.

toggle caption Andrew Leyden/Getty Images

"I know there were a lot of people that showed up from West Virginia specifically that were just like, I want to help, and then later they found out that they were taking out trash and setting up (logistical equipment). I think they later fell off mission as soon as they could get off," he said.

Sponsor Message

Patrolling the streets

As the deployment continued, troops were assigned less to beautification projects and more to presence patrols around the city — which the task force says are an effort to deter crime — and settled into a routine that one guard member described as "mundane" and another as "monotonous."

"At some point, I found myself going, well, at least this isn't that bad. At least I'm not doing anything illegal, and that's always counterbalanced with, like, this is wasting everyone's time," one said, adding that it became clear that the "point of the mission is presence."

One member who served in Afghanistan likened the patrols to tactics commonly used by the U.S. military during the War on Terror in communities to instill goodwill and monitor the opposition.

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Another said the lack of clear goals made the deployment feel never-ending, even as Trump falsely claimed there was "almost zero crime" in D.C. and touted its success.

"If it's safe now, then why are we here?" one guard member asked. "You don't really know when good is good enough, or when we can go home. It's just a continuing thing."

Two recent studies have found that the National Guard presence has had no effect on violent crime in the city, while it has minimally decreased more opportunistic crime, like petty theft and vehicle break-ins. Both also found that local policing could produce better outcomes for less money.

The deployment comes with perks

A majority of the nearly 4,700 guard members deployed to D.C. are from other states or U.S. territories, most of which are led by Republicans, and have volunteered for the assignment. All three guard members said that despite their concerns, they understood why people might raise their hand.

"It's a good paycheck, and I can't blame them for wanting to better their own financial situation when the economy is how it is right now," one said, noting that many of the troops are very young, come from more rural communities and might not have steady income back home.

Sponsor Message

There are a host of other incentives as well, from per diems to boosts to their retirement benefits.

The guard member from West Virginia said that normally, on domestic deployments, he was used to sleeping on the floor of an armory, maybe without electricity, and eating ready-to-eat military meals. But this D.C. deployment was much more comfortable.

"The food on the mission was very good. My hotel was very nice," he said, noting that was different even from other times he had come to D.C. on deployment for events like the inauguration.

The thousands of out-of-state guard members have been staying in hotels throughout the city for more than a year. Recently, the federal government awarded a nearly $300 million contract — the largest of its kind ever — to a local company for thousands of furnished, luxury apartments, saying the move would ultimately save money on extended lodging for the troops in D.C.

That guard member said that when elected officials or other leaders would come visit the troops, they would always ask how they could make it better.

"There was never a discussion of whether you should be here. It was always, 'What do you need?'" he said. "Which is nice as a military member, but once we see what all this is going to cost in the very end, it's probably not going to feel so great."

An estimate from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office found that the D.C. deployment at its current level costs about $3 million per day. The Pentagon estimates extending the deployment until 2029 will cost an additional $1.4 billion. A total cost estimate by the nonpartisan watchdog Project on Government Oversight for the deployment is around $3.4 billion.

A personal cost

The deployment has also had a human cost, after a gunman shot two guard members from West Virginia patrolling near the White House last November. One of those members, 20-year-old Spc. Sarah Beckstrom, was killed. It was a pivotal moment in the deployment.

"I remember feeling just really sad," one guard member said, starting to tear up a bit. "And I kept thinking — did they have to be here?"

Another said the killing similarly made him question the necessity of the deployment in real terms.

toggle caption Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

"The thing that really stuck out to me was how absolutely futile that death felt, and that was hard to live with," he said, noting he still thinks about Beckstrom almost daily and sometimes visits the spot where she was shot, even though he didn't know her personally. "After her death, this mission became untenable for me emotionally."

Sponsor Message

Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, called the shooting a "direct challenge to law and order in our capital," and the White House responded by adding hundreds more troops to the city.

The guard member from West Virginia said he's been specifically angry about the shooting, saying he's had to work in therapy about guilt he's felt for not being there when it happened.

"We were made a target, and I don't know that anybody did a very good job of planning for the worst-case scenario," he said.

Blanchard refuted that, saying that "no mission is without risk" and the loss "remains deeply felt across the National Guard."

"Force protection and the safety of our Soldiers and Airmen remain paramount. We continually assess the operating environment and adapt to changing conditions to better protect the force while accomplishing the mission," he said in a statement.

A harm to the National Guard's reputation

The extended and growing deployment — and the administration's unprecedented use of the National Guard in other parts of the country — has led to a rising anti-guard sentiment, which all three members acknowledged.

Throughout D.C. in the areas most patrolled by the troops, signs are plastered on lampposts and chalked on sidewalks urging "National Guard Go Home" and "Troops out now." Residents regularly approach the patrols and speak their mind, sometimes with what one of the guard members called "misdirected anger."

toggle caption Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images

The guard member from West Virginia said it was the first time he'd ever not had the community in a domestic deployment welcome the help, since the guard usually shows up after floods or natural disasters.

All were concerned that there was damage being done to the reputation of the National Guard.

"If we continue down this path, where this kind of 'presence patrol' mission becomes the new definitive image of the National Guard, it's going to completely rebrand everything that was noble about the National Guard into being mundane at best and threatening at worst," one guard member said.

Sponsor Message

"I would like to think there would be enough mechanisms to have checks and balances that would be able to say overtly that's not what we want to see in our country," another one said.

The member paused before adding: "I don't know if that's the case right now."

World.title: Sean Grayson, former deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says
World.content:
Sean Grayson, former deputy convicted of killing Sonya Massey, dies in prison, lawyer says

toggle caption Illinois State Police/via AP

CHICAGO — Sean Grayson, a former Illinois sheriff's deputy whose fatal shooting of Sonya Massey inside her home became a flashpoint over police use of force, died Sunday while serving a 20-year prison sentence.

Grayson's attorney, Daniel Fultz, confirmed that his client died earlier Sunday but declined to provide any further details.

Grayson, 32, was convicted of second-degree murder in October in the fatal shooting of Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman who had reported a possible prowler outside her Springfield-area home. Body camera video of the July 2024 encounter showed Massey crouching in her kitchen and apologizing moments before Grayson shot her in the face.

He was sentenced in January to the maximum 20 years in prison.

Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer before Massey's killing, and his attorneys said at his sentencing that the disease had spread to his liver and lungs. In May, only months into his sentence, he sought medical release under an Illinois law for prisoners with terminal illnesses or serious medical conditions. The Illinois Prisoner Review Board denied his request last month.

Sponsor Message

Massey called 911 early on July 6, 2024, to report someone prowling outside her home. Grayson and another Sangamon County sheriff's deputy responded.

Video showed Grayson directing Massey to remove a pot of hot water from the stove. As she held the pot, Massey told the deputies, "I rebuke you in the name of Jesus."

Grayson threatened to shoot her, drew his handgun and ordered her to drop the pot. Massey apologized and ducked behind a kitchen counter before Grayson fired three times.

The other deputy, Dawson Farley, later testified that he did not consider Massey a threat and drew his own weapon only after Grayson did.

Grayson was fired after the shooting and charged with first-degree murder. Jurors convicted him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder after Grayson argued that he feared Massey would throw the hot water at him.

Massey's killing drew national attention and protests and raised questions about how Grayson had moved through several law enforcement agencies before being hired by the Sangamon County Sheriff's Office.

Illinois lawmakers later passed the Sonya Massey Act, requiring law enforcement agencies to more closely review an applicant's previous employment records before hiring an officer.

The Justice Department also opened a civil rights investigation after Massey's death and later reached an agreement with Sangamon County, its sheriff's office and other agencies requiring changes to policing and emergency response. Those changes included additional training for interactions with people with behavioral health disabilities and development of a mobile crisis response program.

World.title: High-intensity sprints can trigger molecular changes in the bloodstream
World.content:
High-intensity sprints can trigger molecular changes in the bloodstream

Jesussanz/Getty Images

We all know a sprint feels different than a longer, take-it-slow kind of workout.

Your heart is pounding. You gasp for air. Maybe your muscles burn.

Now, new research reveals this kind of high-intensity training provokes a remarkably robust response throughout the bloodstream. The training substantially mobilizes more proteins and other molecules in the hours after exercising.

The findings were published by a team of scientists in the U.S., Australia and Sweden. The results do not mean that sprint workouts and other forms of high-intensity interval training, or HIIT, are better than moderate exercise where your heart rate remains at a steady level.

Sponsor Message

But the data does suggest that pushing yourself in these all-out, short bursts of effort may yield unique benefits for health and fitness, according to Dr. Paul Cohen, whose lab at Rockefeller University led the study, which recently appeared in the journal Cell Reports Medicine.

In a series of experiments, Cohen and his colleagues collected blood from young, healthy adults before and after they exercised, and combed their blood for thousands of proteins and other metabolites.

For example, participants were divided into two opposing camps: One completed six sets of a 30-second maximum effort on the bike, each spaced by 4 minutes of rest.

The others did a 90-minute moderate-paced ride.

When they ran their analysis, it was clear the sprint group had "many, many more changes," explains Cohen. "What we can conclude is that sprinting does have a greater effect on remodeling the molecules in the bloodstream."

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

The practical implications of those changes need to be teased apart in future trials; however, the study did find some initial clues. They overlaid the results from their study participants with a massive database of 50,000 people, collected from the U.K. Biobank.

Sponsor Message

That evaluation showed the proteins that were altered in the sprinters were associated with improved cardiovascular and metabolic health.

In another part of the study, the research team saw that fat cells behaved differently when drenched with blood collected from the HIIT folks, including changes involved in many genes that regulate fat and whole-body metabolism.

"That's further evidence and much more causal evidence that something in the blood following sprint training can remodel the molecular landscape of other tissues, like fat tissue," Cohen says.

This latest work reflects a broader effort in the field of precision medicine to unpack all the ways molecules — in blood vessels, muscles, the liver and other organs — respond to exercise, including different intensities.

"We know now there's very orchestrated events happening under the hood during exercise," says Scott Trappe, director of the Human Performance Lab at Ball State University. "All these organs are communicating, it's like a super highway and the circulation is that highway."

Trappe is also an investigator in a National Institutes of Health initiative to uncover the molecular inner workings of physical activity. He says this new data clearly shows that "there are some potential benefits you're leaving on the table if you don't do high-intensity exercise."

Though he and other experts emphasize that HIIT may not be practical, or even safe, for everyone.

"I don't view this in the light of high intensity versus moderate," he says. "There's a continuum and all of this stuff is good."

In the study, the participants were young, physically fit, and predominantly males, and that limits how much you can extrapolate to other groups, especially those who are older and less conditioned.

The cycling protocol itself — six sets of 30-second maximum sprints — could prove enormously taxing for the average person, he notes.

Overall, the human studies comparing high- and moderate-intensity exercise suggest they're largely comparable to each other when you look at measures of fitness and other areas of health, says Todd Astorino, an exercise physiologist at California State University, San Marcos. He has spent almost two decades studying HIIT.

The real upside with high-intensity training — assuming you're healthy enough to do it — is how much you benefit from a small investment of time, he explains.

Sponsor Message

"Sometimes, I think people worry too much about time, or frequency," he says. "If you amp up the intensity, you can do a hell of a lot less of that and still get meaningful adaptations and responses."

For example, Astorino says new data from a grant he's involved in shows two sprints a day totaling less than 40 seconds can lead to meaningful improvement in VO₂ max – a measure of cardiorespiratory fitness – within just 6 to 8 weeks.

The work from Cohen's lab and others is all driving at the goal of eventually developing nuanced exercise prescriptions — and possibly drugs — that can be tailored to the individual.

"Perhaps some individuals have a greater response to sprint training, whereas others might do better with moderate intensity training," he says. "This is just the first step towards providing those kinds of recommendations."

World.title: Thousands forced to evacuate parts of Reno, Nevada, as new wildfire rages
World.content:
Thousands forced to evacuate parts of Reno, Nevada, as new wildfire rages

toggle caption Haven Daley/AP

Some 42,000 people in Reno, Nev. have been forced to evacuate, and another 45,000 have been told to prepare to leave, as a fast-growing wildfire spread toward neighborhoods in the northern part of the city on Sunday.

The blaze, known as the Hawk Fire, has grown to more than 15,000 acres since it began Saturday in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains, according to data posted by the National Interagency Fire Center's Inciweb late Sunday.

"We can confirm that the fire was human caused," Shane Akerson, a battalion chief with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District and one of three incident commanders for the Hawk Fire, said at a press conference late Sunday morning. "However, that is still undergoing active investigation."

Sponsor Message

He said at least six people, including three first responders and three civilians, have been injured, and several properties have been destroyed. Some 800 emergency responders are battling the blaze.

The zone of people urged to "go now" reached the edge of the University of Nevada on Sunday. Officials say people evacuating should be prepared to stay away from home for several days, as unpredictable winds have complicated the fight to contain the blaze.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo has activated the National Guard and declared a state of emergency in Washoe County, which includes Reno and parts of Lake Tahoe. This releases federal resources needed to help contain the fire.

"This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," Lombardo said Saturday in a statement posted on social media.

As the fire moves into more heavily urban areas, authorities said tens of thousands of people in areas with "be ready to evacuate" status should stay alert and have "go bags" prepared in case they have to leave suddenly. Sheriff Darin Balaam of Washoe County also urged residents to keep tabs on Watch Duty, an app and website that provides real-time data on nearby wildfires and other natural disasters.

Sponsor Message

"If you can get out now, I would ask you please to do that," Balaam said, saying that would make it easier for firefighters and first responders to do their job.

The Reno-Sparks Convention Center is receiving evacuees, and hundreds of people spent Saturday night there, NPR member station KUNR reports .

Officials first received reports of the Hawk Fire just after 11 a.m. Pacific Time on Saturday. "Red flag" fire conditions – warm temperatures, low humidity and strong winds – helped fuel the blaze, according to Richard Edwards, fire chief at Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue, one of the teams combating the wildfire.

"The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us, as it's being driven by the winds," Edwards said in a video posted to social media Saturday.

"The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas, creating a lot of challenges for our firefighters to save homes and protect lives," he said.

toggle caption Noah Berger/AP

Balaam noted that the Hawk Fire is the third major wildfire to hit northern Nevada in the last few weeks. The Bug Fire, which began Aug. 8 just north of the Hawk Fire, has burned nearly 94,000 acres and is now around 94% contained. The Stallion Fire, which started two days later, is now 98% contained after claiming just over 40,000 acres.
