World.title: The Jewish-Mexican food traditions hiding in plain sight
World.content:
My friend Jorge Fitz once told me a story about his childhood visits to the town where his grandfather grew up, Juliantla, just outside of Taxco, Mexico. He remembers many particular things about the way the town celebrated festivities and holidays, but one thing that stuck out in his memory was a special braided bread they made called pan de Juliantla.

As an adult, Jorge said he started making Jewish friends, and when he saw pan de Juliantla on their tables, he wondered how they knew about it.

“Jorge, that’s challah bread,” they would respond.

He later learned that Juliantla is believed to be the first Jewish settlement in the Americas, complete with a spiritual cleansing bath known as a mikveh that dates back to the 16th century.

As far as Jorge could tell, a majority of the townspeople didn’t realize where many of their customs and food came from. He and his parents definitely didn’t know about their Jewish ancestry until much later.

Hearing this story illuminated just how deeply rooted Jewish food is in Mexican culture, so much so that even when origins have been forgotten, they remain an integral part of community life.

Waves of migration and a culinary legacy

The first Jews to grace Mexican shores sailed in on the ships of Spanish conquistadors during the 1500s and 1600s. They were fleeing the Catholic Inquisition of the Iberian Peninsula, but found little solace in the New World as the Inquisition migrated across the ocean.

Many of these early Jews “converted” to Catholicism while continuing to practice their own religion in secret. In Spanish, they are called “conversos,” or the converted. In English, we often refer to them as Crypto Jews.

With these Sephardim came cinnamon, grapes, figs, dates, almonds, cherries, apricots, olives and olive oil, nutmeg, ginger, cardamom and mustard, as well as black pepper, thyme, basil, clove, fennel, oregano, cumin and other Mediterranean spices.

They also had a strong tradition of pickling what they brought to the New World. In northern Mexico, cabrito, slow-roasted baby goat, is a traditional dish among the Sephardic Jews of the Iberian Peninsula. Similarly, the region’s dessert bread known as pan de cemita and la capirotada, a kind of bread pudding, are also attributed to those early Iberian Jewish immigrants.

The second wave of Jewish immigrants to Mexico arrived at the end of the 1800s from the failing Ottoman Empire. Jews who were part of the diaspora from Spain and Portugal, now living in the countries of the Levant, came because of economic opportunities in Mexico. They arrived from what is today Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, and because they were not fleeing persecution, their culture, religion and food were much more visible.

Preserving culture in the neighborhood oven

A third wave of Jewish immigrants came to Mexico during and between the two world wars. Some had plans of continuing on to the United States but were turned away at Ellis Island because of the Immigration Act of 1924, which severely limited the numbers of Southern and European immigrants allowed into the country.

These immigrants brought the Ashkenazi dishes of Eastern European countries like Poland, Ukraine and Germany — hearty soups and stews made with root vegetables like borscht, matza ball soup, gefilte fish, schmaltz (rendered chicken fat), tzimmes, gribenes and braised meats like brisket.

Food is paramount for any immigrant community trying to preserve their identity. The Jewish community was no different.

When Syrian Jews moved into Colonia Roma at the beginning of the 20th century, they not only built one of the city’s oldest synagogues but also opened a community oven down the street where special traditional breads were baked and sold to worshipers coming from services. At the local market were kosher butchers, while elderly folks sat in neighborhood cafes sipping thick, Turkish-style coffee and eating the sweets of home.

Unlike some of the immigrant groups I have researched, the diverse Mexican-Jewish community not only preserved the traditional dishes of their culture, but also, over the generations, adapted and innovated with local ingredients and cooking methods, creating a distinct Judeo-Mexican cuisine.

The fusion kitchen and home recipes

“Sabor Judío,” published in 2024, is a recipe collection by two authors whose Jewish grandmothers passed down handwritten recipe books. They gathered together a comprehensive archive of recipes from kitchens across the Mexican-Jewish community. Among the book’s pages are traces of many cuisines — Mexican mestizo, Spanish, Sephardic-Iberian, Sephardic-Middle Eastern and Ashkenazi.

Yiddish blintzes with huitlacoche (Mexican corn smut considered a local delicacy), matza chilaquiles, a variation of shakshuka with poblano peppers and Mexican oregano, and brisket tacos with three-chile salsa are all included in the collection. Irma Appel’s stuffed poblano peppers with guacamole include a smattering of gribenes (often referred to as Jewish bacon), and Pati Jinich, of PBS’s “Pati’s Kitchen,” provided her recipe for jalapeño-mushroom matza ball soup.

Then there are traditional Mexican recipes that the Mexican-Jewish community has adopted as their own, cooking them for high holidays and other festivities. That includes nopal and tomato salad made in advance to eat cold during Shabbat, or ceviche with prepared horseradish on top, supposedly invented during a Passover Seder.

Not everything is kosher, but the community’s many identities are on full display.

Scanning through the menus of Jewish restaurants in Mexico City, however, it’s hard to find the fusion dishes represented in “Sabor Judío.” For whatever reason, these dishes hold sway in family kitchens, but haven’t yet made it to commercial dining rooms.

Where to find Jewish food in Mexico City

Maybe the world isn’t ready for spicy gefilte fish?

That’s not to say that you can’t get glimpses of them — the salami chilaquiles at Klein’s in Polanco is a delicious example. You’ll also find chiles making guest appearances in the Israeli dishes at Merkava, and kosher cafe Guacho Grill has al pastor tacos made with fish and chicken, as opposed to the traditional pork.

So maybe fusion is yet to take off in restaurants, but at places like Klein’s or Niddo, which once described itself in an interview as Jewish-Mexican-Canadian, diners will at least find Jewish and Mexican dishes coexisting on the table.

Plenty of other expressions of Jewish food can be encountered throughout the city — Mendl, for instance, has incredible U.S.-style deli sandwiches and bagels with lox. And at Pat Patz, chef Mijeal Seidel has a labneh recipe that he adds dill to as a shout-out to his Eastern European side, along with tons of other dishes worth exploring.

You may have to make some fusion dishes at home, but a taste of Jewish-Mexican heritage is definitely available across Mexico City.

Lydia Carey is a freelance writer and translator based in Mexico City. She has published extensively both online and in print, sharing her insights about Mexico for over a decade. She lives a double life as a local tour guide and is the author of “Mexico City Streets: La Roma.” Follow her urban adventures on Instagram and see more of her work at mexicocitystreets.com.

World.title: How the Middle East has shaped Mexico for almost 2,000 years
World.content:
I’m sitting in the courtyard of Guanajuato’s Museo Iconográfico del Quijote, admiring the stone arches and columns, waiting for a chamber music concert to begin. I probably walk through at least one courtyard a day in Guanajuato because they’re everywhere in town – not just in museums, but in restaurants, universities, government buildings and parks. Even the classic Mexican colonial home has a courtyard with a fountain in the center, surrounded by rooms.

Mexican courtyards reflect the influence of the Moors, the North African Islamic group that ruled Spain for 800 years and whose ornate tilework, intricate geometric patterns and decorative calligraphy influenced the art and architecture of Spain. After the fall of the Moors in 1492, Spain continued to use Islamic patterns in its designs, creating a unique style that blended Islamic and Christian elements known as mudéjar, which later made its way to Mexico.

But it’s not just courtyards that bear the mark of the Moors. From architecture and folk medicine to crafts and textiles, here’s a quick roundup of the Islamic group’s lasting impact on Mexican culture.

Alhambrismo

This is an architectural style in Spain and Latin America inspired by the decorative Islamic arts of the Alhambra, a palace and fortress complex in Granada, Spain, with Moorish elements such as horseshoe arches, intricate stucco and colorful tilework.

A well-known example of this is the Kiosk of Santa Maria la Ríbera, an ornate octagonal pavilion made of wrought iron with a glass cupola dome on the top, in Mexico City’s Alameda Park.

Churches

In many colonial Mexican churches, you can see echoes of the mudéjar architectural style, including azulejos, blue-glazed tiles that adorn domes, bell towers and facades; intricate geometric carved-wood ceilings resembling inverted ship hulls; and arches and doorways.

Oaxaca’s famous Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, for example, displays these design elements in the intricate geometric arabesque patterns on the ceiling and the genealogical tree of the temple’s namesake saint.

Inward-facing living

I remember when my husband and I first saw the house we bought in Guanajuato. Although one of its assets was a close-up view of the dome atop one of the city’s signature churches, San Francisco, we could barely see it from the tiny window in one of the bedrooms.

Unlike in the U.S. and Canada, traditional Mexican houses face inward, revealing their Moorish and Andalusian roots, with walled enclosures and internal gathering spaces.

Urban layouts

While Spanish colonial urban planning in the Americas officially ordered a strict grid system, some historic Mexican towns like Guanajuato and Taxco have narrow, winding streets, reflecting the medieval and southern Andalusian urban layouts shaped by centuries of Moorish influence.

Tiles, pottery and ceramics

Moorish craftsmen influenced Iberian ceramic styles, including tin-glazed pottery, by integrating geometric patterns and calligraphic bands into their work. When the craft was established in Puebla during the colonial period, artisans carried over these traditional Iberian-Islamic design elements, including abstract script borders and traditional brushstroke motifs.

Puebla’s famous Talavera pottery also blends Indigenous styles with Spanish and Moorish glazed-tile traditions.

Crafts and textiles

Mudéjar geometric inlaid woodworking and carpentry techniques influenced traditional lacquerware and furniture crafts in regions like Michoacán and Guerrero. Precise interlaced framing merged with Indigenous wood-carving and pre-Hispanic lacquering, creating colonial furniture like desks with repetitive geometric paneling and floral touches.

As for weaving, the traditional Mexican sarape displays complex linear, diamond and star-centered layouts that show cross-cultural parallels to Middle Eastern flat-weave blanket traditions.

Curanderismo (folk medicine)

Moorish and Islamic medical practices influenced curanderismo, the herbal medicine still widely practiced in Mexico. Ritual cleansing, petitionary prayers and talismanic magic elements arrived via Spanish traditions that had absorbed Moorish folk customs.

For example, the belief that the “mal de ojo,” or “evil eye,” can cause physical discomfort like fever, crying and restlessness was brought to the New World via Spanish and Moorish folk magic.

Middle Eastern influences beyond the Moors

Influential as the Moors were, they are not the only Middle Eastern influence in modern Mexico.

Following the fall of the Moors, many Sephardic Jews fled from the Middle East to colonial Mexico to escape the Inquisition. Later waves of Sephardic Jews arrived from the crumbling Ottoman Empire in the early 20th century. These communities established synagogues, cultural institutions and social networks, primarily in Mexico City.

While Mexico has seen periods of antisemitism throughout its history, modern Mexico hosts one of the largest and most vibrant Jewish communities in Latin America, mostly in Mexico City.

Meanwhile, the Lebanese diaspora in Mexico — currently standing at more than 500,000 descendants — has shaped the nation’s culture, cuisine and commerce since the late 19th century.

In the 1890s, they left to escape political oppression, heavy taxes, religious conflict and military conscription. At the same time, Mexico’s then-president, Porfirio Díaz, encouraged foreign immigration and trade, offering a welcoming environment and growing business opportunities.

During the period between the 1890s and 1930s, more than 100,000 mostly Lebanese immigrants arrived from Arabic-speaking nations, settling predominantly in the Yucatán, but also in Veracruz, Puebla and Mexico City.

In the early 20th century, the Lebanese community contributed around 50% of the total immigrant input to Mexico’s economy, and it remains one of Mexico’s most successful immigrant groups.

I’ve known for years that words like ¡ojalá!, albañil, and azotea are Arabic in origin, but I had no idea about other enduring Middle Eastern influences. The next time I use the Talavera dish I bought in Puebla, I’ll appreciate its ancient Moorish history, going back almost 2,000 years.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Fugitive swaps, a strawberry spat and a stronger peso
World.content:
Mexico and the United States spent the week of Aug. 17 trading shows of security cooperation, from fugitive handovers to a new drone-technology pact, culminating Wednesday in a federal operation in Michoacán that saw nine alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel arrested and set off narco-blockades at more than 20 points across the state.

That cooperation ran alongside friction on other fronts. Mexico is contesting a proposed U.S. antidumping tariff on strawberry exports and objecting to Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Central America rather than home, as trade uncertainty lingers more than a month after the U.S. declined to renew the USMCA free trade deal in its current form. Domestically, the fallout from the U.S. visa revocation of former president López Obrador’s son continued to shadow the government’s messaging on fuel-smuggling enforcement. Against that backdrop, the peso’s push below 17 to the dollar stood out as a rare point of good economic news, as the central bank held its interest rate steady on lingering inflation concerns.

The week also brought a new Mexico-made electric vehicle, a national debate over kids and social media, and a presidential sick day. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Fugitive returns and a new drone pact mark security cooperation

Mexico and the United States kept up a steady drumbeat of security announcements this week. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said U.S. authorities returned three wanted fugitives to Mexico in a single day — one linked to the CJNG, one wanted for murder in Zacatecas and one for fraud — while separately handing over six more fugitives wanted for crimes including murder and firearms offenses. Jalisco police also captured Antoni Covarrubias, wanted for second-degree murder in California, in Puerto Vallarta, which Johnson called the ninth high-profile U.S.-targeted arrest in the state in recent weeks. At the same time, the U.S. and Mexico conducted a joint security exercise along the El Paso-Ciudad Juárez border, and the two countries signed a declaration of intent on drone technology that will let Mexico’s Defense Ministry access the U.S. Army’s marketplace for unmanned aircraft systems, though no models, quantities or purchases have been agreed.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch drew public praise from DEA Administrator Terry Cole at the 40th International Drug Enforcement Conference in Buenos Aires, where García Harfuch said U.S. agencies are processing 155 arrest warrants tied to Mexican investigations and reported that Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit has frozen more than 8.6 billion pesos in assets. He also cited a more than 50% drop in daily homicides, from 86 to 42, over the past two years, a figure attributed to his ministry’s own count of arrests and seizures.

The Michoacán operation capped the week’s security news: Soldiers and National Guard troops arrested nine people, including two women identified as relatives of CJNG plaza boss Heraclio “Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez, who evaded capture as the operation set off blockades that were largely cleared by Wednesday afternoon.

That flow of cooperation announcements ran alongside a separate dispute over fuel smuggling and politics. Sheinbaum said at Tuesday’s mañanera that fuel smuggling, or huachicol fiscal, is “practically over” in Mexico thanks to customs interventions and arrests — a claim she offered in the context of defending her government against opposition criticism. That criticism stems partly from the U.S. revocation of the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President López Obrador, which Sheinbaum has called a political matter, saying he “was not” ever on authorities’ radar for criminal involvement. The fuel-trafficking case itself advanced this week when Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, accused of leading a Pemex-linked smuggling ring, was extradited from Argentina and jailed at the Altiplano maximum security prison. The case has damaged the Navy’s reputation and drawn indirect allegations, which Sheinbaum has rejected, involving López Beltrán.

Strawberries, Vietnam imports and a Canada call test trade ties

Mexico is contesting a U.S. Commerce Department finding that could impose antidumping tariffs on Mexican strawberries, which supplies 98% of U.S. strawberry imports. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard called the U.S. criteria “arbitrarily applied” and inconsistent with USMCA provisions; a final ITC ruling isn’t expected until early 2027, and the case could affect roughly 5,000 Mexican producers and 151,000 jobs if it proceeds. Sheinbaum has warned the case could set a precedent for challenging other Mexican agricultural exports.

Separately, Mexico’s imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first half of 2026 to $18.4 billion, a jump that has raised suspicions — flagged in a recent White House report naming Mexico a “Tier 1” transshipment risk — that Chinese goods are being routed through Vietnam to dodge Mexico’s tariffs on non-free-trade-agreement countries. Mexico has denied being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods bound for the U.S.

Against that backdrop, President Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed North American trade by phone on Thursday. Carney’s office said the two underscored the importance of renewing the USMCA pact soon, and separately thanked Mexico for deploying more than 400 firefighters to help combat wildfires in British Columbia. The call came as Trump-imposed tariffs on Canadian goods, delayed this week, loomed for Saturday absent a deal. (The U.S. tariffs on Canada ultimately went into effect after trade talks collapsed late Friday night.)

Peso strength collides with a cautious Banxico

The peso dropped below 17 to the U.S. dollar this week, dropping below 16.9 on Friday, largely on dollar weakness following a U.S. Treasury bond buyback announcement. The currency has appreciated nearly 6% in 2026, a gain Banxico credits with helping cool inflation.

Even so, the central bank held its benchmark rate at 6.5% earlier this month. In meeting minutes released this week, four of five board members cited persistent services inflation as a driver of that decision. Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, but Banxico now doesn’t expect it to reach its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027. The bank also flagged Middle East tensions as an upside risk to oil prices. Separately, INEGI’s preliminary July data showed the economy growing 2.7% annually, which Rodríguez called “another piece of good news” following 2.1% growth in the second quarter.

Other business and finance news this week:

Mañanera themes: EVs, phone lines and a presidential sick day

On Monday, Sheinbaum said she opposes a social-media ban for minors like Australia’s, calling the idea “very problematic” and noting enforcement challenges, while Education Minister Mario Delgado announced a nationwide teacher consultation on classroom device rules ahead of the Aug. 31 school year.

At Thursday’s press conference, Sheinbaum unveiled a prototype of Olinia Carga, the government’s second domestically developed electric vehicle, a light-cargo EV that can carry 650 kilograms and will sell for around 150,000 pesos starting in late 2027. The same day brought a new arrest in the 2024 kidnapping case of Sinaloa Cartel figure “El Mayo” Zambada.

On Friday, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, standing in for an ill Sheinbaum, told U.S. Ambassador Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica rather than to Mexico.

Elsewhere, millions of Mexican cell phone lines were suspended after an Aug. 15 mandatory registration deadline passed, though regulators say most affected users can still recover service. Mexico also abstained from an OAS vote, which passed 29-1, to convene an emergency session on Nicaragua’s move to bar opposition candidates, with representative Alejandro Encinas citing Mexico’s non-intervention principle. Friday’s mañanera, run by Rodríguez after Sheinbaum announced she had the flu, also touched on new archaeological finds in a Chiapas cave tied to Zoque ritual traditions.

Regional news roundup:

And some good news to close out the week:

Looking ahead

Several threads left open this week are likely to develop further: Security cooperation with the U.S. continues to strengthen, while trade friction between the two countries shows no sign of easing. On a practical note, cell phone users facing the next registration deadlines — Aug. 31 for numbers ending in “1” — should act before their lines are suspended.

World.title: From the archive: How to whistle like a true Mexican
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in January 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of whistling.

I have known no jealousy like the jealousy I feel when I hear Mexicans’ elaborate category of effortless whistles.

Okay fine, they’re not effortless. They just sound that way because they learned how to do it when they were kids. You know, like speaking Spanish.

Indeed, whistling is part of the language in some meaningful ways. There are specific whistles used for getting people’s attention. There are whistles for saying “Hey buddy, what’s up?” from across the street. There are whistles for saying, “But of course, my horse” — okay, maybe not exactly that, but a kind of “You know it!” with that adorable tone. There are whistles to say, “Wowza, nice butt, strange woman I don’t know!” Some whistles say, “Okay, back up your car now, a little more, a little more, a little more, stop!” There are even whistles to tell people where they can stuff it. Careful with those.

And I am going to learn them all.

A realistic goal

Well, I’m going to try. Forget turning my health or finances around; it’s too big a task. I need something I actually stand a chance at being able to bite off. Even though the prospect of practicing them takes me back to the deep humiliation I felt trying to string a four-word sentence together in Spanish while the three-year-old next to me rattled off deep, complex sentence after deep, complete sentence, I’m committed. I did it once, and I can do it again!

I won’t necessarily use them all, or use them frequently. In fact, I’m fairly certain that men whistle much more than women around here, anyway. Like cursing, it falls into a decidedly “male” category of behavior, and is seen as somewhat crass and unladylike.

I’ve also noticed that whistling is more prevalent among lower socio-economic classes than among the more well-to-do. Part of this is simply cultural habit, growing out of the need to communicate at great distances. It’s more pleasant sounding, and clearer, than shouting. If you’re willing to do some digging, there are actually some fascinating examples of whistles-as-language. There’s a cool short video about this below.

But I don’t need to be communicating over great distances in the Oaxaca countryside. I just want to have some fun.

Indigenous Whistle Language In Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

And I don’t want to go too fast, but I’m also an eager learner. This video is pretty cute, by the way, as an introduction to the meanings of different whistles.

Here are the specific ones that I want to learn:

Learning how to whistle in Mexico (in different styles, for different purposes)

The whistle to get someone’s attention

Say you’re walking along a busy street and you need to get someone’s attention. Maybe it’s a vendor, or maybe a taxi that didn’t notice you! This whistle is perfect for it. It’s also important for me personally, because my voice does not carry at all. My loudest is not very loud, and the strain on my voice physically hurts! This can either be a quick low-high sound, or the more universally recognized high-low-slightly higher.

The ‘you can count on me, buddy’ whistle

I mostly want to learn this one because I think it’s both hilarious and adorable. My partner does this one sometimes, and even though it’s kind of a joke, I am 100% charmed.

‘Hey, friend on the other side of the street!’

Finally, I’ve just got to learn this whistle. It’s short and sweet, and I don’t care that I’ve hardly ever heard it from a woman’s lips.

So those are the three goals. Three distinct whistles — I can kind of do a “pucker” whistle now, but not very well — should be manageable in a year, right?

In the meantime, I’m dying to know: can you whistle? Can you do any specifically Mexican whistles? I especially want to know how many women out there can — please let me know in the comments!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Argentina’s Central Bank Reserves Reach a Record US$50.655 Billion
World.content:

Argentina · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Argentina’s central bank posted record gross reserves of US$50.655 billion on August 21, 2026.

— How big a jump The bank added US$313 million that day, mainly from gold revaluation.

— The real story Gross reserves are a superficial measure; net reserves remain undisclosed.

— The catch The record is partly accounting, not all new cash, and risk country still above 500.

— Who it touches Foreign investors, expats, and anyone watching Argentina’s economic stability.

— What comes next Congress debates a reform to bar central bank financing of the Treasury.

Gross reserves hit a seven-year high, but the net position remains unclear.

Argentina central bank reserves reached a record US$50.655 billion on 21 August 2026. The bank added US$313 million that day, and most of it came from revaluing its gold.

The BCRA building in Buenos Aires, where the central bank manages Argentina’s reserves.

Argentina Central Bank Reserves: What Is Behind the Number

The BCRA, Argentina’s central bank, said gross reserves hit US$50.655 billion on August 21, 2026. That is the highest level in seven years, according to reports from Ámbito Financiero, El Cronista, and Infobae.

The daily increase of US$313 million was driven by a revaluation of the bank’s gold holdings. This is an accounting adjustment, not fresh foreign currency from trade or loans.

Gross reserves include assets like gold and foreign currencies. They do not reflect what the bank can quickly use to defend the peso.

Analysts warn that net reserves, which subtract short-term liabilities, are likely much lower. The BCRA has not published official net reserve figures.

The record is partly a paper gain, not new cash. That matters for anyone judging Argentina’s ability to pay imports or debts.

For a country with a history of currency crises, the size of usable reserves is key. Gross figures can mask underlying vulnerabilities.

Congress Moves to Change the Central Bank’s Charter

A bill to reform the BCRA’s organic charter has cleared committee. It is set for a vote in the Chamber of Deputies on August 26, 2026.

The reform would forbid the central bank from financing the national Treasury. This is a major step toward ending the practice of money printing to fund government spending.

The bill is identified as expediente 0171D, according to El Argentino Diario, Letra P, and Infobae. It is part of a broader package, including fiscal amnesty and patent reforms.

The reform could boost investor confidence by limiting inflation pressures. But the final text and its implementation remain unclear.

If the reform passes, the race’s record would not be at risk from government borrowing. That could make the record more sustainable.

Investors and citizens alike see this as a test of fiscal discipline. The outcome will shape monetary policy for years.

Country Risk at 505, Yet Shares Rose

Argentina’s country risk, as measured by J.P. Morgan’s EMBI+ index, closed at 505 basis points. That was a drop of 30 units, or 5.6%, in a single day.

A lower risk country score suggests investors see less chance of default. But 505 is still high compared to investment-grade countries.

Meanwhile, the S&P Merval stock index rose 1.3% in pesos on the same day, reaching 2,913,184 points. That gain came despite the high risk score.

Stocks and bonds can move differently, reflecting varied investor expectations. The day’s data shows mixed signals about Argentina’s financial health.

Even with the survey, the risk premium remains above 500 basis points. That shows lingering doubts about long-term stability.

For a foreign investor, the gap between stock optimism and bond caution is a warning. Diversification is wise in such conditions.

Market Odds on Milei’s Reelection

A local consulting firm, GMA Capital, calculates a 53.5% implied probability of President Javier Milei being reelected. This estimate comes from the forward rate between two Argentine bonds, AO27 and AO28.

This is not a poll or a prediction. It simply reflects what bond prices imply about future political outcomes.

Investors watch these market-based odds for signs of policy continuity. A higher probability suggests markets expect Milei’s reforms to continue.

But market signals can change quickly with new data or news. The 53.5% is a snapshot, not a forecast.

The record might reinforce confidence in Milei’s economic team. Yet bond markets remain cautious about the future.

Political stability matters as much as reserve levels for long-term investors. The two are closely linked.

Debt Auction Aims to Roll Over Trillions

Argentina’s next debt auction has maturities worth around 14.6 trillion pesos (US$2.8 billion). The goal is to renew those debts and attract dollars through a new bond, the Bonar 2029.

The Ministry of Economy and the Secretariat of Finance are managing the auction. Success would help cover the government’s financing needs without central bank help.

The auction comes as the BCRA reform would limit monetary financing. This makes attracting private investors even more important.

Observers note that the exact date and results of the auction are not yet public. Expectations are high, but actual demand will matter.

If the auction fails, the government might pressure the BCRA for funds. That would undermine the meaning of the record.

A successful rollover would show market trust in Argentina’s fiscal path. That trust is fragile but growing.

What Argentina Central Bank Reserves Mean if You Live or Invest Here

For investors and expats in Argentina, the record gross reserves might look like a sign of strength. But because they include gold revaluation, the real capacity to intervene in the currency market is uncertain.

The proposed BCRA reform would prohibit financing the Treasury, a move that could reduce inflation. That would change the investment climate significantly.

Foreigners should watch whether net reserves improve, not just gross figures. The gap between gross and net tells the real story.

If the reform passes, Argentina could become more predictable for long-term investment. Until then, keep an eye on the auction and market reactions.

The record is a headline number, but not the whole story. Net reserves and policy reforms matter more for daily life.

Expat workers and retirees often convert dollars to pesos. That exchange rate depends on reserve strength and market confidence.

Official Exchange Rates on August 24, 2026

The BCRA’s official communication A3500 for August 24, 2026, has not been published in available sources. The latest confirmed rates are from August 20 and 21.

On August 21, the official dollar rate was 1,497.45 Argentine pesos per US dollar. That reflects the ongoing depreciation of the peso.

For comparison, the Brazilian real traded at 5.1706 per dollar, and the Mexican peso at 16.9188. These rates help investors gauge regional currency trends.

Since the August 24 rate is unconfirmed, rely on the latest available data. Check the BCRA website for the official update.

Even with the poll, the peso continues to lose value slowly. That is a sign of persistent inflation pressures.

Foreigners sending money home or planning budgets need current rates. Check official sources before transactions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between gross and net reserves? Gross reserves are everything the central bank holds, including gold and money it owes back. Net reserves strip out what is borrowed, and Argentina central bank reserves are reported gross. How does the BCRA reform affect investors? If passed, the reform prohibits the central bank from financing the Treasury. This could reduce inflation and make Argentina more attractive for long-term investment. Why did the Merval rise while risk country remains high? Stocks and bonds reflect different expectations. The Merval rose 1.3% on August 21, while risk country fell slightly to 505, showing mixed market sentiment. What does ‘gold revaluation’ mean for reserves? It means the reported increase in reserves comes from marking gold to current market prices, not from new cash inflows. It boosts gross reserves but not necessarily usable dollars. Where can I check the official exchange rate for August 24, 2026? The BCRA’s official rate for that date is not yet published. Check the BCRA website or reliable financial news sources for updates. Is the BCRA record reserves figure sustainable? The record is partly due to gold revaluation, which is not new cash. Sustainability depends on net reserves and policy reforms.

Africa Intelligence Brief — Monday, August 24, 2026

What Nobody Has To Do

Key Facts Congo. The first verification inspectors of the eastern Congo ceasefire reach Minembwe today, nine months after the Doha framework agreement of 15 November 2025.

Every state announces more than it enforces. What distinguishes them is the size of the gap and whether anybody is permitted to measure it.

A Ceasefire Nobody Checked For Nine Months

Minembwe, today

The first verification inspectors of the eastern Congo ceasefire reach Minembwe today. The agreement they are verifying was signed four months ago.

In the interval it existed as a text and as a claim. Both parties could assert compliance and neither assertion could be tested.

Why that matters

An agreement without verification cannot be violated in any recorded sense, which means the incentive structure it was meant to create does not exist. Inspectors arriving nine months late will document a situation, not a sequence.

A Policy That Binds Nobody

Namibia, approved but not in force

Namibia has gazetted a local-content policy for its upstream oil industry, setting out what operators should do for Namibian workers and suppliers. It currently obliges nobody to do any of it.

That is not necessarily bad faith. Policies are often published before the legislation that gives them teeth, and Namibia is drafting into a basin that has not produced a barrel yet.

An Agreement Nobody Will Describe

Libya, in Tunis

Libya’s rival delegations initialled an agreement on elections, and the committee itself then denied the accuracy of leaked accounts of what it contained.

An agreement whose contents are contested by the body that convened the talks is a document rather than a settlement.

The constraint is rarely the writing of rules and almost always the existence of somebody with both the standing and the appetite to apply them.

And The Numbers Nobody Will Explain

Abuja and Accra

Nigeria has drawn about US$1.5 billion of a US$5 billion facility from Abu Dhabi and has not explained its terms. Reporting describes it as structured through a total return swap, a form that keeps the obligation off the places where obligations are usually counted.

Ghana’s central bank lost about 1.7 billion dollars on a gold purchase programme, according to the International Monetary Fund. That figure exists because an outside body went looking for it.

The One Announcement That Binds

Washington, with a date on it

The World Bank barred a Kenyan technology contractor and its founder from Bank-financed work for a minimum of five years, with release conditional on compliance over a Somalia contract. That is an announcement with an enforcement date attached.

It is also, tellingly, the only one this week issued by an institution that was not a party to the thing it was ruling on.

Elsewhere

Kenyan banks hold about seventeen billion dollars of their own government’s debt. South Africa sells Zimbabwe roughly eight times what it buys back, and French firms booked 532.1 million euros (about US$620 million) of orders from Morocco in 2025, against deliveries of 83.3 million euros, far above the prior year, though the report does not publish a comparable 2024 figure.

What This Means From Latin America

Guyana has moved to reverse four months of falling oil output with a fifth offshore project. Namibia, at an earlier stage in the same story, has just published a local-content policy with no binding force.

The comparison is the useful one. Both are new producers writing the rules for revenue they have not yet earned, and only one of them has production to bargain with.

The wider shape is familiar here. Every resource economy in this hemisphere has a shelf of local-content policies, disclosure requirements and monitoring agreements, and the ones that changed anything were the ones with an enforcement date on the page.

The Bigger Picture Verification is the cheapest part of any agreement and the part most often deferred. Signing is a political event with cameras; inspecting is a logistics problem with a budget. Across three very different files this week — a ceasefire, an oil policy and an election deal — the announcement arrived intact and the enforcement arrived late, weak or contested. A South Sudanese committee has meanwhile ordered the finance ministry to start clearing salary arrears, without setting a date, ahead of a December election. Paying people is the one obligation that cannot be deferred by drafting.

Africa Intelligence Brief August 24, 2026: What We Are Watching

Minembwe — Whether a second inspection is scheduled matters more than what this one finds.

— Whether a second inspection is scheduled matters more than what this one finds. Nigeria’s Abu Dhabi facility — The structure is the question, not the size.

— The structure is the question, not the size. Ghana’s gold inquiry — Watch whether the inquiry is given real scope.

— Watch whether the inquiry is given real scope. Libya’s initialled text — An agreement its own convenor disputes is not yet an agreement.

— An agreement its own convenor disputes is not yet an agreement. Namibian local content — The legislation, if it comes, is where this becomes real.

— The legislation, if it comes, is where this becomes real. The World Bank debarment — The week’s only announcement with an enforcement date, and it came from outside.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is happening in eastern Congo today?

The first verification inspectors of the ceasefire arrive at Minembwe, nine months after the Doha framework agreement of 15 November 2025. Nothing had been independently checked in the interval.

What did Namibia announce?

A local-content policy for its upstream oil industry, gazetted, setting out expectations for Namibian workers and suppliers. It carries no legal obligation on operators; legislation would be needed to give it force.

What is the dispute over Libya’s election deal?

Rival delegations initialled an agreement in Tunis, and the committee that initialled it has denied leaked accounts of its contents, and the head of the Presidential Council has criticised the secrecy.

What is Nigeria’s Abu Dhabi loan?

A five billion dollar facility that Nigeria has drawn on without explaining its terms. Reporting describes the arrangement as structured through a total return swap, which the finance minister confirmed publicly on 19 August, while declining to publish a spending breakdown.

World.title: Mexico’s Economy Grew 1.4% in Q2, Inflation Stays in Target
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Mexico · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Mexico’s GDP grew 1.4% in Q2 2026 versus Q1 2026.

— How big a jump The annual growth rate was 2.1% compared to Q2 2025.

— The real story Monthly readings for June have been reported inconsistently.

— The catch The 1.4% is quarterly, not annual, and core inflation sits above 3%.

— Who it touches Foreign investors and expats who track the peso (MXN) and local borrowing costs.

— What comes next Banxico, Mexico’s central bank, now expects inflation to hit 3% only by Q4 2027.

Quarterly rebound reflects solid growth, despite inconsistent monthly data and persistent services inflation.

Mexico Q2 GDP 2026 shows the economy grew 1.4% in the second quarter, compared to the first three months of the year. The data comes from INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, and is adjusted for seasonal swings.

Mexico’s GDP grew 1.4% in Q2 2026, while IGAE monthly readings for June have been reported inconsistently.

The quarterly growth figure explained

The headline number for Mexico Q2 GDP 2026 is a quarter-on-quarter rate. It means the economy was 1.4% larger in April, May, and June than in January, February, and March.

This is a seasonally adjusted figure. It removes normal calendar effects like holiday shopping or harvest seasons to show the true trend.

A separate annual rate shows a different picture. Compared to the same quarter last year, Mexico’s GDP expanded by 2.1%.

The total nominal value of the economy reached 37,530,380 million pesos (US$2.2 trillion) in Q2. That is up 6.3% from a year earlier.

This growth follows a rough start to 2026, when the economy shrank in the first quarter. The rebound suggests some recovery, but it is not yet a strong trend.

For context, this quarterly rate is similar to the 1.4% seen in Q4 2025. It is slower than the 2.0% pace of the year before, signaling a moderate expansion.

Why the monthly activity index is uncertain

Mexico Q2 GDP 2026 may look solid, but the IGAE, a monthly proxy for GDP, has reported June readings inconsistently. Some sources show a rise, others a fall, and the official data remains unclear.

This uncertainty means we cannot confirm a direction for June. The quarterly figure, however, is solid and well-documented.

The services sector, the largest part of the economy, reportedly shrank 0.1% in June. Industry, however, grew by about 0.2%.

Primary activities like farming and mining also contracted during the month. This points to an uneven recovery.

For someone living in Mexico, a falling IGAE can mean fewer job openings in retail and hospitality. It often signals slower consumer spending ahead.

The conflicting reports for June match a pattern seen in previous mid-year slowdowns. It is not yet a recession signal.

Inflation sits inside the target but remains stubborn

Annual inflation reached 3.26% in the first half of August 2026. This is within Banxico’s target corridor of 2% to 4%, and it is the sixth straight half-month period inside that range.

However, core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, was 3.93%. That is much closer to the upper limit.

Non-core inflation, including those volatile items, was much lower at 0.96%. The problem is clearly in core services prices.

High services inflation affects everyday costs like restaurant meals and haircuts, which are common for locals. It also makes it harder for the central bank to cut rates.

For investors, stubborn core inflation means the central bank will likely keep borrowing costs higher for longer. This affects bond yields and the peso.

The catch: services inflation delays the final goal

The 1.4% quarterly GDP figure is a solid growth rate, but it is quarterly, not annual. The annual rate has been reported at both 2.1% and 1.9%, but we use INEGI’s published 2.1%.

On inflation, the headline 3.26% is inside the target zone, but core inflation at 3.93% is above the 3% center. Because of this, Banxico has pushed back its forecast for hitting the 3% target to the fourth quarter of 2027.

This delay affects anyone with a mortgage or business loan in pesos. High rates keep borrowing costs elevated.

For expats planning to buy property, the rate outlook means fixed-rate loans may stay expensive. Variable rates could rise if inflation surprises.

The core inflation figure shows that while headline inflation is within range, underlying pressures remain. This is a key reason for Banxico’s cautious stance.

What this means for foreigners in Mexico

Given the uncertain monthly data in Mexico Q2 GDP 2026, expats and investors should be cautious. The economy is not showing consistent momentum.

Persistent services inflation means the central bank is unlikely to cut rates aggressively. The target rate stands at 6.50%.

High rates make borrowing in pesos more expensive for businesses and homeowners. They also make cash deposits more attractive for savers.

The peso’s official FIX rate was 16.9018 per US dollar on 24 August 2026. This is the rate banks use for settling international transactions.

If you receive remittances, the exchange rate and high local interest rates will affect your effective income. Timing your currency conversions wisely matters.

For savers, high rates on Mexican bank deposits can yield better returns than in many other countries. However, currency risk remains.

The outlook for the rest of 2026

Mexico Q2 GDP 2026 growth was a positive sign. The unclear June data is a warning that the third quarter could be weaker.

Banxico, Mexico’s central bank, has to balance a weak economy against stubborn services prices. Cutting rates too fast risks the second, and holding them too long risks the first.

Most analysts expect rates to stay high for now. The central bank’s own minutes suggest patience until prices cool down.

The next key data point will be the July IGAE figures. If the decline continues, it will confirm a mid-year slowdown.

If you are planning a trip or a move, a softer economy can mean easier hotel and restaurant prices late in 2026. It can also mean a weaker peso, which stretches money brought in from abroad.

But a slowdown also raises the risk of peso depreciation. That would make imports and foreign travel costlier for residents.

Braskem, a major Brazilian petrochemical company, filed for extrajudicial recovery on August 24, 2026. This Braskem extrajudicial recovery targets roughly US$10.9 billion (R$56.1 billion) in financial debt.

What Extrajudicial Recovery Means

Extrajudicial recovery is a negotiated path for a company to restructure debt outside of court. The company presents a plan to creditors, and once approved, a court homologates it.

This differs from judicial recovery, which happens under court supervision from the start. It also differs from Chapter 11 in the United States, which is a formal court process.

Press reports put creditor support at around a third when the request was filed. Braskem’s own notice does not publish a percentage, so treat that figure with care.

The approved plan covers only financial obligations, not debts to suppliers or customers. This is a key distinction from broader recovery processes.

No asset sales are part of the current plan. Any such sales could happen later, but no date has been set.

The Size Of The Debt

The debt targeted for restructuring is approximately US$10.9 billion. In local currency, this equals about about R$56 billion, based on an exchange rate of R$5.15 per US dollar.

This figure represents only Braskem’s financial debt. It does not include obligations to suppliers, customers, or other stakeholders.

Braskem described the process as having a ‘limited, strictly financial scope’ in its official statement. The company communicated this to Brazil’s securities regulator, the CVM.

Two Separate Legal Processes

Braskem Idesa is a joint venture in Mexico, a distinct entity from the main Brazilian company. Its Chapter 11 process does not affect the Brazilian recovery directly.

The Braskem extrajudicial recovery in Brazil is a negotiated, court-homologated path. Chapter 11 is akin to a judicial reorganization under court supervision.

Understanding these terms helps investors avoid confusion. Each process has different rules, timelines, and implications for creditors.

What Has Not Been Announced

No asset sales are part of the current recovery plan. Braskem has not announced any intention to sell assets at this stage.

There is also no formal plan for a share offering, often called a follow-on. Only generic mentions of possible capitalization exist, with no decision made.

Correcting Common Misunderstandings

Some headlines claim Braskem ‘filed for extrajudicial recovery.’ This is technically correct, but it does not mean the process is already court-approved.

— The real story Forno da Saudade has no reservations or waiters; customers order at a counter.

— Where it is At Rua Patrocínio, 1, in Carlos Prates, northwest of Belo Horizonte’s center.

— What comes next Open Monday to Saturday 4:30pm-0:30am, Sunday 3:30pm-11:30pm; arrive early.

In Belo Horizonte, a pizzeria’s customers spill onto a public square, turning it into a dining room, dance floor, and lookout.

The Belo Horizonte pizzeria Forno da Saudade turns a public square into its dining room. Customers sit, eat, and dance in Praça Zigue-Zague, which the house uses as an extension of its space.

A Square as Dining Room

In fact, the Belo Horizonte pizzeria Forno da Saudade occupies a large old house facing Praça Zigue-Zague. According to Estadão Paladar, the square works at the same time as dining room, pavement, dance floor, and lookout.

Therefore, the public space becomes part of the venue. In fact, the city’s tourism portal notes there is live music and forró for dancers at the address.

The square’s name, Praça Zigue-Zague, means Zigzag Square. Meanwhile, this public space is a key part of the dining experience.

The square’s public nature means anyone can join the gathering. However, the house uses this open space as its own dining room.

Belo Horizonte pizzeria’s neighborhood location

Forno da Saudade sits at Rua Patrocínio, 1, in the Carlos Prates neighborhood. This residential area lies on high ground northwest of Belo Horizonte’s center.

Belo Horizonte, often shortened to BH, is the capital of Minas Gerais state in southeastern Brazil. It is the country’s sixth-largest city, about 430 km north of Rio de Janeiro.

The address is Rua Patrocínio, 1, in Carlos Prates. In addition, the city’s tourism portal lists this exact location.

Carlos Prates sits on high ground northwest of the city center. In addition, the neighborhood is residential and quiet.

The Meaning Behind the Name

The name Forno da Saudade translates roughly as ‘the oven of longing. ‘ Meanwhile, saudade is a Portuguese word for a warm longing for something absent.

So the name itself evokes a sense of nostalgia. This fits the cozy, communal atmosphere of the square.

The name evokes a sense of nostalgia for what is absent. However, the venue itself is a permanent, welcoming place.

The name evokes a warm longing for what is absent. Still, the venue itself is a permanent, welcoming place.

How Service Works

The pizzeria does not take reservations and has no table service. Instead, you order at a counter, receive a paper ticket or ficha, and collect your food and drink yourself.

According to BH Dicas, you can sit in the square itself or at some tables. There are no waiters, and entry is free, though food and drink are paid for.

You order at a counter and receive a paper ticket. After that, you collect your food and drink yourself, with no waiters.

Monday Forró Nights

On Mondays, the square hosts forró, a northeastern Brazilian dance music played with accordion, zabumba drum, and triangle. G1 Minas lists the forró at Forno da Saudade starting from 6pm.

Meanwhile, a specialist forró listing gives the start time as 8pm. Both times are published, so arrive early to catch the music and the lively atmosphere.

Forró is a northeastern Brazilian dance music played in couples. In addition, it is a weekly fixture in Belo Horizonte bars and squares.

Both published start times are 6pm and 8pm, attributed to G1 and a forró listing. Meanwhile, the square becomes a dance floor for couples.

Who Runs the Pizzeria

Moreover, the pizzeria is run by Grupo Viela, a local hospitality group. Rafael Quick is the owner and a member of Grupo Viela, according to BHAZ.

The venue occupies a large old house up in Carlos Prates, as described by Rede 98. It’s a permanent establishment, not a temporary event.

Rafael Quick is the owner and a member of Grupo Viela. Meanwhile, the group runs this pizzeria-bar in a large old house.

Grupo Viela runs this pizzeria-bar in a large old house. Moreover, Rafael Quick is the owner and a member of the group.

The Sign Controversy

The pizzeria has had its run-ins with city hall. In 2025, BHAZ reported a dispute over its illuminated sign, raised publicly by former city councillor Gabriel Azevedo.

However, the city hall denied this. The PBH stated that inspectors gave guidance to remove banners from a cultural heritage building, but no fine was recorded.

The owner said the sum related to a banner announcing a temporary closure, not the sign. The city hall denied any fine related to the sign.

As a result, the inspectors’ union said the issue was with the law, not enforcement.

No Reservations, No Cover

The house does not take reservations, and entry is free. Estadão Paladar’s service note confirms the hours and no-reservations policy.

Rede 98 advises arriving early, as the square fills up. The forró gathering is described as free and public space.

Entry is free, and the square is a public space. However, you still pay for your food and drinks.

Plan Your Visit

Forno da Saudade is open Monday to Saturday from 4:30pm to 0:30am, and Sunday from 3:30pm to 11:30pm. It’s best to arrive early, especially on Monday for the forró.

While menu prices are not published, you can expect pizza and focaccia. The square is public, so you can enjoy the open-air dining experience.

The venue is open Monday to Saturday from 4:30pm to 0:30am. Meanwhile, Sunday hours are 3:30pm to 11:30pm.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Forno da Saudade located?

The Belo Horizonte pizzeria is at Rua Patrocínio, 1, in the Carlos Prates neighborhood. It faces Praça Zigue-Zague, which serves as its outdoor dining area.

Does Forno da Saudade take reservations?

No, the pizzeria does not take reservations. Entry is free, and you order at a counter, then collect your food and drink yourself.

What are the opening hours?

It’s open Monday to Saturday from 4:30pm to 0:30am, and Sunday from 3:30pm to 11:30pm. Arrive early, as there is no reservation system.

Is there live music on Mondays?

Yes, on Mondays there is forró in the square. G1 Minas says it starts at 6pm, while a forró listing says 8pm, so check both times.

Samba do Trabalhador — Renascença Clube, Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí. Moacyr Luz’s “workers’ samba” has run on Mondays since 2005, more than twenty years — a roots-samba roda born for musicians who only had Mondays off. The house opens at 4.30 pm, the samba starts at 5, and the group plays until about 9.45 pm. Tickets are R$30 (about US$6) in advance through Sympla, R$40 (US$8) on the door. The room is covered, so unlike the Pedra do Sal it runs whatever the weather. It is a beloved, joyful, unpretentious institution.

Lapa is closed tonight — Carioca da Gema, Rio Scenarium and the rest of the neighbourhood’s samba houses do not open on Mondays. Carioca da Gema runs Tuesday to Saturday, opening at 7.30 pm with the show at 8.30 pm and a R$30 (about US$6) cover midweek. If you want Lapa, come back tomorrow.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Late afternoon (4:30 pm) — Samba do Trabalhador opens in Andaraí, an early, all-evening affair.

Early evening (6–7 pm) — The Vik Muniz show at CCBB before it closes, or dinner near the port.

Main event (7 pm onward) — The Pedra do Sal roda gets going and fills through the evening.

Later (8:30 pm onward) — The roda at the Pedra do Sal is at its fullest; the Samba do Trabalhador runs until about 9.45 pm.

Getting home — Rideshare door-to-door; the port and Andaraí both quieten quickly once the music stops.

Scenes & Sounds

Street samba — The night’s heart: the free Pedra do Sal roda in the port, Rio’s flagship Monday samba. Where: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde.

Roots samba — Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador, a Monday institution up in Andaraí since 2005. Where: Renascença Clube (Andaraí).

Samba houses — All of Lapa’s rooms are shut on a Monday, Carioca da Gema included; it reopens Tuesday. Bip Bip in Copacabana is traditionally a Monday choro night, but publishes no schedule. Where: Bip Bip (Rua Almirante Gonçalves 50, Copacabana) — check first.

Culture — CCBB is open with the Vik Muniz show; a rare Monday option in the centre. Where: CCBB (Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro).

Closed tonight — Rio Scenarium and Carioca da Gema both rest on a Monday and reopen midweek. Where: Carioca da Gema from Tuesday, Rio Scenarium from Wednesday.

Pick Your Night

Free and essential: The Pedra do Sal roda — the pick of the night.

An institution: Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí.

Indoors and seated: The Samba do Trabalhador — the Renastença is covered, so rain is not a risk.

Culture first: The Vik Muniz show at CCBB before it closes.

Quiet: Most of Lapa is closed — Monday is a night for the samba, not the strip.

Where to Go

Pedra do Sal — Saúde (Pequena África) The stone steps in the old port where Carioca samba was born — a free, open-air largo with a loose, street-party energy, and its flagship roda on Mondays. Tonight: The Monday roda — open-air samba from around 7 pm into the night. Best time: Monday is the flagship; get there early for the atmosphere before the crush. Cost: Free to attend. Drinks from bars and vendors on a cash basis — carry small bills. Address: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde Getting there: VLT to the port, or rideshare door-to-door. Metro Uruguaiana is about 1.3 km away through a quiet Centro after dark — not the walk we would recommend. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Wear comfortable shoes and keep an eye on your belongings in the crowd.

Samba do Trabalhador — Renascença Clube, Andaraí Moacyr Luz’s legendary Monday roda, an institution of roots samba, running since 2005, in a Zona Norte social club, drawing a mixed, devoted crowd. Tonight: Moacyr Luz and the Samba do Trabalhador, several sets across the late afternoon and evening. Doors 4:30 pm. Best time: Get there near the 4:30 pm opening for a spot; it fills up. Cost: Tickets from around R$40 (US$8) via Sympla or Sympla. Buy ahead. Address: Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí Tickets: eventim.com.br Getting there: Rideshare is easiest to Andaraí, in the Zona Norte. Arrange your ride home too. Good to know: An early, all-evening affair — very different in rhythm from a late Lapa night.

Carioca da Gema — Lapa Lapa’s most awarded samba house, going since 2000. It is closed tonight — the house runs Tuesday to Saturday. Tonight: Live samba/MPB, doors from 6 pm, band around 8:30 pm. Check the site for tonight’s act. Best time: Monday to Thursday 6 pm–2 am; calmer and more local at the start of the week. Cost: Cover around R$30 (US$6) early in the week. Card and cash. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá 79, Lapa/Centro Website: barcariocadagema.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk into Lapa. Rideshare to the door at night. Good to know: A reliable indoor fallback if the largo’s crowds aren’t for you.

CCBB Rio — Centro The Banco do Brasil’s grand cultural centre in a neoclassical landmark — free, high-quality exhibitions, and open on Mondays. Tonight: “Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu” and other shows. Open until 8 pm; last entry around 7 pm. Best time: Wednesday to Monday, 9 am to 8 pm. Closed Tuesdays. Cost: Free; collect a ticket at the box office or on the CCBB site. Café on site. Address: Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro Website: ccbb.com.br/rio-de-janeiro Getting there: Metro Uruguaiana or Carioca, short walk. A short ride to the port afterwards. Good to know: A calm early-evening stop before the Pedra do Sal roda nearby.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Centro / Saúde / Gamboa: The old port and the cradle of samba — the Pedra do Sal is its Monday heart. Alive for the roda, quiet otherwise, so travel by car.

Andaraí / Zona Norte: A residential northern district, home to the Renascença Clube and Samba do Trabalhador. Rideshare in and out.

Lapa: Closed on a Monday, with no exceptions. The neighbourhood comes back from Tuesday.

Copacabana: Home to Bip Bip, traditionally a Monday choro night, though the bar publishes no schedule. Its big samba rodas are Thursday and Sunday. An easy beachfront base.

Santa Teresa: Bohemian hilltop of cobbled lanes and artist bars. A relaxed early dinner; rideshare up and down.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

A quiet Monday — the big queer parties run Thursday to Sunday, so tonight is low-key. The Pedra do Sal roda, though, is a mixed, welcoming, everyone-together kind of night.

Everyday-friendly spaces — The port roda and the Renascença are relaxed and open to all.

Money & How Paying Works Free at the largo: Pedra do Sal is free to attend; drinks are cash-based from surrounding bars and vendors. Carry about R$150 (US$30) in small notes. Tickets: Samba do Trabalhador sells through Sympla — R$30 (US$6) in advance, R$40 (US$8) on the door. Buy ahead. Cover: Lapa’s houses are shut tonight. From Tuesday, Carioca da Gema charges about R$30 (US$6), added to your bill separately from drinks. Tipping: 10% is usually added to the bill as ‘serviço’. Check before adding more.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: MetrôRio runs roughly 5 am to midnight Monday to Saturday. Check the last-train time for your line before you rely on it.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and the safest way home from the port and Andaraí late at night. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

The port at night: Lively at the largo, quiet around it — book a car door-to-door rather than walking to find one.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets, and keep it away in the largo crowd. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Andaraí: Residential and off the tourist track — rideshare directly to and from the club.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Monday such a big samba night in Rio?

Tradition — Monday was historically the musicians’ day off, so the rodas grew up around it. The Pedra do Sal’s Monday gathering and Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador are both institutions, making Monday one of the best samba nights of the week.

Is Pedra do Sal free, and is it safe?

It’s free and open-air, and generally fine when it’s busy, which it is on a Monday. Take only what you need, keep your phone away in the crowd, and rideshare door-to-door rather than walking through the quiet streets around it.

I’ve just landed at GIG (Galeão) tonight. Where should I go?

Straight to the Pedra do Sal — the roda runs into the night and the port is about a 25–35 minute rideshare from Galeão. Carry small cash for drinks, and take a rideshare door-to-door.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

Not at all. The music does the work and the crowds are welcoming. A smile, a cold beer, and cash for the drinks are all you need.

Sources: Riotur — Pedra do Sal Monday roda, Riotur — Samba do Trabalhador, Carioca da Gema — opening days, Rio Scenarium — opening days, CCBB Rio — Vik Muniz. Currency converted at R$5.1625 = US$1, the Banco Central do Brasil PTAX rate for 21 August 2026., visitrio.com.br (Pedra do Sal)

World.title: Paraguay Waterway Toll Fight Reopens Over Argentine Charge
World.content:
Paraguay · TRADE

Key Facts — What happened Paraguay’s shipping sector is reviving its fight against Argentina’s toll on the Paraguay-Paraná waterway.

— The toll US$1.30 per net registered tonne on the northern stretch from Santa Fe northwards.

— The real story The toll can absorb a large part of the margin on agricultural goods, hitting exporters.

— The catch The dispute has run since 2023 with no resolution; no fresh Argentine statement was found for August 2026.

— Where it hits Paraguayan cargo uses this corridor to reach the Atlantic, shared by five countries.

— What comes next Paraguay’s claim within Mercosur remains open, with no ruling or award reported.

Paraguay’s shipping sector is reviving its push against Argentina’s toll on the Paraguay-Paraná waterway, a charge that can eat into agricultural profits.

A barge convoy on the Paraná at Encarnación, on the route Paraguayan grain takes to the sea.
