The Paraguay waterway toll is back on the table. Paraguay’s shipping sector is reviving its effort to cut what Argentina charges on the Hidrovía Paraguay-Paraná.

Argentina says the fee funds waterway maintenance. Paraguayan shipowners say it eats into farm export margins.

The Paraguay Waterway Toll Dispute Reopens

However, Paraguay’s shipping sector is reviving its effort to reduce the impact of the toll charged by Argentina on the Hidrovía Paraguay-Paraná. The report from La Razón on Wednesday 19 August 2026 says the sector seeks to reactivate efforts to lower the toll’s impact.

The toll can absorb a large part of the margin on agricultural products, according to Paraguay’s shipping sector. This warning comes from the sector as a whole, not from any specific chamber or federation.

The dispute has been running since 2023, with no closure found in August 2026. Meanwhile, both governments maintain their positions on the waterway toll.

What Is the Paraguay-Paraná Waterway

The Hidrovía Paraguay-Paraná is a system of navigable rivers; in fact, it carries transport between Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay. It uses mainly the Paraguay and Paraná rivers and serves as the main export corridor for Paraguayan cargo to the Atlantic.

The waterway is shared by five countries; therefore, its importance to Paraguay is huge. For example, Paraguayan cargo relies on this corridor to reach global markets.

The waterway is the main export corridor for Paraguayan cargo to the Atlantic. However, it is shared by five countries, each with its own interests.

The Toll Rate and Its Stretch

The international toll on the northern stretch of the waterway, from Santa Fe northwards, stands at US$1.30 per net registered tonne. Santa Fe is an Argentine river port city that marks the boundary of this stretch.

By contrast, other tariffs on Argentina’s Vía Navegable Troncal reach US$4.30 per net registered tonne on other stretches. The two figures apply to different stretches and should not be merged.

The northern stretch, from Santa Fe northwards, carries the US$1.30 per net registered tonne toll. In addition, other stretches have tariffs reaching US$4.30 per net registered tonne.

Argentina’s Justification for the Toll

Argentina has maintained the toll and justified it as financing the maintenance of the waterway. This position was documented in coverage from El Destape Web on 23 September 2023 and La Política Online on 2 November 2023.

Argentina’s stance is part of the dispute; in addition, it must be reported alongside Paraguay’s position. The toll applies to vessels including Paraguayan-flagged ones on the Vía Navegable Troncal.

Argentina’s justification, from 2023 coverage, is that the toll finances waterway maintenance. However, no fresh official statement from Argentina was found for August 2026.

Paraguay’s Challenge Since 2023

Since 2023, Paraguay has challenged the toll Argentina imposed and has raised a claim within Mercosur, the Southern Common Market. Paraguay argues the charge affects free navigation of the waterway and the competitiveness of its exports.

The dispute has never been closed. Paraguayan coverage records a formal complaint and diplomatic tension over the toll, but no definitive resolution has been reached.

Paraguay’s claim within Mercosur argues the toll affects free navigation. However, no ruling or award has been reported on this case.

The Waterway’s Cargo Volumes

Overall, the Hidrovía is forecast to move 28 million tonnes during 2026, according to Mundo Fluvial Marítimo on 14 August 2026. This figure describes the entire waterway, shared by five countries, not just Paraguay, although it is often misunderstood.

Moreover, in 2023, the river sector carried 24 million tonnes. Almost 46 per cent of the goods came from Paraguay, as reported on 4 October 2024.

This is a different claim from the 2026 forecast. The 2026 forecast of 28 million tonnes covers the entire waterway, not just Paraguay.

In contrast, the 2023 figure of 24 million tonnes is also waterway-wide, with Paraguay’s share at almost 46 per cent.

Paraguay’s Growing River Fleet

Meanwhile, Paraguay’s shipping sector is expanding. In addition, plans add around 15 new tugs and more than 400 barges over the next two years.

This is according to La Nación on 21 January 2026. This growth reflects Paraguay’s ambition as a regional river power.

Asamar, a Paraguayan shipping association, reports 3,445 Paraguayan-flagged vessels operating on the waterway, including 2,700 dry bulk barges and 380 tugs. Their combined static cargo capacity is 4,507,737 tonnes, plus 10,812 twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, the standard container measure.

Plans add around 15 new tugs and more than 400 barges over the next two years. However, this growth is separate from the fleet counts reported by different sources.

Different Fleet Counts Over Time

Various sources have given different fleet counts over the years. For example, Asamar reported more than 2,500 units in April 2024, while La Nación cited at least 3,200 barges in September 2023.

In addition, Paraguay’s industry minister told ABC Color on 1 August 2024 that the country has 2,200 barges. In fact, it boasts being the third largest fleet in the world.

That claim is the minister’s own wording and should be attributed to him. The industry minister’s claim of being the third largest fleet is his own wording.

Meanwhile, the various counts reflect different dates and sources.

What the Paraguay Waterway Toll Means for Trade

The Paraguay waterway toll is a key issue for Paraguayan exports, as the waterway is the main corridor to the Atlantic. The toll can absorb a significant part of agricultural margins, affecting competitiveness.

Overall, the dispute remains unresolved, with both sides holding firm. The Paraguay waterway toll will continue to be a point of tension between the two countries.

The toll’s impact on agricultural margins is a key concern for the sector. However, no total cost or annual bill has been calculated from the toll rate.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Paraguay waterway toll?

Paraguay’s waterway toll is a fee Argentina charges on ships using the Hidrovía Paraguay-Paraná. This applies to the Vía Navegable Troncal, which lies inside Argentina.

Why is Paraguay challenging the toll?

Paraguay argues the toll affects free navigation of the waterway and the competitiveness of its exports. Since 2023, Paraguay has raised a claim within Mercosur, but no resolution has been reached.

How much cargo moves on the waterway?

The whole Hidrovía is forecast to move 28 million tonnes in 2026. In 2023, the river sector carried 24 million tonnes, with nearly 46 per cent of that cargo coming from Paraguay.

What is Argentina’s justification for the toll?

Argentina maintains the toll and says it finances the maintenance of the waterway. This justification was documented in 2023 coverage and remains Argentina’s standing position.

Sources: La Razón; Mundo Fluvial Marítimo; Asamar; La Nación (Paraguay); ABC Color; Revista Protagonista; Primera Edición; El Destape Web; La Política Online.

World.title: PACT, Government to launch Youth Climate Academy and Climate Education initiative
World.content:
PACT, Government to launch Youth Climate Academy and Climate Education initiative

By Zoila Palma: Following the opening ceremony for Belize Climate Week 2026 on August 21 in Punta Gorda, the Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT) facilitated a series of afternoon engagements focused on strengthening youth leadership and building environmental resilience.

A key development was the signing of a letter of intent between PACT and the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management to establish a Youth Climate Academy.

The proposed Youth Climate Academy represents a strategic partnership aimed at equipping young Belizeans with the knowledge, skills and tools needed to participate meaningfully in climate action.

The afternoon programme also featured the official launch of the National Climate Change Education Policy (NCAEP), an initiative designed to strengthen Belize’s capacity to respond to climate-related challenges.

The launch concluded with the presentation of 32 scholarship awards to representatives from various organizations who will participate in piloting the programme.

World.title: Belize Climate Week 2026 launched in Toledo, promoting innovation and climate resilience
World.content:
Belize Climate Week 2026 launched in Toledo, promoting innovation and climate resilience

By Zoila Palma: The 5th National Climate Week officially got underway on Friday, August 21, 2026, with an opening ceremony at the Punta Gorda Sporting Complex in Punta Gorda Town.

The four-day event, organized by the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management through the Climate Change Department, is being held under the theme, “Where Innovation Meets Impact: Driving Resilience, Scaling Technology, and Expanding Inclusion in Climate Action.”

Climate Week 2026 began with a community parade and will continue through Monday, August 24, featuring panel discussions, interactive activities and exhibition booths.

The initiative provides an opportunity for Belizeans to learn more about climate change, share ideas and explore practical solutions to help communities become more resilient.

Prime Minister John Briceño delivered the keynote address during the opening ceremony.

The event is also highlighting the evolution of Belize’s climate policy, including the Climate Change and Carbon Market Initiatives Act 2026, which is expected to play an important role in advancing the country’s climate agenda.

Minister of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management Orlando Habet said the government is working to strengthen Belize’s legal and institutional framework while improving access to climate financing and technology.

“The government is putting the foundations in place, strengthening the legal framework, turning national commitments into investment priorities,” Habet said.

The decision to host Climate Week in Toledo is also intended to highlight the contributions of women, Indigenous peoples and youth to climate action and decision-making.

CEO Milagro Matus said Toledo provides an ideal setting for discussions on resilience, noting that “Climate action is now part of national development” and is connected to how Belize grows food, manages waste, protects forests and seas, builds communities and prepares for the future.

World.title: PM Briceño begins official visit to Honduras, eyes stronger Belize-Honduras cooperation
World.content:
PM Briceño begins official visit to Honduras, eyes stronger Belize-Honduras cooperation

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister John Briceño was formally welcomed in Honduras on Sunday, August 23, 2026, with a red-carpet and military reception marking the start of his official visit to the neighboring country.

Briceño is scheduled to meet with Honduran President Nasry Asfura as both governments seek to strengthen bilateral relations and expand cooperation.

The official visit is expected to focus on shared priorities between Belize and Honduras, with discussions aimed at identifying opportunities for deeper collaboration.

The engagement comes as both neighboring countries continue to explore areas of mutual interest and strengthen ties across various sectors.

Briceño travelled to Honduras with a Belizean delegation that includes Minister of Health and Wellness Kevin Bernard, Chief Executive Officer in the Office of the Prime Minister Narda Garcia, CEO in the Ministry of Health and Wellness Julio Sabido, and CEO in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Ambassador Oscar Arnold.

During the official military reception, Briceño also met with Belizean cadets Fernando Valladarez and Perfecto Aldana, who are currently pursuing their studies at the Honduran Military Academy.

World.title: Back to School: Thousands of High School students begin 2026–2027 school year
World.content:
Back to School: Thousands of High School students begin 2026–2027 school year

By Zoila Palma: The 2026–2027 academic year officially begins today for high school students across Belize, as thousands of students return to classrooms nationwide to begin a new chapter in their educational journey.

Over the past several days, students and parents have participated in orientation sessions designed to help students transition into their new school environments.

Students have been introduced to school rules and expectations, met their teachers and classmates, and familiarized themselves with their new surroundings.

For many students, the start of the school year represents an exciting milestone as they work toward their academic goals and future careers. Schools have been preparing lessons and activities to welcome students and create an engaging learning environment throughout the academic year.

The students entering classrooms today will eventually become the professionals and leaders who shape Belize’s future, including doctors, educators, scientists, engineers, attorneys and other contributors to national development.

Along the way, they are expected to encounter new opportunities, friendships, experiences and challenges.

As students begin the new school year, they are being encouraged to embrace both the successes and challenges ahead.

Every setback can provide an opportunity to learn and grow, while determination, faith and perseverance can help them overcome obstacles.

World.title: 23 year old Belize City baker shot dead, body found hours later
World.content:
23 year old Belize City baker shot dead, body found hours later

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 23 year old Belize City baker was shot dead early Sunday morning, with his body discovered hours after the shooting.

Police received information around 7am that a body had been found in a yard on Arlington Drive, near a green apartment building.

The man has been identified as Christopher Smith Jr., 23, of Linda Vista Street.

Initial investigations indicate that residents in the area heard several gunshots shortly after 1am. Smith was found six hours later lying motionless on his back in the yard of a residence on McKenzie Lane.

Police observed what appeared to be a gunshot wound to the left side of his head and another to his left shoulder.

Four expended 9mm casings were recovered from the scene.

His body was identified by his father, Christopher Smith Sr., a police officer.

Police investigations into the circumstances surrounding the shooting continue.

World.title: Jorge Rosales wins convention, eyes historic third term as Benque Mayor
World.content:
Jorge Rosales wins convention, eyes historic third term as Benque Mayor

By Zoila Palma: Incumbent Mayor Jorge Rosales has secured the PUP’s mayoral candidacy for the 2027 municipal elections after defeating Jenny Martinez at the party’s convention in Benque Viejo del Carmen on Sunday.

Rosales received 458 votes, edging Martinez, who polled 449 votes in a closely contested race.

The victory puts Rosales on course to seek an unprecedented third consecutive term as Mayor of Benque Viejo del Carmen.

If successful in the 2027 municipal elections, Rosales would make history as the first mayor in the border towns to serve three consecutive terms, further extending his tenure in local government.

Rosales first entered the mayoral race in 2020 after years of working in the construction industry and community development.

Born on March 7, 1973, he is the eldest of 12 children of Irene and Marcos Rosales. He attended Mount Carmel Primary School, Mopan Technical High School and later Belize Technical College before establishing his own construction company.

As Mayor, Rosales has continued to promote municipal services and development initiatives in Benque Viejo, working alongside the town council on projects aimed at improving the community.

His latest convention victory now gives him the opportunity to return to voters in 2027 and ask for another term, with the potential to make history by becoming the first mayor of the border towns to serve three consecutive terms.

World.title: Leader of the Opposition warns 12% hotel tax could hurt Belize tourism
World.content:
Leader of the Opposition warns 12% hotel tax could hurt Belize tourism

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton is calling for rigorous public scrutiny of the Belize Tourism Board’s proposal to raise the hotel accommodation tax from 9% to 12%.

In a statement titled “Do Not Tax Tourism Into Decline,” Panton described the move as a 33% increase in the tax rate that would add directly to the cost of hotel stays.

She warned that the change could push visitors to shorten their stays, choose cheaper lodging, spend less on tours and restaurants, or pick competing destinations altogether.

“Even a modest decline in bookings or length of stay can have significant consequences in a tourism-dependent economy,” the statement reads, pointing to hotels, tour operators, restaurants, transport providers, tour guides, water taxi operators, artisans and farmers who rely on visitor spending.

Panton said small and medium sized businesses would feel it hardest, as they operate on narrow margins.

She is calling on government and the BTB to publish revenue projections and expected effects on occupancy, employment and small business activity before proceeding.

She also demanded an independent audit of the $50 million tourism infrastructure bond.

World.title: Jorge Rosales defeats Jenny Martinez in PUP convention in Benque Viejo
World.content:
Jorge Rosales defeats Jenny Martinez in PUP convention in Benque Viejo

By Zoila Palma: Incumbent Benque Viejo del Carmen Mayor Jorge Rosales has retained his position as the PUP’s mayoral candidate after narrowly defeating Jenny Martinez at Sunday’s PUP convention.

Rosales secured 458 votes, edging Martinez, who received 449 votes.

Among those present was former PUP area representative Jorge “Milin” Espat.

Espat expressed disappointment with the convention process, particularly the disqualification of two candidates from Martinez’s team.

“The people are displeased with the representation of the town,” Espat said during an interview.

Espat also questioned the decision to disqualify the two candidates, arguing that voters should have been given the opportunity to choose from all eligible candidates.

“I am very unhappy that there were two teams and two candidates for Team Jenny were disqualified, and I do believe it’s supposed to be a choice for the people, give the people a choice and an opportunity to select the candidates that will represent them,” he stated.

Espat also said he was also disappointed with the turnout.

“I am very displeased that the internal problems of the party, I would like to say, bring us to this. For me, it’s a very low turnout,” he said.

Rosales now moves forward as the PUP’s mayoral candidate for Benque Viejo del Carmen.

World.title: ‘Long overdue’
World.content:
Minister of National Security and Deputy Prime Minister Dr Horace Chang and Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange are all smiles as they receive the keys to the third Government-run shelter for women facing domestic abuse. (Photo: JIS)

LOCAL gender advocates have welcomed news that work has been completed on a third shelter for victims of domestic abuse.

Minister with responsibility for gender affairs Olivia Grange made the announcement last Friday as she toured the facility at an undisclosed location.

“We made a commitment that we would establish three centres, safe spaces for women, and we have achieved that,” said Grange as she pointed out that prior to the Dr Andrew Holness-led Administration there were no State-run shelters for women wishing to leave violent relationships.

In the last few years the Government completed, and is operating, two shelters for women. Grange said the addition of the third shelter will enable the ministry to offer up to 70 safe spaces for women and their children.

Grange said the completion of this third shelter, which is scheduled to begin providing a safe space for women after September 1, enables the Government to provide much-needed services to vulnerable females across the entire island.

“The completion of this space advances the gender agenda, because what we have been able to do now is to provide the spaces across the island, and we are now better equipped that when we get the call we are able to activate the kind of network that is necessary to move [women in abusive situations] into safe spaces,” said Grange.

On Sunday, gender and development practitioner Judith Wedderburn told the Jamaica Observer that the new shelter was long overdue.

“It is certainly very welcome because, not only from my experience but from the reports of women who do suffer, they have been beaten by a male partner and have experienced gender-based violence. The data does show us that it’s not getting better. More and more reports are coming out that it is happening,” said Wedderburn

According to Wedderburn, she became aware of plans to construct the new shelter through discussions with officials of the Bureau of Gender Affairs, however she was uncertain of the completion time.

“I am acknowledging that I have been in meetings in the last couple months where it was reported by somebody from the bureau that a third shelter was going to be built in a different part of the island, outside of Kingston. My understanding was it was going to serve the western part of the island,” said Wedderburn.

Pointing to a recent article published by the Jamaica Gleaner headlined, ‘The cop who finally listened’, Wedderburn said the presence of another shelter in the country serves as a call to action.

“Two women who recounted years of fear after ending abusive relationships are grateful to a corporal for standing with them. What it said was the woman who had been so badly abused was paying tribute to the only policeman who took her report seriously, the only policeman that supported her. And if you reflect on not just this article but other reports, on many occasions, unfortunately, a woman will not gather up the strength to go to a police station to report the incident,” Wedderburn argued.

Welcoming the initiative Joy Crawford, co-founder and executive director of female support group Eve for Life, told the Observer that the move strengthens the national response to gender-based violence (GBV) and expands access to safety for women and children leaving abusive situations.

“We recommend convening a robust, national GBV shelter working group comprising Government, NGOs, community-based organisations and other stakeholders to improve coordination, effectiveness, and accountability across the shelter system. This should include deliberate efforts to strengthen and expand non-government shelter models, recognising that Government cannot do this alone,” said Crawford.

She told the Observer that the country needs more diverse, accessible safe spaces across the island for survivors with different needs, including women with children, women with complex needs, adolescents, and other vulnerable groups.

“NGOs and community organisations play vital roles in victim identification, referral, psychosocial support, and sustained engagement. Formal referral pathways and partnerships can help survivors access appropriate services and safe accommodation earlier,” added Crawford.

For advocacy officer at Jamaica Coalition for a Healthy Society Philippa Davies, the provision of a third shelter by the Government is a commendable initiative but it is unfortunate that the problem of GBV exists.

“It is always better that society encourages, teaches, and supports healthy, safe relationships between men and women. As such, the family is the fundamental foundational institution of any society. The very real need for such places is evidence of family pathology, which is often passed on through generations,” said Davies.

She argued that the Government needs to establish a Ministry of the Family to address the critical role of the family and the need to prioritise its welfare.

“This would include strongly encouraging women and men to exercise discernment when choosing romantic and life partners, and to seek wise advice before and when challenges arise. It is scientifically established that the brain hormones released during sex bonds partners to the point of overshadowing danger signals such as the potential for or the occurrence of abuse,” added Davies who argued that the Government should also consider providing support for men who may be victims of abuse.

In announcing the completion of the new facility Grange said the Government-run shelters not only provide safety but also provide a therapeutic environment for women to rebuild their lives.

“We not only ensure that we protect them, but we help them to gain skills where they don’t have skills, we provide counselling, we have adequate space that we can facilitate a family — mother and children,” said Grange.

She revealed that during the last few years, one shelter hosted a mother and five of her children, while another mother gave birth while residing at another shelter.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang, acting in his capacity as chairman of the Citizens Business Group — a Government team that is mandated to manage social interventions across the country — said the establishment of Government-run shelters for women has been a big part of a programme to seek to impact, in a positive way, a number of vulnerable communities in Jamaica and, in particular in this case, women who have suffered abuse.

Chang noted that in the past few years the ministry has established domestic violence intervention centres at selected police stations as part of the strategy to eliminate domestic violence.

World.title: People and culture give Ja tourism edge, says Tortuga Resorts CEO
World.content:
Member of Parliament for St James East Central, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett (front row, third right), members of his East Central Education Fund team, and chief executive officer of Tortuga Resorts Leonardo Schlesinger (front row, right), stand with recipients of the constituency’s 2026 tertiary awards at the Montego Bay Convention Centre last Thursday. Horace Hines

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Leo Schlesinger, chief executive officer of Tortuga Resorts which recently acquired Hyatt Hotels’ interest in Playa Hotels & Resorts brand, says Jamaica’s greatest competitive tourism advantage is its culture and people — which no other destination can reproduce.

“Many countries have beautiful beaches. Anyone can copy a beach [but] nobody can copy Jamaican culture — that is Jamaica’s true competitive advantage,” Schlesinger told the St James East Central Scholarship and Welfare Fund’s annual tertiary awards at Montego Bay Convention Centre last Thursday.

According to Schlesinger, the warmth, energy, music, food, humour and authenticity associated with Jamaica give the island a distinctive appeal in the global tourism marketplace.

“Guests may forget the room they stayed in [but] they never forget how Jamaicans make them feel,” declared Schlesinger.

He said the value of that cultural advantage extends well beyond tourism branding as culture has become an important economic asset for Jamaica.

“When tourism is 30 per cent of the economy, culture is, in a very real sense, one-third of the Jamaican economy.

“Culture is not just heritage; it is a tool for the future. We often talk about culture as something to preserve. In Jamaica’s case, we should also think of culture as something we use to create the future,” added Schlesinger.

Tortuga Resorts has expanded its footprint in Jamaica through the acquisition of the former Playa properties — including Secrets, Breathless, Hyatt Ziva, Hyatt Zilara and Dreams resorts — and Schlesinger said the company plans to maintain its focus on the Jamaican market.

“We are deeply invested in Jamaica, and we intend to keep investing in the country,” said Schlesinger.

He argued that tourism’s economic impact reaches far beyond hotels, with visitors generating opportunities for airport workers, taxi operators, hotel employees, farmers, fishermen, construction workers, retailers, musicians, and other service providers.

The Tortuga Resorts CEO warned, however, that Jamaica’s ability to sustain its competitive advantage would ultimately depend on the quality of its human capital.

“The countries that succeed will not necessarily be the ones with the most resources. They will be the ones with the best educated, most adaptable, and most innovative people,” he said.

Schlesinger said while Jamaica faces significant challenges — including climate change, hurricanes, labour constraints, immigration, and infrastructure gaps — its people remain its most valuable resource.

“If you invest in a person in their education, skill, confidence, and creativity, the person grows,” he said. “Knowledge grows when it’s shared. Skills grow when they’re practised. Ideas grow when people collaborate,”

He called on universities to move beyond simply preparing students for employment and underscored that tertiary institutions have an equally important responsibility to develop critical thinkers and responsible citizens who will question, analyse, distinguish fact from opinion, listen to ideas they disagree with, and think independently.

“A healthy democracy does not just need educated professionals, it needs educated citizens,” he added.

For his part, Member of Parliament for St James East Central, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett said he wants his contribution to education and human capital development to be his enduring legacy.

Bartlett revealed that 60 tertiary students from the constituency received scholarships from his education programme, valued at just under $10 million this year.

He said the scholarship programme — which began 47 years ago at the start of his political life in St Andrew Eastern and has continued for the past 30 years in St James East Central — reflects his long-standing commitment to education as a vehicle for social mobility and national development.

“If I should be asked, ‘What is it that you would really like to be remembered by 100 years from now?’ — and somebody wants to remember this fat-faced fellow from Westmoreland — I would want to be remembered as the person who made a difference in the lives of the people in this country,” Bartlett said.

“And I would like to be remembered as the one who recognised that education was the surest way for social mobility and human advancement,” added Bartlett.

World.title: Burger Gully residents welcome MP’s relocation plan
World.content:
Residents who live closest to the banks of the gully in the community known as Burger Gully are the ones Member of Parliament Philip Paulwell wants to relocate.x

SEVERAL residents of the flood-prone east Kingston community of Burger Gully have welcomed the announcement from Member of Parliament for Kingston Eastern and Port Royal Phillip Paulwell that close to 150 of them will be relocated.

Paulwell made the disclosure during his address at his annual constituency conference at Vauxhall High School just over one week ago.

“I am willing to relocate; a lot of people are willing too. We really want to see it happen. We a feel it, man. As high as the windows them be, water goes through them. All the stoves and fridge you seeing here, a wash them wash out a people house,” said one female resident as she pointed to several flood-damaged appliances.

“This has been happening for more than 40 years. I have been living here for 38 years and it has been flooding since then,” added the woman who noted that many persons are forced to start over when their homes are flooded during heavy rain.

Her sentiments were echoed by Alton Giscombe, a shopkeeper in the area.

“When it floods, the water comes straight into the shop; I have to place my goods on top of crates. Two a me fridge them mash up,” said Giscombe.

“I am comfortable with relocating because I wouldn’t want for the gully to be flooded again and it flood out my things them,” Giscombe added.

For Frank Smith, another resident, while he appreciates the initiative, he would rather the gully walls be adjusted to prevent the frequent flooding.

“They could have raised the gully a little higher and everybody could be happy. If they carry the gully wall another four feet or five feet high I think we would be happy because the water would just go down,” said Smith, who added that he recently learnt about the relocation initiative.

According to Smith, when the gully overflows its banks the water enters his house and destroys everything.

“Over the years I have been flooded out like six times. You have a time water come here and it don’t trouble me but when the gully bursts, it floods my home.

“Even right now my car is there. When I came out of my house the last time [the gully] burst, it flooded the car. It destroyed my transmission, seat, and engine — everything full of water,” Smith said, pointing to an abandoned car along the side of the gully.

For Hyacinth — who has lived in Burger Gully for 54 years — even though she is not directly affected by the flood waters, the initiative is welcomed.

“The last time the gully come dung it barely came into my house, [and] it did not destroy my stuff. But if it is safer and the community that we will be living in is okay, I will go,” said Hyacinth even as she underscored that she will miss her current community if she relocates.

The flooding of Burger Gully, an informal settlement also called 17 1/2 Mountain View Avenue, has been an ongoing problem but worsened last year as sections of the gully which runs through the community were damaged by flood waters.

According to Paulwell, the Government has already allocated $30 million to repair the gully, with work expected to be completed by next month.

He told the Observer that lands have been identified in the communities of Mountain View and Rockfort for the relocation of Burger Gully residents, but he is awaiting a response from minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan.

“I have identified three different parcels of land in and around the community. It is for the ministry now to come and do the proper surveying of the land,” Paulwell said.

World.title: Voice House expands
World.content:
Some of the 50 students selected from across the island for the free Singing Summer Intensive hosted by Tessanne Chin Foundation rehearse an item in preparation for the programme’s final showcase on August 23 at Louise Bennett Garden Theatre.

Singer and recording artiste Tessanne Chin, through her charitable foundation, just hosted over 50 talented children — her largest cohort to date — for a 4th annual Summer Singing Intensive training camp.

The programme’s signature end of camp showcase — this year titled Out of the Box — got underway on Sunday, August 23, at Louise Bennett Garden Theatre (Ranny Williams Centre).

The group was coached by Chin and a team of highly qualified performance instructors, among them Evad Campbell, Lori Burnett, Diana Sancho, Victoria Taffe, and Kelly Barrett.

This year’s edition also marks a major milestone for one of Jamaica’s most prominent singers who has plans to expand her year-round performing arts academy, called The Voice House, at a newly dedicated home now located in Liguanea, St Andrew.

She also pointed out that the dynamic performance ensemble associated with the programme will also now be known as The Voice House.

“It has always been my dream is to create a space where children can develop their voices and their confidence all year long. Through The Voice House we will offer comprehensive training in singing, voice acting, stagecraft, and performance development, giving young talent a structured pathway to grow their skills throughout the year,” shared Chin.

“Over the past three years we have been successfully hosting an after-school programme and our kids have been consistently engaged for several corporate and entertainment events, demonstrating the high-calibre output that we are delivering. We see so much potential to deliver so much more under our expanded programme,” she further highlighted.

Looking ahead, Chin and her team are laying the groundwork to establish a talent agency for children, creating a safe, structured avenue for young performers to access auditions, bookings, and industry opportunities both locally and internationally.

“Our new home has and will continue to allow us to give them the kind of consistent, world-class training that builds not just performers, but empowered young people,” she added.

Chin’s vision is being strengthened by the support of some of Jamaica’s most influential artistes, including Sean Paul, who this year has generously offered scholarships to help children access the year-round programme and pursue higher education in the performing arts.

She also noted the kind contributions of this year’s sponsors Tastee, Supreme Ventures, Sagicor, Sandals Foundation, CHASE Fund, Digicel Foundation, Lasco, GraceKennedy Group, Loshusan, and Wisynco.

She also expressed gratitude for her production partners and Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC) for their involvement in making the programme a success.

World.title: ‘JUST HAVING FUN’
World.content:
Oblique Seville (foreground) celebrates winning the men’s 100m event at the Silesia Diamond League athletics meeting in Katowice, Poland, on Sunday. Photo: AFP

World Champion Oblique Seville says his men’s 100m victory at the Wanda Diamond League meeting in Silesia, Poland, on Sunday, sets him up well for the remainder of the season.

The Jamaican ran a meet record 9.83 seconds (1.4m/s) during the Kamila Skolimowska Memorial, effectively securing his place in the Diamond League final set for Brussells, Belgium, in two weeks.

Kenny Bednarek ran a season’s best 9.87 for second and fellow American Christian Coleman was third in 9.93. Jamaican Ackeem Blake ran 10.26 in his first-round race and failed to advance.

Seville, 25, said he is also eyeing success at the first-ever Ultimate Championships set for Budapest, Hungary, in mid-September.

“I am in pretty good shape and I feel pretty good about the win. I am in great shape for the Ultimate Championships. The victory feels nice — especially as I ran close to my personal best — and I am just having fun,” he said.

After placing second at the London Diamond League last month, he qualified for Sunday’s final after running 9.90 (1.9m/s) in the preliminaries. He then broke the meet record of 9.87 that was held jointly by three men, including compatriot Kishane Thompson.

“There are great things ahead of me,” Seville said. “Many sprinters ran under 10s, that is really special. For the rest of the season I would like to keep winning, and the next win should be in Brussels.”

Brianna Lyston was the best-placed Jamaican in the women’s 100m, placing fourth in 10.96(0.6m/s). The race was won by American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, who maintained her unbeaten run all year with a season’s best-equalling 10.78. Jefferson-Wooden defeated St Lucia’s Olympic Games champion Julien Alfred who ran a season’s best 10.83. Another American, Sha’Carri Richardson, placed third in 10.96.

Tina Clayton, who had a good start, faded to sixth place with 11.01, while her twin sister Tia was ninth with 11.24.

Megan Simmonds was second in the 100m hurdles, running 12.62 (0.2m/s) behind American Alaysha Johnson who won in 12.52. Poland’s Pia Skrzyszowska placed third with 12.64.

Ackera Nugent, who raced in Finland four days prior, was fourth with 12.64, while two-time world champion Danielle Williams was fifth in 12.70.

Nickisha Pryce ran a season’s best 49.49 for second in the women’s 400m as world champion Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic clocked 48.87 to win for the fifth-straight time on the Diamond League circuit.

Salwa Eid Naser of Bahrain finished third with a season’s best 49.57 while Stacey Ann Williams was sixth with 49.81.

Three days after he competed at the Diamond League in Lausanne, Switzerland, Orlando Bennett was fifth in the 110m hurdles in 13.25 (-0.7m/s).

American Ja’Kobe Tharp, who had finished at the back of the race in Switzerland, rebounded to win with 13.05 in a clean sweep of the top three places for Americans. Trey Cunningham was second with 13.08, just ahead of Jamal Britt (13.09),

Rajindra Campbell was sixth in the men’s shot put with 21.61m as Italy’s world leader Leonardo Fabbri won in dramatic fashion, coming from fourth place with 22.08m in fourth round.

Early leader Jordan Geist of the United States was second with 21.96m while his country man Joe Kovacs was third with 21.86m.

Olympic Games champion Roje Stona was sixth in the men’s discus throw with 67.65m while national champion Ralford Mullings threw a season’s best 66.44m for seventh after starting with two fouled efforts.

Mykolas Alekna of Lithuania set a Diamond League and meet record 72.58m to beat Kristjan Ceh (68.93m) of Slovakia and Daniel Stahl (68.25m) of Sweden.

Alekna broke his own own Diamond League record of 71.70m set in London last year and the meet record 68.60m set by Germany’s Robert Harting in 2013.

Commonwealth Games medallist Ackelia Smith finished eighth in the women’s triple jump with 13.97m (-0.7m/s) as Saly Sarr won with a Senegalese national record 15.08m (0.2m/s). Sarr defeated the Cuban pair of Leyanis Perez Hernandez, who recorded 14.91m (-0.2m/s), and Davisleydi Velazco, who jumped 14.84m (1.2m/s).

Lamara Distin was ninth in the women’s high jump, clearing 1.89m. Yaroslava Mahuchikh of Ukraine equalled the meet record of 2.00m to win. Mahuchikh topped her compatriot Iryna Geraschenko (1.98m), with Australia’s Commonwealth Games champion Eleanor Patterson (1.98).

World.title: How Dis Mek: RIVER RAFTS
World.content:
Visitors to the island boarding a raft at the start of the Rafting on the Martha Brae tour. (Photos: Gavin Jones)

RIVER rafting is one of Jamaica’s popular vacation activities for locals and visitors alike but have you ever considered the mechanics behind the making of the rafts?

Claude Johnson, raft captain #102 at Rafting on the Martha Brae, explained to the Jamaica Observer’s How Dis Mek the process behind the making of rafts during an interview on the banks of the Martha Brae river in the hills of Trelawny, where dozens of his coworkers’ rafts were docked.

Bamboo, Johnson explained, is ideal for raft creation because each joint on a stalk is essentially an air-filled sealed vacuum, allowing the stalks to float extremely well.

“The reason why we choose bamboo is because it’s air-packed, so as the joints don’t burst, everything is okay. The bamboo can take [withstand] up to a thousand [pounds] on it. You see the more length you have, the more weight you can take on top of it. You can build it 28 feet, 29 feet — those lengths are the good lengths,” said Johnson.

He explained that even if some of the bamboo joints pop open, due to age or sun damage, as long as the others remain sealed the integrity of the raft is maintained.

The use of rafts in Trelawny is well documented. Initially, rafts were used to ferry goods from rural Trelawny to the parish capital of Falmouth. Recreational rafting began in the 1970s under the Jamaica Tourist Board and has been operated by River Raft Limited since 1985.

Raft captains must be fully trained and certified before they can operate, with lessons in controlling the raft and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) certification compulsory.

Once licensed, the captains are responsible for the creation of their own rafts. To create the raft, captains need what they refer to as a “dozen stalks of bamboo”.

“If you don’t have any and you can’t go into the field to cut it, you have some people cut it and sell it for $10,000 for a dozen, [but] when we say dozen we mean 14 bamboo to make a raft,” Johnson explained.

Then to move forward, captains need a partner, because raft building is a two-person job.

Working alongside Richardo Geinues, Captain #114, Johnson demonstrated that the stalks must first be cut to the same length, placed exactly next to each other, and bound tightly to create a flat surface.

Captains use ratcheting straps to tightly bind the stalks and prevent any chance of movement. Before the binding, the stalks are pierced at one end, at the same spot, to allow for a stick to be threaded through them and bound with metal wire and pliers.

The tension from the metal wire keeps the stalks together, forming the flat bed of the raft. Then another stalk is cut into five pieces and threaded in a similar manner on top of the raft.

World.title: Absentee dad got married, now wants custody
World.content:
DEAR MRS MACAULAY, My daughter migrated and my grand-daughter, who is nine, has lived with me and my husband for almost three years. Her father rarely visited, but got married recently and suddenly wants full custody. The child barely knows him. Do we have any legal standing to prevent this?

From your very concise letter, I cannot say whether your daughter had applied for and obtained a legal order of custody, care and control of her child. I deduce that your grandchild lived with her mother, your daughter, for the first six years of life, until she migrated. I also conclude that your daughter left her child in yours and your husband’s care when she migrated, thus making you both the guardians of her child. I assume that this was not done by a deed, but by word of mouth and the physical handing over of the child to you.

You have also not stated the details of your daughter’s request. Was it until she made an application and obtained the necessary visa for her daughter to join her abroad, or was it until the child attains majority? And also, was the “father” pursuant to the Registration (Births and Deaths) Act, registered as the father of the child? Or was he so declared by an order of a court?

It seems that all arrangements were done with the absence and non-intervention of your grandchild’s putative father. You also make no mention of whether he ever provided any maintenance for the child during the years the child has been with you and your husband, or while with your daughter. All these are pertinent questions as to his status, which the court ought to consider on his application for legal custody, whether full or joint, with you and/or the mother of the child.

It seems to me that you have concluded that because your daughter is abroad, she cannot intervene in any application made by the father, or file an application herself for legal custody (which she should have done before her departure and during the years of the non-interest or non-involvement of the putative father). But matters in the Family Court or the Supreme Court can be heard by video conferences/

Zoom when a party is abroad (or in Jamaica but unable to attend personally). There is therefore no reason why your daughter cannot act herself or join with you to intervene in any action by the father.

The question you want answered is whether you and your husband as grandparents can intervene in the court to stop the presumed father from obtaining a legal custody order. By the way, I know of instances like this when such fathers get police officers to accompany them to “collect” their children, and these officers insist that the father has the legal right to the child. But in such circumstances, the officer should advise the father to go and apply for custody in the Family Court, and the application must be served on the person with whom the child is residing. It is for the court to decide and make any order for the custody, care and control of a child who has not had any relationship with his/her presumed father. A police officer is not a judge or jury in any legal matter.

If this happens, do not accede to any pressures of a police officer. Rather, call the station and speak with the officer in charge and report what is happening. Such matters where the father has been absent from the life of his purported child for years must be decided by in a court of law and not a police officer.

Your position raises several issues of facts and law which need to be considered and determined by the court in the circumstances you have sparsely related. The court, pursuant to the Children (Guardianship and Custody) Act, has a discretion, when a child was allowed to be brought up by another person (you and your husband), and where a father abandoned or deserted the child, to make an order that is not averse to the best interests and welfare of the child.

It is my opinion that you and your husband could act both as the guardians of the child and grandparents who were made the guardians by your daughter who had full custody of the child while the father showed hardly any interest in the child. I am also assuming that your grandchild is still with you, and you refused to just hand the child over to this father, because you and your husband are the child’s guardians appointed by the mother who had full custody and care and control.

So you can intervene as the

de facto guardians and apply to be so declared, and for full legal custody of the child, with the consent of your daughter, evidenced in an affidavit sworn to by her. These applications must be made in the Supreme Court.

I must advise you, however, to retain an attorney-at-law to represent yours, your daughter’s, and your grandchild’s interests by preparing and filing the necessary applications and affidavits in support in the Supreme Court or Family Court of your parish, whichever is relevant. If the father has applied, file your defence as quickly as possible. Remember, your daughter can also be a party to the application.

It is such a pity that your daughter, like so many others, made these important decisions which direct the lives of so many children without first seeking and obtaining legal advice. Legal consultation and advice protect the rights and lives of so many, and ultimately save anguish, worry and money.

Your lawyer can also add that an access order be made to enable the father to have specific access periods with the child, so that a relationship can develop between them as the law intends, and also to ensure that the rights of the child are recognised, respected and upheld.

So please act as quickly as you can to obtain the services of a lawyer to act for you all in this very important matter.

All the very best.

Margarette May Macaulay is an attorney-at-law, Supreme Court mediator, notary public, and women’s and children’s rights advocate. Send questions via e-mail to allwoman@jamaicaobserver.com. All responses are published. Mrs Macaulay cannot provide personal responses.

World.title: Fire Brigade gets critical gear
World.content:
Granville Gayle (left), CEO of National Safety Limited, presents donated equipment to Jamaica Fire Brigade officials (from second left) Deputy Commissioner Sean Martin, Acting Deputy Commissioner Julian Davis-Buckle, and Commissioner Stewart Beckford.

NATIONAL Safety Limited, Jamaica’s leading provider of industrial safety and emergency response solutions, has facilitated the donation of critical fire fighting and rescue equipment from global emergency services leaders Rosenbauer and Holmatro to the Jamaica Fire Brigade.

The equipment was handed over recently by Granville Gayle, chief executive officer of National Safety, to head of fire brigade Commissioner Stewart Beckford.

The donation is in support of the Jamaica Fire Brigade’s continuing recovery and operational enhancement efforts following the impact of Hurricane Melissa last October.

Through National Safety’s long-standing relationships with international manufacturers Rosenbauer and Holmatro, the organisations responded positively to the brigade’s needs by providing essential equipment designed to enhance the safety and effectiveness of front-line firefighters and rescue personnel.

Rosenbauer’s contribution includes 100 HEROS NFPA firefighting helmets together with a range of accessories, spare parts, helmet-mounted lighting systems, and related components — providing valuable protective equipment for firefighters operating in hazardous environments.

Holmatro’s donation consists of specialised lifting bag systems and supporting equipment used in rescue and recovery operations.

These tools are designed to assist emergency responders in lifting, stabilising, and moving heavy objects during rescue incidents, helping to improve operational efficiency and enhance victim recovery efforts.

Speaking at the handover ceremony Gayle emphasised the importance of collaboration between industry partners and emergency services.

“National Safety is honoured to serve as the bridge between our valued international partners and the Jamaica Fire Brigade. We recognise the vital role the brigade plays in protecting lives and property across Jamaica, and we are proud to support initiatives that help equip our firefighters with the tools they need to carry out their duties safely and effectively,” said Gayle.

He argued that the initiative underscores National Safety’s ongoing commitment to advancing occupational safety, emergency preparedness, and resilience throughout Jamaica.

“By working closely with internationally recognised manufacturers and local stakeholders the company continues to support organisations which play a critical role in protecting communities and saving lives,” added Gayle.

Fire chief Beckford expressed appreciation for the gesture and acknowledged the significance of the donation.

“We are deeply grateful to National Safety, Rosenbauer, and Holmatro for this generous contribution. These resources will strengthen our firefighting and rescue capabilities and support the dedicated men and women who serve on the front lines every day,” said Beckford.

World.title: Ukraine faces €23B defense funding hole as Western cash comes too slow
World.content:
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham was in Kyiv Monday for a meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing.

European Council President António Costa, Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldovan President Maia Sandu, Estonian President Alar Karis, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and other Nordic and Baltic leaders also attended in person, while French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz joined remotely.

“Ukrainian people deserve not just continued support but our gratitude ... I am determined we [the coalition of the willing] will work together to deliver the support you need,” Burnham said in a statement.

The funding gap originated after the defense ministry brought forward spending originally planned for the second half of the year, while the EU’s €90 billion loan was delayed by roadblocks from Hungary.

“At the beginning of the year, decisions were made at the ministry to use in the first half of the year funds that were intended to be disbursed in the second half," Zelenskyy said during a meeting with reporters on Saturday. The shortfall comes on top of €30 billion in funding Europe has already pledged to Ukraine this year as part of the €90 billion loan.

Purchases made included "fiber-optic drones, middle-strike drones, interceptors,” former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told POLITICO in June.

World.title: Far-left firebrand Mélenchon gaining ground in French presidential race, poll shows
World.content:
The National Rally leader has long been the favorite to win, and Mélenchon’s rise raises the risk of a runoff between two candidates who hold deeply skeptical views of the EU and NATO.

In one scenario tested, which includes three candidates from the political center, the France Unbowed leader would receive 16 percent of the vote ahead of former prime ministers Édouard Philippe on 14 percent, and Gabriel Attal on 8 percent. Le Pen came in well ahead of all of them with 35 percent.

Without Attal in the contest, the poll found Mélenchon and Philippe would be tied for second place at 17 percent each. Moderates have for weeks voiced concern that the field is too crowded and risks ceding the election to the political extremes.

“I’ve been warning for months of the likelihood of a face-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” said government spokesperson Maud Bregeon, who is supporting Philippe’s candidacy. “The likelihood of this risk has increased, unsurprisingly.”

World.title: Star news anchor steps down as her partner launches French presidential bid
World.content:
Léa Salamé is seen ahead of the evening news broadcast in Paris on Oct. 7, 2025. | Stephane de Sakutin/AFP via Getty Images

Journalist Léa Salamé said she will temporarily step down from her role anchoring French public television’s primetime news broadcast, the 20h, while her romantic partner, the MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, runs for the French presidency.

“The 20h is a strategic platform where interviews with the candidates and campaign reports will be among the highlights of the coming year,” Salamé said in an Instagram post on Monday announcing her decision. “Wherever the campaign takes place, I’ll step aside. Everywhere else, I am and will remain a journalist.”

Since taking her seat in the anchor’s chair of the 20h on France TV, Salamé has faced questions over the potential conflict of interest if Glucksmann, who has long signaled his presidential ambitions, were to join the race to replace Emmanuel Macron next year. Glucksmann announced his candidacy Sunday on TF1, France TV’s main competitor when it comes to the evening news.

World.title: Sam and Anne’s guide to the term ahead
World.content:
After a summer of setting out his stall, Andy Burnham now faces the hard task: turning ambition into action.

In the last of the summer boxset, Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy take a deep dive into five big challenges facing the government in the coming months.

From defining the 10-year plan to unresolved pressure at home and abroad, the duo give their take and analysis on a critical parliamentary term ahead.

With party conferences and a key budget on the horizon, can Burnham’s government deliver on the change it has promised?

World.title: What Ukraine needs to survive another winter
World.content:
We’re back! And so are Ukraine’s key backers. On the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence from the Soviet Union, leaders meet in Kyiv this Monday to discuss new pledges of support for the country.

On the podcast, Zoya Sheftalovich and Chief Foreign Affairs Correspondent Nick Vinocur discuss what support Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is looking to secure from the Coalition of the Willing ahead of another difficult winter.

Next we look at elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt in Germany, where the far-right Alternative for Germany is on course for a sweeping victory. If it wins an outright majority, its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, could become the first AfD state premier.

Plus: e-scooters get a reprieve until the end of the year in Brussels, much to Nick’s delight. The Brussels government announced it had found a way around a legal ruling that threatened to remove the scooters from the streets on Sept. 1.

World.title: The shipping industry profits from conflict and looks East
World.content:
This past May and June, while the Strait of Hormuz crisis was at its peak and a fifth of the world’s traded oil was looking for a way around the blockage, researchers from Kapa Research were interviewing the businesses that move the cargo. We spoke with 314 shipowners and C-suite executives ​from​​​ the world’s leading shipping groups and asked them how they see the years ahead. ​ ​​The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94​​​ percent​​​​​​​ express optimism about their company’s prospects​, and 70​ percent​​​ believe global shipping is in better shape today than it was five years ago.

The Global Shipping Outlook 2026 is Kapa Research’s quantitative study of the industry’s leadership, with respondents across every major shipping region, from Europe’s main maritime cent​er​​​s to the United States and Asia. Because fieldwork ran at the height of the crisis, the survey is a rare real-time record of how shipping leaders think under pressure.

Geopolitical crises in Ukraine, the Red Sea and the Middle East are named the most serious problem​s​ for shipping today by 76​ percent​​​ of respondents, the top concern in every region we surveyed. Yet when we asked what the Hormuz crisis means for their own company, 40​ percent​​​ said it creates new opportunities and only 23​ percent​​​ see significant obstacles. ​ ​​Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business​​.​ The logic is pragmatic. Conflict pushes ships onto longer routes, longer routes absorb vessel supply​​ and freight rates rise while demand for goods persists. Shipping moves against the cycle. When instability rises, so do revenues.

The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94​​​ percent​​​​​​​ express optimism about their company’s prospects.

​​The industry also treats this as a lasting reset rather than a temporary challenge. 76​ percent​​​ expect the effects of the Hormuz crisis on global shipping to outlast six months, and opinion splits almost in half on whether this is the sector’s most serious crisis of the past 50 years, ​which covers​​​ the oil shocks, the tanker war, the global financial crisis and C​ovid​​​-19. One phrase from our interviews captures the mindset behind optimism: ​“​​​​Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.​​”​​​​

We therefore asked the uncomfortable question directly. Does global shipping today want peace​​ or does it benefit from turmoil? The peace camp wins, but only just: 54​ percent​​​ to 46​ percent​​​. Even among those who say the crisis hurts their own company, a third concede that the industry gains. Such cando​​r is rare in any sector, and it tempers any expectation that shipping will lobby hard for de-escalation. Markets gaining on volatility do not vote against it.

Confidence, however, does not mean that the influence equilibrium stays the same. Asked which power will affect developments in global shipping the most in the years ahead, 76​ percent​​​ of our respondents point to the East, meaning China and India, while 17​ percent​​​ choose the West. China is rated the leading shipbuilding nation by 69​ percent​​​, the operator of the most competitive fleet by 62​ percent​​​ and a near-universal 96​ percent​​​ ​​call its role important for ​​strengthening ​​global shipping. Trust, though, has not moved East with the tonnage. Only 17​ percent​​​ rate Chinese ship management highly, while traditional maritime powers such as Greece, Norway​​ and Germany continue to be recognized as the industry’s superior managers.

The same shift appears when executives rate the world’s leaders. Xi Jinping​, the president of China,​ stands alone at the top with a net favourability (percent of positive minus percent of negative views) of ​​+44, ahead of Narendra Modi​, the prime minister of India,​ at +24, while the bottom of the ranking is crowded with political leaders at the cent​er​​​ of today’s wars and confrontations. For an industry that plans in decades, predictability seems to weigh more than political alignment, and maritime leaders reward the global actors who ensure a more predictable environment.

Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business​​.​

The study’s technology section shows where the next edge will be decided. Shipping’s digital core has advanced from its experimentation phase. Remote monitoring and voyage optimi​z​​​ation are standard equipment, used by over seven in ten companies, while a second wave, predictive maintenance and ​Internet of Things ​​​sensors, is scaling, and a third, ​artificial intelligence (​AI​)​ analytics and digital twins, is only emerging. Each wave reaches roughly half the companies of the one before it. Tradition survives alongside the sensors, since 70​ percent​​​ still track fleet performance with the noon report (a holdover from the age of sail). ​AI​​​ is the divide to watch​:​​​ 65​ percent​​​ of companies already use or pilot AI, yet only 7​ percent​​​ use it extensively​​ and adoption splits along tonnage lines. Among fleets above one million deadweight ​​tonnes, 79​ percent​​​ work with AI, against 50​ percent​​​ in the mid-sized tier. Scale buys data, teams and budgets, the returns compound, and command of AI and cybersecurity will help set the new shipping hierarchy. As one shipowner told us, “Better positioning produces better data, which produces better positioning.”

No such technology will replace shipping crews. The shortage of skilled personnel remains the third most serious problem in the ranking, at 37​ percent​​​, and companies respond with high safety standards, competitive pay, internet access on board and training. Two findings point to a deeper change​:​​​ 72​ percent​​​ of companies intend to employ more women at sea​​ and 74​ percent​​​ now call ESG​ (environment, social, governance)​ performance important to their overall business strategy.

Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.​ One response from the interviews

Shipping carries about four​-​​​fifths of world trade, so the way its leaders think matters far beyond the industry. What they told us at the peak of a crisis is that volatility is now structural, that the cent​er​​​ of maritime gravity is shifting East, and that they plan to keep moving through whatever comes. Governments, corporations and international organi​z​​​ations facing the same instability have lessons to draw from ​their​​​ resilience.

​​The full Global Shipping Outlook 2026 report is available ​here​​.

​​A special thanks to LAROS by Prisma Electronics SA for their insights and support in this year’s study.​

World.title: Britain told EU citizens to trust its settled status system. Then it mixed up identical twins.
World.content:
The eVisa database keeps a record of a person’s full name, date of birth, nationality, and a facial photograph. But these traits are by definition often a very close match for identical twins, including Webb, whose name is similar to that of her sister.

Many such cases

Monique Hawkins, acting CEO of the3million, which campaigns for the rights of EU citizens living in the U.K., said problems with the eVisa system sometimes left people unable to prove their identity when they needed it most.

“We have seen many cases where someone else’s immigration status is entangled with another person’s eVisa account. We had hoped, after repeatedly raising this issue, that the Home Office had taken more steps to prevent it happening. It just shows how, despite claims that the eVisa system is highly resilient, it can fail people at the critical moments they need it to work,” she said.

Hawkins said it was “crucial that people have a genuinely stable means by which to prove their status” and described the digital-only system as “rushed,” adding: “We regularly see people not only denied boarding, but also compensation, as carriers and the Home Office play a blame game shifting responsibility between each other.”

While a Home Office spokesperson did not dispute Webb’s account, they defended the eVisa system, arguing it had worked for many people.

“Over 10 million people have already successfully used eVisas to prove their immigration status,” the spokesperson said. “As we expand our digital system, we are committed to data accuracy and ensuring that the safeguards in place to support eVisa users are accessible to anyone reliant on the digital system. In the rare cases where errors are identified, the majority of cases are resolved within 24 hours.”

World.title: Ukraine widens its targets — and its tolerance for causing civilian casualties
World.content:
The numbers help illustrate the change. In 2025, Ukrainian attacks inside Russia killed 253 civilians, according to the United Nations, which says it was not able to independently verify the numbers. This year, in the month of July alone, Russian authorities reported that 79 civilians were killed and 601 injured, a marked increase in the casualty rate.

Zelenskyy has said that Wildberries is a legitimate target because it has been “used by the aggressor to ensure the supply of sanctioned components for the production of drones and navigation equipment.” Russian soldiers supplement their equipment by purchasing items from Wildberries.

Maryana Bezuhla, a Ukrainian lawmaker and one of the most outspoken critics of Zelenskyy and Ukraine’s military leadership, is unapologetic about the increased risk to civilians. “Russia’s logistics system is used to wage the war of aggression against Ukraine,” she told POLITICO. “Russia has been targeting Ukrainian civilians all the years of the war.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied accusations from Ukraine that Wildberries handles military supplies but conceded to journalists that “the situation is indeed difficult” for the company.

Dmitry Peskov attends a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow on June 3, 2026. | Pool photo by Ramil Sitdikov via AFP/Getty Images

There is no indication that Ukraine is deliberately targeting civilians — even as Russia continues to hit apartment buildings, hospitals, schools and other civilian infrastructure with ballistic missiles and drones. And yet, there is no indication that the rising civilian toll in Russia is causing Kyiv to reconsider its approach.

“It is a very important thing to stress from the outset, that any civilian casualties resulting from Ukrainian attacks are collateral damage,” said Jaroslava Barbieri, Ukraine expert at Britain’s Chatham House. “No Ukrainian strikes have deliberately targeted civilian districts.”

World.title: Volkswagen workers condemn ‘disastrous’ communication over job cuts
World.content:
Volkswagen workers have sharply criticised the company’s management amid growing uncertainty over possible job cuts and the future of several German factories.

 

In a survey of employee morale initiated by the works council last week, employees accused the board of “disastrous communication," AFP reported on Monday.

The chance to express their criticism and expectations of CEO Oliver Blume and the rest of the board via the company intranet led to ranking the communication as employees' number one grievance, even ahead of concerns about job security or possible factory closures.

According to the German Press Agency, employees and their families were left "uncertain and frightened."

The consultation was organised by Volkswagen’s works council ahead of a series of meetings between senior executives and employees.

CEO Oliver Blume and other board members are beginning a tour of Volkswagen sites for meetings with workers this week, and executives are expected to provide initial answers to the questions and responses to the criticism during these nine extraordinary works meetings, the first of which will take place on Tuesday, 25 August, in Wolfsburg.

It will be followed by others at followed by others at sites including Emden, Zwickau, Braunschweig and ending in Hannover on 31 August.

Volkswagen is seeking deeper cost cuts as the group struggles with fierce Chinese competition, weaker demand and US tariffs.

In a separate intranet post seen by AFP on Sunday, Blume said: "The situation is more than critical," adding that the firm was not making enough money to "ensure we have the means over the long term for new technologies, new products and our locations".

Volkswagen reported an 11.6% decline in its first-half operating result to €5.9bn, while its operating margin fell from 4.2% to 3.8%.

Volkswagen has already agreed to about 50,000 job cuts across brands, including its namesake as well as others like Audi and Porsche, but Europe's largest carmaker has since said cutting another 50,000 positions could be required.

Uncertainty also surrounds four German plants: Volkswagen sites in Emden and Zwickau, the Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles factory in Hannover and Audi’s plant in Neckarsulm.

Volkswagen's supervisory board are discussing turnaround plans.

Blume said Sunday that Volkswagen and the rest of Germany's car industry are facing "the biggest upheaval in their history" from global headwinds and Chinese competition.

Other German carmakers have also warned about the country’s high production costs. Mercedes-Benz chief executive Ola Källenius said last month that costs at the company’s German operations were about 70% higher than at its plants in Hungary.

Reports about possible further job cuts at Volkswagen have angered unions, which have accused Volkswagen’s management of failing to communicate openly with employees.

Blume confirmed in July that the equivalent of up to 50,000 additional positions could be affected, but said the figure had been leaked to the media without his approval.

World.title: As bitcoin soars people ask who is Giancarlo Devasini, Italy's richest man?
World.content:
Bitcoin is back in the spotlight after a week-long rally pushed the cryptocurrency above $79,000, with gains of more than 20% in just a few days.

 

The rally has been driven by fresh flows into spot Bitcoin ETFs, expectations of greater liquidity in the United States, a more favourable climate for cryptocurrencies in Washington and a squeeze on traders betting against Bitcoin.

But there is a distinctly Italian twist to the story. While Bitcoin returns to centre stage, Italy's richest man is someone who built his fortune at the heart of the crypto economy.

At 62, Giancarlo Devasini, chairman of Tether — the company behind USDT, the world's largest stablecoin — has amassed a fortune estimated by Forbes at $89.3 billion, making him the world's 23rd-richest person.

His fortune is almost twice the $48.8 billion attributed to Italian businessman Giovanni Ferrero and also well ahead of Andrea Pignataro, whose wealth is estimated at $42.6 billion. It is the first time since 2007 that an Italian other than a member of the Ferrero family has occupied the top spot.

He didn't get rich by buying Bitcoin

To say that Devasini made his money "with Bitcoin" is striking, but not entirely accurate. His wealth was built through the broader crypto economy, above all through Tether and the ecosystem that has developed around cryptocurrencies.

Tether issues USDT, a stablecoin designed to maintain a value close to one US dollar. It has become a kind of transit currency for the crypto world, allowing market participants to move money quickly between exchanges and digital assets without having to return to the traditional banking system.

This is where the scale becomes enormous. At the end of 2025, there were more than 186 billion USDT in circulation, while Tether reported more than $10 billion in profits for the year.

A large share of its reserves is invested in US Treasury securities. By the end of 2025, Tether's direct holdings of US Treasuries exceeded $122 billion, while its total exposure, including indirect holdings, was above $141 billion.

Forbes estimates that Devasini owns around 45% of Tether. It is this stake, valued according to the company's size and profitability, that has propelled his estimated wealth to such heights.

From medicine to digital finance

Born and raised in the Casale Monferrato area of northern Italy, Devasini studied medicine and specialised in plastic surgery. But his medical career did not last long. His path instead led him towards IT, e-commerce and eventually digital currencies.

One of the earliest traces of Devasini's entry into the Bitcoin world dates back to 2012, when, according to a Financial Times investigation, he appeared on a Bitcoin forum offering to sell CDs and DVDs for bitcoin. At the time, the cryptocurrency was worth a tiny fraction of its current value.

Then came Bitfinex, the cryptocurrency exchange, and above all Tether.

Tether began life as Realcoin in 2014 before being renamed later that year. Devasini, already closely involved with Bitfinex, went on to become a central figure at the stablecoin company.

A few years later, Paolo Ardoino, a computer scientist from the Italian region of Liguria, joined Bitfinex. He is now Tether's chief executive and has become the public face of the company. Ardoino has said he first met Devasini while working on Bitfinex's software.

The phantom billionaire

Despite a fortune estimated at almost $90 billion, Devasini has largely remained in the shadows, giving few interviews, making few public appearances and attracting relatively little media exposure.

It is far more often Ardoino who speaks publicly about Tether and its activities. Devasini, by contrast, appears to prefer staying behind the scenes, becoming one of the richest people on the planet without building the kind of public profile associated with many other billionaires.

... and then came Juventus

Devasini's story came to the fore when Tether entered the world of Italian football.

In February 2025, the company announced the purchase of a stake in Juventus, initially equivalent to more than 5% of voting rights. By April, Tether had increased its stake to more than 10% of the club's share capital, making it the club's second-largest shareholder after Exor.

By later that year, Tether's stake had risen to around 11.5% of the club's share capital, with the company also gaining representation on Juventus' board of directors.

The move offered a striking juxtaposition: a company whose chairman built his fortune in the cryptocurrency industry had become a major shareholder in one of the most famous names in Italian football, bringing the world of digital finance into one of the country's most traditional sports.

And it did not stop there. Tether has also sought to expand its presence in sport and entertainment while diversifying its investments beyond stablecoins.

The business behind Devasini's $89bn fortune

As Bitcoin resumed its rally, reaching an intraday high of around $79,500, Tether continued to operate on a different level. Its business is not simply a bet on Bitcoin rising in value, but is built around financial infrastructure underpinning a huge share of the crypto market.

This is what sets Devasini's fortune apart. He is not the archetypal billionaire who bought Bitcoin when it cost next to nothing and then waited for its value to soar. Instead, he helped build one of the key instruments through which money enters, exits and circulates in the cryptocurrency economy.

And while Bitcoin makes headlines each time it breaks another threshold, the "phantom billionaire" from Casale Monferrato remains a far more discreet figure, operating behind a company that handles hundreds of billions of dollars and has, according to Forbes, become valuable enough to turn a little-known Italian businessman into the country's richest person.
