Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Armenia-Azerbaijan exports could begin ‘soon’: Pledges, figures and remaining barriers
World.content:
Exports from Armenia to Azerbaijan

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists that “exports from Armenia to Azerbaijan could begin in the near future”. He also said that bilateral trade was already on the agenda. According to Pashinyan, Azerbaijani specialists visited Armenia in September 2025 and January 2026 to discuss infrastructure issues, including power lines, railways and pipelines.

The statement comes against the backdrop of tangible but still highly asymmetrical trade relations between the two countries, which began to take shape following the signing of the declaration in Washington in August 2025.

Official data and figures

According to Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee, Azerbaijan exported around $17.4m worth of goods to Armenia between January and July 2026. The shipments consisted mainly of petroleum products, particularly diesel and petrol. Over the same period, Azerbaijan’s indirect imports from Armenia amounted to just $960. This figure was recorded in March, with imports falling to zero in subsequent months.

Following the lifting of transit restrictions in October 2025 and the start of the first fuel deliveries in December, Azerbaijan has facilitated both direct exports to Armenia and the transit of goods from Russia and Kazakhstan, including grain, fertilisers and other products. Volumes remain small, but the direction of travel has changed: borders that had been closed for decades have effectively begun to open.

There has yet to be any official commercial export from Armenia. In January 2026, Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said the two sides had exchanged lists of potential goods for bilateral trade. These included aluminium foil and raw materials for its production, ferromolybdenum, textiles, flowers, greenhouse produce including tomatoes and peppers, raw materials for brandy production, and other goods.

The specific contents of the lists and the expected volumes of shipments have not yet been officially published. Further development of trade will depend on agreements between companies.

What could be traded, and why?

Azerbaijani experts note that, at the initial stage, developing trade in industrial goods and raw materials appears more realistic than focusing primarily on food products. Vugar Bayramov, an MP and member of the Milli Majlis Committee on Economic Policy, citing preliminary estimates, puts the potential annual trade turnover for 38 categories of goods at up to $300m. These include food and industrial products as well as raw materials. In his view, mutual supplies of goods other than fuel could begin between the two countries in the near future.

Economist Natig Jafarli says the process is developing gradually. According to him, Azerbaijan has an advantage in energy resources, while potential Armenian exports could include agricultural products, fish, fruit and iron ore. However, Azerbaijan is not yet importing goods from Armenia, while the necessary infrastructure, including bank transfers, insurance and contractual mechanisms, has yet to be fully established.

Akif Nasirli, chairman of the Centre for Liberal Economists, believes food products could also be viable export candidates, including fruit and vegetables such as apricots, peaches, cherries, tomatoes and peppers, as well as fish, mineral water and wine. In his view, restrictions on the Russian market are forcing Yerevan to seek alternative export markets.

Former Finance Minister Fikret Yusifov has previously argued that, if trade relations are restored, a trade deficit for Armenia would be inevitable, but that these economic ties should nevertheless be developed for the sake of peace.

There is also a widespread view among experts that food and beverages are psychologically more sensitive categories of goods. Construction materials, cable and electrical products, industrial raw materials, chemicals and light-industry goods, by contrast, may be perceived considerably more favourably.

Psychological barrier

This is one of the deepest and most sensitive aspects of the issue. Expert assessments published by Caliber note that memories of the 44-day war remain fresh. The appearance of products labelled Made in Armenia on shop shelves could initially provoke mixed reactions, ranging from curiosity to social media campaigns. Trust in food and beverages, including wine and brandy, is particularly important, as some consumers may have irrational concerns about their safety. With industrial goods and construction materials, by contrast, the country of origin is less visible to consumers and purchasing decisions tend to be more pragmatic.

During a transitional period, neutral packaging in English or Russian, or rebranding, could potentially be used. The appearance of Azerbaijani fuel on the Armenian market has already created a precedent for a kind of “economic truce”. A similarly pragmatic approach could work in the opposite direction, although this will not happen automatically.

In both societies, support for peace does not yet necessarily translate into an equally positive attitude towards goods from the neighbouring country. Traders from border areas who wished to remain anonymous, as well as entrepreneurs with experience of informal “re-exports” through Georgia using channels that have existed since the 1990s, say that price and quality could eventually become the decisive factors. However, this process could take years.

Practical obstacles and possible timeframes

Issues surrounding certification, phytosanitary controls, customs procedures, bank transfers and insurance have yet to be fully resolved.

Logistics currently operate mainly through Georgia. Direct rail links and the TRIPP corridor are still at the infrastructure development stage. Competition also remains high, with suppliers from Turkey, Russia and Iran already present in the market alongside domestic producers. The competitiveness of Armenian goods will therefore depend on their price, quality and logistics costs.

Under an optimistic scenario, small-scale shipments of industrial goods and raw materials could begin within several months to a year. A more realistic scenario would see trade gradually expand over one to three years, while under a pessimistic scenario, political fluctuations and public reaction could delay the process considerably.

What to watch next

Key indicators could include the first genuine commercial shipments from Armenia appearing in customs statistics, the introduction of banking mechanisms for cross-border payments, official approval of a list of potential goods for trade, and changes in the procurement policies of retailers such as Bravo, Araz and others.

Independent polling and sociological research in both countries will also be needed to assess public attitudes towards goods labelled “Made in …”. Without such data, statements about future trade will remain largely expressions of intent.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan likely to expand payment integration for tourists - HUMO (Exclusive)
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 24. Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan may expand payment connectivity between financial systems, allowing tourists from both countries to use their usual payment methods while traveling, the Head of Business Development for EMEA and the Caucasus and a representative of HUMO told Trend on the sidelines of the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum in Tashkent.

According to him, there is active rapprochement between the two countries at the intergovernmental level, including against the backdrop of growing tourist flows. “A large number of tourists from Uzbekistan are visiting Azerbaijan today, and we also expect guests from Azerbaijan,” Ergashev said.

The HUMO representative noted that the development of payment infrastructure could provide more convenient payment options for citizens of both countries. “They will be able to make payments through our network using their own apps, which we are ready to integrate between the payment systems of Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan,” he said.

Speaking about the development of Uzbekistan’s payment market, Ergashev noted that the country is actively transitioning to cashless payments, while cash payments are gradually taking a back seat. “Uzbekistan is precisely the testing ground in Central Asia where cash payments are fading into the background as much as possible. For the most part, everything here is done cashless,” he noted.

According to him, as of July 1, businesses in the country are required to have a single QR code for accepting payments, which also contributes to the development of cashless infrastructure.

He added that tokenized payment solutions are also being developed in Uzbekistan, allowing transactions to be made using various devices, including wearable gadgets. “We already have tokenized solutions where people pay not just with a card, but, for example, with a ring or some other gadget,” Ergashev said.

The representative of HUMO also reported on work being done on a tokenization project to enable the future launch of services such as Apple Pay and Google Pay, noting that the development of such solutions could further contribute to an increase in cashless payments.

World.title: Presidents and First Ladies of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan visit Poi-Kalyan Complex in Bukhara (VIDEO)
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BUKHARA, Uzbekistan, August 24. On August 24, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva, President of the Republic of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev, First Lady Ziroatkhon Mirziyoyeva, and family members visited the Poi-Kalyan Complex in Bukhara, , Trend’s special correspondent reports.

The name of the complex means “the pedestal of the Great.” One of its main monuments, the Kalyan Minaret, was built in 1127.

The Kalyan Mosque is the largest mosque in Bukhara. Constructed in the 16th century, the mosque can accommodate up to 12,000 worshippers at a time.

The Mir-i Arab Madrasah, located within the complex, is a religious educational institution. The madrasah was built in the 16th century by Abdullah Yamani, also known as Mir-i Arab.

World.title: Presidents and First Ladies of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan visit Ark Fortress in Bukhara (VIDEO)
World.content:
BUKHARA, Uzbekistan, August 24. On August 24, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva, President of the Republic of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev, First Lady Ziroatkhon Mirziyoyeva, and family members visited the Ark Fortress in Bukhara, Trend’s special correspondent reports.

The Ark Fortress was constructed in the 4th century BCE. Its present appearance was mainly formed in the 17th–18th centuries. In the early 20th century, the fortress served as a winter residence of the rulers of Bukhara. Currently, the fortress covers an area of four hectares. A major portion of the fortress was destroyed in 1920. Since 1947, the Bukhara State Museum-Reserve has operated within the fortress.

World.title: ABB Davr Bank project launched with participation of the Presidents of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan (PHOTO)
World.content:
On August 23 in Tashkent, the ABB Davr Bank project was officially launched with the online participation of President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and President of the Republic of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev. The launch took place as part of a ceremony marking the inauguration and groundbreaking of projects being implemented by Azerbaijan in Uzbekistan.

President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, speaking at a joint press statement with the President of Uzbekistan, described the event as the entry of a leading Azerbaijani bank into the Uzbek market.

The project envisages ABB acquiring a controlling stake in Davr Bank, one of Uzbekistan’s commercial banks, and subsequently operating in the country under the ABB Davr Bank brand.

As previously reported, on August 22, during the 4th Uzbekistan–Azerbaijan Interregional Forum held in Tashkent, Abbas Ibrahimov, Chairman of the Management Board of ABB, and Lutfulla Ubayev, founder and Chairman of the Supervisory Board of Davr Bank, signed an agreement on ABB’s acquisition of a controlling stake in Davr Bank.

The signing marked the launch of the project and ABB’s entry into Uzbekistan’s financial market, in line with the geographic expansion objectives set out in the Bank’s 2026–2028 Strategic Development Plan.

Operating under the ABB Davr Bank brand, the Bank will provide universal financial services to corporate and retail customers across all regions of Uzbekistan. ABB Financial Group will bring to the Uzbek market its proven corporate governance framework, expertise in digital transformation, innovative artificial intelligence-based solutions, and comprehensive financial services for small and medium-sized businesses.

With a population of nearly 40 million and an economy demonstrating sustained and rapid growth, Uzbekistan offers significant opportunities for the development of new banking practices and solutions. ABB Davr Bank will seek to contribute to this development, with a particular focus on creating additional opportunities for the country’s small and medium-sized enterprises.

A focused presence in the Uzbek market will also open up significant new opportunities for ABB, further strengthening the regional and international standing of ABB Financial Group as a well-established Azerbaijani brand.

Abbas Ibrahimov, Chairman of the Management Board of ABB, expressed his gratitude to the Presidents of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, as well as to the relevant government authorities that supported the process, for creating the conditions for ABB’s entry into the Uzbek market: “It is a great honour for us that the first historic step towards ABB’s geographic expansion objective for its new strategic period has been taken in brotherly Uzbekistan.

We view this project as the beginning of our long-term presence in Uzbekistan and aspire to become a trusted financial partner for businesses, individuals and the country’s economy. Our ambition is to create new opportunities, support economic development and contribute to the further strengthening of cooperation between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.”

Lutfulla Ubayev, founder and Chairman of the Supervisory Board of Davr Bank, said: “With this transaction, we are taking banking services to a qualitatively new level. The expertise, innovative technologies and strong capital base of our new partner will enable Davr Bank to offer advanced financial products to its customers in the shortest possible time. This partnership will provide our Bank with even greater stability and create the foundation for a major technological leap forward.”

Detailed information about ABB’s modern, useful and universal products and services is available at the Bank’s branches and service offices, on its official website at abb-bank.az, through the 937 Information Centre, and via the Bank’s official social media channels.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan sees strong job creation amid economic reforms
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. Kyrgyzstan created more than 273,000 new jobs in 2025.

This was announced in a statement published by the press service of the Kyrgyz President, citing President Sadyr Zhaparov’s remarks in Bishkek during the opening ceremony of the Ak-Keme hotel on August 24.

"Thanks to the ongoing reforms, more than 273,000 new jobs were created in Kyrgyzstan in 2025. Kyrgyzstan is opening its doors wide to the world. As the number of tourists, entrepreneurs and foreign visitors coming to our country grows, the quality of services provided to them should also improve. This is particularly important for Bishkek, the heart and face of our country," he said.

According to him, the capital hosts state and official visits, international meetings, forums and other major events.

"Therefore, having hotels, conference halls and service infrastructure in Bishkek that meet international standards is of great importance,” the head of state said, expressing confidence that the fully renovated Ak-Keme hotel, with its 174 rooms, conference and business meeting halls, restaurants and other facilities, will contribute to this goal.

According to Trend's analysis, the creation of more than 273,000 jobs highlights the impact of Kyrgyzstan’s ongoing economic reforms on employment and business activity.

The expansion of tourism and international business activity is also increasing demand for modern hospitality and service infrastructure, particularly in Bishkek. The development of hotels, conference facilities and related services could help the capital accommodate a growing number of foreign visitors while supporting employment and economic activity.

World.title: Ukraine marks Independence Day as UK vows support despite Russia's threats
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has used a defiant speech on Ukraine's Independence Day to declare that the country wants peace but will not just surrender to Russia at any price, as foreign leaders pledged their support.

Flanked by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa, Mr Zelenskyy praised the resilience of the Ukrainian people during more than four years of war with Russia.

"Ukraine absolutely wants peace, but it is not ready to simply surrender," the Ukrainian president said, warning that Russia would not halt its aggression even if Ukraine ceded to its demands for more territory in the country's east.

Wearing a traditional Ukrainian embroidered shirt, Mr Zelenskyy thanked several foreign leaders for travelling to Kyiv to show their continued backing, on the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's break from the Soviet Union.

Hundreds of thousands of soldiers have died in fighting since Russia's invasion began in February 2022. (Reuters: Gleb Garanich)

Mr Burnham, who took office last month, said his choice of Kyiv for his first foreign visit showed the importance he attached to assisting in Ukraine's defence.

"We are with you in this struggle all the way, heart and soul," Mr Burnham said.

The British prime minister vowed to continue that support "despite Russia's outrageous threats to my country."

The British government announced on Monday it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start production of European SCALP long-range cruise missiles in Ukraine, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia.

In response, the Kremlin said the use of classified British technology would "add fuel to the fire" of their worsening relations, after it warned London last week there would be "consequences" for supplying drones to Kyiv.

Allies to hold military talks

Mr Burnham was scheduled to co-chair a virtual meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" — a group of countries backing Ukraine — with French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The leaders were expected to discuss Ukraine's request for more air defence systems to stop Russian ballistic missiles pounding Ukrainian cities.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is among world leaders in Ukraine to mark the country's Independence Day. (Reuters: Henry Nicholls)

Mr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Ukraine's war effort was being complicated by a $US27 billion ($37 billion) defence funding gap this year.

He also warned that Russian could escalate the conflict later this year by mobilising some 300,000 additional troops after parliamentary elections in September.

Paying tribute to Ukrainian people and soldiers defending Ukraine in the war, Mr Zelenskyy called on allies to give it "everything" needed to stop the war.

"We are not asking you to fight for us," he said.

Hundreds of thousands of people have been killed, and swathes of Ukrainian territory have been laid waste, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

US-led peace talks to bring a lasting end to the war fell apart earlier this year as Ukraine refused Russian demands to cede more territory.

Technological display

Fighting continues along a 1,200 kilometre front line and Ukraine has succeeded in bringing Russian advances overall to a virtual halt this year.

Hovering in the sky above Kyiv, a squadron of aerial drones carried out a demonstration of the Ukrainian military technology, which has helped to keep Russian forces in check.

Ukraine's drones could crash Russian banks On the outskirts of Russian cities, warehouses belonging to the country's largest online retailer are being struck by Kyiv's drones, with some analysts saying it could lead to a financial crisis.

Naval drones swept along the Dnipro river, while unnamed ground vehicles — some equipped with heavy machine guns — trundled in formation along one of the city's main commercial avenues.

While praising the achievements of Ukraine's defence industry during the war, Mr Zelenskyy called for an increase in cruise missile production to take the fight to Russia this winter.

Exploiting Ukraine's critical shortage of anti-ballistic missiles, Russia has stepped up its campaign of air strikes at cities far from the front line this summer.

Ukraine has also increased its long-range attacks on Russian refineries and logistics infrastructure, aimed at undermining Moscow's war effort.

It hit four logistics hubs owned by Russia's second-largest online retailer Ozon in southern Russia in drone strikes on Monday, the company said.

In a sombre moment, the Ukrainian leader rewarded fallen soldiers with state awards, which he presented to their mothers and family members.

He also announced the return of 10 Ukrainian servicemen, who were previously listed as missing in action, as part of a special prisoner exchange with Russia.

"We remember each and every one who remains in captivity," Mr Zelenskyy said, promising to do everything possible to bring them home.

Reuters

World.title: Swan's assistant takes-over as Essendon coach
World.content:
Mark McVeigh, a former Essendon player and Sydney assistant coach, will take over as Essendon's senior coach after what the club said was an "extensive" and "deliberate" selection process.

McVeigh, 45, won the role ahead of Bombers great and ex-coach James Hird, as well as Jaymie Graham and Murray Davis.

Essendon confirmed the announcement on Monday afternoon, a day after the stricken club's narrow loss to Port Adelaide.

McVeigh would take over "effective immediately", the club said in a statement.

The official announcement came following a day of speculation and a message of congratulations from former teammate and Bomber's legend, James Hird.

"I put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that's the way it goes," Hird said on Nine yesterday night.

James Hird (L) and Dean Solomon (C) speak with Mark McVeigh (R). (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Brad Scott was sacked on May 25, with Dean Solomon taking over as interim coach for the rest of the season.

Solomon rounded out the Bomber's worst season in club history with a 10-point defeat to Port Adelaide on Sunday.

McVeigh commits to building Essendon's 'next great era'

The search for a new coach has involved a tumultuous selection process, with opinion sharply divided on whether Hird should win another tenure in the role.

Club president Andrew Welsh, who played at Essendon alongside McVeigh and Hird, said the appointment was a unanimous board decision.

"Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands," Welsh said on the club website.

"We are building the next successful era for Essendon, with a view to playing finals, winning finals and competing for premierships.

"We weighed every candidate against what this role actually demands, and Mark was the clear stand-out."

Hird congratulates McVeigh A 'very disappointed' James Hird congratulates former teammate Mark McVeigh, as the Bombers prepare to unveil their new coach.

McVeigh played 232 games for Essendon and returns to the club on a three-year contract after nearly 14 years away, which also included working as an assistant coach at the Greater Western Sydney Giants.

He also acted as caretaker coach at the Giants in 2022.

"We're not looking backwards, we're building the next great era of this football club," McVeigh said.

"That's not built on promises. It's built on our standards, our actions and the work we put in every single day."

AAP/ABC

World.title: New Zealand prime minister proposes Australia-style social media ban
World.content:
New Zealand's Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has unveiled a proposed law banning children younger than 16 from using social media platforms, citing what he said on Monday was "harm being done to a generation" of young people.

Social media ban spreads More and more countries are following Australia's lead and introducing social media bans for children, but US policies are piecemeal and vary from state to state.

If re-elected in November, Mr Luxon is seeking to make his conservative government the latest worldwide to enact age restrictions for social media platforms after Australia enacted its world-first under-16s social media ban in December 2025.

"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," Mr Luxon said in a statement.

He said 2025 research showed a third of New Zealand teenagers spent at least five hours a day on social media.

" Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep, and education. "

Platforms would be fined 10 per cent of their revenue

New Zealand's proposal includes platforms including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook. (Reuters: Asanka Brendon)

Under the law, platforms including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook could be fined up to 10 per cent of their global revenue for failing to meet their obligations — taking "reasonable steps" to check users were older than 16.

Age-check providers want social giants tested In a damning submission, an age-check firm warns big fines may be seen as a "small price to pay" if copping them allows Australia's ban to be "wrongly" be portrayed as a failure.

This could include "existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal ID," according to material supplied by Mr Luxon's party.

Like Australia, New Zealand would not penalise parents or children under the proposed bill. However, its penalty system differs from Australia's approach of imposing a maximum fine of $99 million.

Excluded from both Australia's ban and New Zealand's proposed law are messaging platforms such as WhatsApp, online gaming platforms like Roblox and AI apps with productivity uses — including ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot.

Proposal comes amid criticism of Australia's ban

Loading...

Mr Luxon's government has considered such a law since Australia's world-first social media ban for under 16-year-olds took effect in December 2025.

Since Australia's law came into force, countries including Canada, Brazil and Indonesia have enacted bans too, while many other countries are studying or developing laws.

Albanese's social media ban has a shark problem Years into Australia's quest to get teens off social media, the Albanese government is suddenly in a hurry.

Child safety advocates and some parents have welcomed age restrictions, while privacy groups say the rules can be cheated and that forcing users to supply identification raises privacy concerns.

Professor Nicholas Carah, director of the Centre for Digital Cultures and Societies at the University of Queensland, says there are "two big problems that other countries ought to learn from the Australian experience".

"The first is that the ban doesn't actually work in practice. Young people are still easily able to access social media," he said, echoing reports that more than eight in 10 Australian teenagers are still using social media three months after the ban was enacted.

"The other problem is that the ban is regressive, it fails to recognise that social media platforms are important places for young people to learn, to socialise and to express themselves.

" If social media platforms harm young people then the real task is to make them safe. "

Hannah Storey, Head of Children and Young People's Digital Rights at Amnesty International, echoes this sentiment and adds that an under-16s social media ban does not address the harm platforms can inflict on adults too.

"Bans rely on age verification measures, which raise significant privacy concerns, while doing nothing to address the underlying design choices that make many platforms addictive and amplify harmful content," she told the ABC.

"Children who get around bans, and adults who remain on the platforms, will continue to face the same risks.

"We should use the momentum behind this issue to focus on making platforms safe by design for all users, rather than restricting who can access them."

NZ government divided on proposed ban

Some New Zealand political parties plan to vote against the law. (Reuters: Marty Melville)

New Zealand's proposed law has been vehemently opposed by the other two parties that make up the government along with Mr Luxon's centre-right group National — libertarian ACT and populist NZ First.

Both minor parties repeated on Monday their plans to vote against the law.

Politicians from the largest opposition party, centre-left Labour, have not decided if they would vote for it, leader Chris Hipkins said.

However, there would not be enough time for politicians to hold a vote on the proposal before New Zealand's parliament dissolves on October 1 ahead of November's general election, Mr Luxon said.

Bills in New Zealand are required to pass three rounds of voting, usually over a period of months, before they become law.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Suspended sentence, $100 fine for man's naked attack on country ambulance
World.content:
A man who smashed his head through the windscreen of an ambulance while naked on a public street in Western Australia's Goldfields has been handed a suspended sentence and $100 fine.

Brian Charles Parfitt attacked the ambulance, and the paramedics inside, on December 7 last year after he had been spotted behaving erratically on the streets of Boulder, 600km east of Perth.

Parfitt, 26, attempted to climb the first ambulance on scene before mounting the second and repeatedly smashing his head into the windscreen.

The paramedics inside drove back and forth in an attempt to dislodge him, before he smashed his head through the windscreen and began crawling inside.

The St John Ambulance staff fled the vehicle and ran to the second ambulance, with Parfitt apprehended a short time later and placed into an induced coma.

Parfitt's lawyers had previously indicated he was having a "mental health episode" at the time of the incident, but further details have not been mentioned during court proceedings.

Video of the incident, which the ABC has chosen not to republish, was circulated widely on social media and sparked a campaign from St John's around the near-constant violence faced by the ambulance service's staff.

Prosecutors said Parfitt threatened bystanders with a pair of scissors taken from the ambulance. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)

Prosecutors urged prison term

As Parfitt faced the Kalgoorlie Magistrates Court on Monday for sentencing, prosecutors urged an immediate jail term.

Police prosecutor Carl Logan said the 26-year-old, who appeared via video link from Casuarina Prison, was naked in the vicinity of women and children, and had threatened to kill a bystander with scissors taken from the ambulance.

Sergeant Logan said Parfitt had a lengthy criminal record, with the attack coming four months after his release from prison on other charges and causing $4,000 damage to the ambulance.

The court heard he had failed to engage with rehabilitation programs and represented a high risk of future offending.

Defence points to family support

Defence lawyer Leneva Polmear submitted a letter from Parfitt's Perth-based father, describing his pride in his son's efforts to turn his life around.

Ms Polmear said the family had made arrangements with a metropolitan crisis support service to ensure Parfitt had access to appropriate help.

Parfitt's attack caused $4,000 damage to the ambulance. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)

Sentencing Parfitt, Magistrate Donna Webb said she had only been willing to consider a non-custodial sentence if the 26-year-old's father was willing to take him in.

She told the court she was also required to factor in Parfitt's significant mental health issues and the 261 days he had already spent in custody.

Describing the 13-month suspended prison term as a likely "last chance", she said Parfitt would need to do everything right to avoid further time in custody.

Magistrate Webb urged the 26-year-old to remain in Perth after his release from prison.

"Kalgoorlie seems to be a trap for you," she said.

Attacks on paramedics rising

Parfitt's offending came amid a significant rise in attacks on paramedics across Western Australia, with incidents rising 11.9 per cent in 2025.

Rebecca Thompson says she was traumatised by the attack. (ABC News: Nic Perpitch)

Kalgoorlie patient transport officer Rebecca Thomspon was on duty and in the ambulance during Parfitt's attack.

"I have three young children at home and I feared for my life whilst I was on that job," she said at the launch of a campaign to tackle violence against paramedics.

"It shouldn't be like that."

She described the incident as the most traumatic moment of her life.

World.title: International company's plan for multi-billion-dollar data centre in regional Qld
World.content:
With the energy demands of artificial intelligence prompting broader policy debates across Australia, regional Queensland is now facing the reality of hyper-scale expansion with a $31.9 billion data centre being proposed for the Western Downs.

The Western Downs Digital Park, set to be the largest facility of its kind in Australia, has been earmarked for a 725.5-hectare plot near Dalby, roughly 250 kilometres north-west of Brisbane.

The company behind the project is Singapore-based developer Zerra DC, which operates hyper-scale data centres across the Asia Pacific.

A coal seam gas well near Wambo Feedlot, on the Western Downs. (ABC Southern Queensland: Nathan Morris)

The site, 37km north-west of Dalby, is currently home to a 24,000-head feedlot owned by Wambo Cattle Company.

Although this proposed data centre is strategically located near major regional power stations, there are ongoing concerns across the country about energy consumption and water security as the development and construction of data centres surges.

A map showing the proposed site of the Western Downs Digital Park and surrounding energy sources. (Supplied: Urbis)

The federal government is currently refining proposed new national rules for how data centres consume energy, including a requirement for them to purchase power from renewable energy sources.

In Southern Queensland, there has been a recent push from the Toowoomba Regional Council to ensure data centres do not encroach on drinking-water sources in the region.

Councillor Rebecca Vonhoff said the council took a national lead in passing a motion.

"We have this prime industrial land, we own our water infrastructure, we provide drinking water to our residents and, most importantly, we have a personal and very deeply felt connection to water, having lived through some devastating droughts," she said.

Water and energy consumption

While the Western Downs Digital Park plans to prioritise air-cooled technology and avoid reliance on town water infrastructure, the construction and operation will still be water intensive.

During construction, it would require about 522 kilolitres of water a day.

That would be followed by 26.9 megalitres per building for a one-time flush-and-fill process, equivalent to the average annual water use of 155 Australian households.

Under regular operation, the centre would use about 16.5kL of water each day.

It would source its water from coal seam gas water, rainwater harvesting, water delivery, recycled wastewater, and on-site surface water, according to the development application.

Western Downs mayor Andrew Smith says there are a lot of questions being raised about the data centre proposal. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Beyond water security, the centre could draw heavily on power networks, but Western Downs mayor Andrew Smith said, as the "energy capital of Queensland", the region was uniquely positioned to handle the load.

"We've built a lot of energy infrastructure in our region that has benefited our region," he said.

"So, if there needs to be more built, well, bring it on."

He said there would be a rollout of community consultation about the proposal.

"Questions around water, questions around power, around geography — they're the main questions that we're hearing out of our community," Cr Smith said.

"But certainly, those questions around water are very real and the applicant will need to deal with those."

Queensland Minister for Water Ann Leahy said the community should have a voice in this proposal, just like any other major project.

World.title: Matildas star receives rousing welcome in return after mother's death
World.content:
Matildas midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross has played her first match in more than five months after taking time away from football to spend time with her mother before her death.

Cooney-Cross was sent on in the 63rd minute as Arsenal recorded a 1-0 pre-season win over Paris FC in Borehamwood.

The 67-time international recorded her first minutes since the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup final in March, when she started in the Matildas' 1-0 loss to Japan in Sydney.

Cooney-Cross announced on January 8 via Instagram that her mother Jessica Cooney was diagnosed with terminal Stage 4 bile duct cancer. She died on July 10.

Arsenal manager Renee Slegers confirmed on March 28 Cooney-Cross was granted indefinite compassionate leave and would remain in Australia after the Asian Cup to be with her mother.

"You're my biggest inspiration and the person I aspire to be," Cooney-Cross wrote on social media after her mother's death.

"Mum, my favourite part is knowing that I'm a little piece of you."

The 24-year-old returned to Arsenal's pre-season training on August 17, with the Gunners' Women's Super League campaign set to begin on Sunday evening against former Socceroo Dario Vidosic's Brighton & Hove Albion.

Cooney-Cross received a rousing ovation at Meadow Park as she was substituted on alongside compatriot Steph Catley.

Loading Instagram content

The former A-League Women's star with Melbourne Victory and Western Sydney Wanderers was involved in the build up to Canadian attacker Olivia Smith's 91st minute winner.

Arsenal's final pre-season match is against Charlton Athletic on August 26.

The Addicks signed Australian trio Emily van Egmond, who marked a national record 170 international appearances during the AFC Women's Asian Cup, alongside fellow Matildas midfielder Leah Davidson and youth international Grace Johnston, following the club's promotion from the Women's Super League 2 in May.

Meanwhile, goalkeeper Jada Whyman is returning to A-League club Sydney FC after a stint in Sweden.

Whyman is yet to play for the Matildas but has been selected in multiple national squads.

World.title: Exclusive CCTV captures the violence facing Coles workers
World.content:
For teenagers looking for their first job, an opportunity in retail is one of the most sought after gigs.

But in Victoria, retail workers are facing growing safety concerns.

In exclusive video obtained by 7.30 and captured during the past four months, CCTV shows shocking incidents of aggressive behaviour towards Coles staff and, at times, other customers.

In one instance, a customer was armed with a hammer and threatens a staff member as they were leaving the store, and in a second attack, a security guard was physically thrown into a check-out machine by a customer.

Loading...

Ruth Sumner, 70, has worked at Coles for 30 years. She said it was time the abuse against workers stopped.

"I enjoy my job. I'd just like to be able to do it without getting abused basically or worrying about whether somebody's going to come flying around the plaza with weapons," she said.

Ruth Sumner says she experiences verbal or physical abuse on a regular basis. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Last year, in a union survey of about 3,000 workers across Australia, 88 per cent of people said they had been verbally abused.

One in four said they had been physically attacked.

Ms Sumner says she feels anxious about her safety when she clocks on for a shift.

"The physical violence, irrespective of what anybody thinks, once is too much. Because once could end somebody's life," Ms Sumner said.

" I've seen aggression progress, especially since COVID. I thought people would come out kinder and they've actually, I don't understand, but their mentality is worse. "

Incidents have almost doubled in two years

Coles's chief operations and supply chain officer Matt Swindells said there had been a dramatic increase in abuse towards staff in Victoria.

"We've had rising instances of what we would call threatening situations, particularly towards our team members and particularly in Victoria over the last two years," he said.

"To give you some idea, they've grown 85 per cent in Victoria over that period.

"Whilst we call them threatening situations, what we really mean are either verbal assaults or physical altercations, or in some instances using product as a weapon, like a bottle of wine or a tin of tomatoes."

Matt Swindells says staff look after each other and protect customers before worrying about stock. (ABC News)

In comparison, Coles said threatening situations across the nation have increased by 65 per cent over the same period. South Australia is the only jurisdiction where it has declined by 16 per cent.

"We would have an internal system that can provide a text alert when incidents occurred, and my phone would go off repeatedly every day, which in itself is pretty sad," Mr Swindells said.

In Coles stores across Victoria, there are more security measures needed than in any other state, like body-worn cameras on staff and motion detection cameras in aisles.

There are also security guards who patrol the stores to keep the peace but only intervene in violence if it is safe to do so.

Coles staff in Victoria wear body-worn cameras to deter violence and most stores have motion security cameras in aisles to track customers. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"There are clear standards that we have, and we work with our security team on what we expect," Mr Swindells said.

"At every moment, the intent of the team, whether it's security or Coles, is to look after each other, protect their customers and protect themselves before we start worrying about protecting stock and putting anyone at risk."

The main challenge for retailers in Victoria is the repeat offenders.

"They will come back, and at some point there has to be an intervention that's more than us over-servicing a customer or the police making an arrest and to come back out on bail within hours," Mr Swindells said.

"We're not here to uphold the law or to be the judge, jury or government, but we clearly would ask for faster support with the workplace protection orders so we can support the police."

Victoria Police has increased the number of police officers patrolling Melbourne's CBD to combat retail crime and anti-social behaviour.

Since March, Victoria Police have flooded the city with double the number of officers patrolling high-risk areas to tackle retail crime and anti-social behaviour. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Assistant Commissioner Jo Stafford told 7.30 arrests were up since March, with 260 arrests made for a range of offences from theft to assaults and public disorder.

But repeat offenders remain a challenge for police and Assistant Commissioner Stafford said the force would support measures that would target them.

"That is an issue for government, but in terms of any initiatives that help protect our workers, Victoria Police would be supportive of," she said.

Workplace protection orders in Victoria

Workplace protection orders are court-ordered bans on violent repeat offenders that restrict them from entering a retail store for a period of time.

Last month Victorian Premier Ben Carroll promised workplace protection orders would be in place across the state by July 2027.

Ben Carroll says the Workplace Protection Order scheme will be introduced to protect workers. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Victorian state secretary of the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association Michael Donovan said the laws need to come into effect much sooner.

"Ideally, we would like to see it before Christmas. It's a very busy period, and there does tend to be a spike in customer abuse and violence," he said.

" This is a crisis and the government needs to address it. "

Michael Donovan says there tends to be a spike in abuse and violence during the Christmas period. (ABC News: Rachel Clayton)

Workplace protection orders are already in effect in the ACT and South Australia.

Mr Swindells said Coles welcomed the Victorian premier's announcement.

"South Australia implemented the same policy from start to finish in six months. So again, we know it can be done. We know it works," he said.

"We welcome the change from the government in Victoria. We would just ask for it to be accelerated."

For Ms Sumner, she is nearing the end of her professional life, but she is speaking out to protect the next generation of retail workers.

"If I drop dead tomorrow, I want to know that I've done something to make life better or help make life better for the people to come after us."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: England bowler Brydon Carse under investigation over nightclub video
World.content:
England bowler Brydon Carse is being investigated over an incident in Derby on Saturday night, according to the England and Wales ​Cricket Board (ECB).

Videos circulating on social media appear to show the Durham bowler in handcuffs being led away from a club by police officers.

"We are aware of an incident which is reported to have taken place in Derby last night and we are currently investigating," an ECB spokesperson said.

"We ​will provide a ‌further update when possible."

Carse is part ‌of England's squad for the second Test against Pakistan starting next ⁠week at Lord's.

He was not on England duty at ‌the time of the alleged ​incident after being an ‌unused member of the squad for the first Test, which England won comfortably at Headingley.

Bazball's complex legacy Brendon McCullum deliberately set out to make England's men's Test team a less complicated team to play cricket for. After four years of Bazball's highs and lows, it leaves a very complicated legacy.

The investigation comes five days after England's returning Test captain Joe Root spoke of the players being "really good role models and ​human ‌beings" after a series of incidents and accusations of a drinking culture.

Controversy has followed England around in recent times with off-field ⁠issues during last winter's tours, including ‌Harry Brook being fined £30,000 ($40,908) after ‌an altercation with a bouncer in Wellington as well as reports of drinking ‌during a mid-Ashes trip to Noosa.

This summer Ben Stokes broke a team curfew along with Gus Atkinson, with the pair ‌dropped ​from the second Test ⁠against New Zealand at the Oval.

Former Test captain Stokes eventually announced his retirement from international cricket while Brendon McCullum was sacked as Test coach, with Root confirming that the team had done away with the curfews under new coach Stephen Fleming.

The ECB would not confirm whether Carse was still ⁠in the squad for the second test against Pakistan. Reuters has contacted Carse's county side Durham ‌to request comment ‌from the player.

In 2024, South Africa-born Carse was suspended ​from cricket for three months for historic betting offences.

World.title: 1000 One Nation voters said why they were voting for Hanson - and what it would take to switch
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalOne Nation 1000 One Nation voters said why they were voting for Hanson - and what it would take to switch Paul Sakkal August 25, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Immigration rather than living costs is the top concern for Australians who have flocked to One Nation, according to research that suggests Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor must convince voters they’ve cut migration if they are to claw back support. A survey of 1000 supporters of One Nation, run by pollster John Utting and Labor strategist Bruce Hawker, shows a key difference between supporters of One Nation and those of other parties is that 91 per cent believe the country is heading in the wrong direction. Among all voters, it is 62 per cent. The poll also maps out the split between Pauline Hanson’s loyal voters – true believers who back her no matter what – and newer supporters who revealed what it would take for them to switch their vote back to the Coalition – and far less likely, Labor. Of the One Nation backers who say the country is on the wrong track, 39 per cent name immigration as a reason. Australia’s border controls and cultural diversity has turned into a flashpoint as Labor scrambles to hit its targets and the Coalition jibes One Nation over its internal policy confusion. In all major polls over the past few years, inflation has reigned supreme as the top issue.



The research painted a picture of One Nation voters, showing they are slightly less well off than the average voter ($101,000 versus the average $109,000 income), more likely to live outside major cities, and 12 percentage points more likely to hold a trade certificate. The majority are men. Utting, who helped conduct Labor’s polling for many elections up to 2019, said that “migration is the real thing motivating One Nation supporters”. “Cost-of-living rhetoric is everywhere these days and people are a bit deadened to it. Migration is the real hotspot. Everyone has a cost of living plan and it is hard to get cut-through,” he said of the research, conducted between August 7 and August 12. The importance that voters place on Australia’s migration system and population, which has grown quicker than it has in other democracies this century, was demonstrated in this month’s Resolve Political Monitor. It found that more than half of voters across the spectrum believed the government was running the portfolio in an “unplanned and unmanaged way”.



Related Article Immigration Pauline Hanson’s deleted post deepens One Nation’s migration muddle Labor abruptly delayed a migration overhaul this month as it agonised over the economic and social consequences of reducing net overseas migration from about 300,000 to 225,000. The Coalition has also been at odds over migration, but Taylor has proposed to cut net migration to 175,000. Utting and Hawker, a key adviser to prime minister Kevin Rudd, conducted weeks of focus groups followed by a survey to understand what was driving Australia’s populist surge. They will present their research at Parliament House in Brisbane on Tuesday. The work was commissioned by the Labor-aligned TJ Ryan think tank. The poll finds that about half of One Nation’s supporters are totally committed to voting for the party at an election due in 2028. The rest, however, can be persuaded in a process Utting described as “chipping away at an iceberg as it comes out of the Antarctic”.



Hawker said of Hanson’s movement: “It’s moving away from just being a party of protest to one which has some pretty entrenched attitudes about the way Australia should be.” The most recent Resolve survey showed core support for Labor, the Coalition and One Nation remained unchanged, with Labor at 28 per cent, the opposition steady on 23 per cent and Hanson’s party on 26 per cent. Opposition MPs were pleased by a poll on Monday, published in Capital Brief and conducted by research firm Demos, showing the Coalition up four points and ahead of One Nation for the first time in many months. The Utting-Hawker survey showed Hanson’s backers detest Labor and Albanese himself. Overwhelmingly, the respondents say that the only thing that could draw them back to the major parties is if Albanese or Taylor developed bold plans to reduce migration. About 27 per cent said a united, credible Liberal Party would win them over, suggesting replacing Taylor with Liberal MP Andrew Hastie may be unwise after months of internal chaos in the Coalition. But two-thirds have barely heard from Taylor, underscoring his challenge with communication.



“One Nation’s rise is as much a story of Liberal failure as of One Nation success. Immigration and

the cost of living created the conditions. Labor is overwhelmingly rejected by these voters, and

the Liberals have not offered them a convincing alternative,” the research states. A critical finding is that One Nation voters are split over migration issues. An anonymous One Nation backer said: “I’m not against immigration. Because the moment you say anything, people assume the worst. My issue is the arithmetic. You can’t bring in that many people and not build the houses.” Another argued: “It isn’t the number so much. It’s who, and whether they want to be part of what’s here.”



Polling shows more than half of those who say they will vote for One Nation will not change their mind. Alex Ellinghausen Asked what they feared, 57 per cent of One Nation supporters said Australia’s culture and identity were changing too quickly while 40 per cent said housing and infrastructure were strained. One Nation’s newer supporters were more likely to take issue with the volume of migration, a view Hawker said was shared by many migrants. However, her more traditional support base believes the background of migrants is of greater concern. Hanson spoke in plain and sometimes incendiary terms about Muslim Australians after the Bondi attack in December, after which One Nation’s vote rose. Hawker said the split emphasised a broader misalignment between Hanson’s core support and her new, expanded base. On issues such as Hanson’s hard line on abortion and sacking lazy workers, the survey showed many of Hanson’s supporters did not agree with her, providing opportunity for her opponents. About 20 per cent of Hanson’s newer supporters said they could change their vote after Hanson’s positions on those issues – plus others such as her relationship with billionaire Gina Rinehart – were put to them. Only 4 per cent of her rusted-on base said the same.
